weeks.theme: Go core from the real repo + network essentials

sections.title: Networking overview
sections.label: Networking overview
sections.md:
*Read before the questions (~20 min)*

This part follows one web request across the network, one layer at a time:

1. **DNS** finds the server's address.
2. **TCP** opens a connection to it.
3. **TLS** makes that connection private.
4. **HTTP** carries the request, through the servers that sit in front of your app.
5. The **browser** turns the response into a page.

Each section explains one layer. The last section puts the whole trip together. Every section ends with the interview
questions it answers: read the section, close it, then answer them out loud.

One term you'll need from the start: **RTT** (round-trip time) is one message there and its reply back. Inside a
datacenter it's under a millisecond; across a continent it's about 100–200 ms. Most network latency comes down to
**how many round trips** a step needs.

---

sections.title: DNS: turning a name into an IP
sections.label: DNS
sections.md:
- Order of lookup: browser cache → OS cache → **recursive resolver** (your ISP's, 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1).
- On a cache miss, the recursive resolver walks the tree: **root** server ("who handles `.com`?") → **TLD** server
  ("who handles `example.com`?") → **authoritative** server ("`shop.example.com` is 203.0.113.7").
- Your machine never talks to root servers itself. The resolver does that work and caches the answer.
- **TTL** (time to live): how long a record may be cached.
  - Low TTL: faster failover when you change IPs, but more DNS queries.
  - High TTL: fewer queries, but a change takes longer to reach everyone.
- Record types:
  - `A` maps a name to an IPv4 address. `AAAA` maps it to an IPv6 address.
  - `CNAME` is an alias to another name.
  - `MX` routes mail, `TXT` holds verification strings, `NS` delegates a zone to other name servers.
- DNS uses **UDP port 53** (one small question, one small answer). It falls back to TCP for large responses.
- DNS returns an **address**, never the page.

sections.title: TCP vs UDP: the transport layer
sections.label: TCP vs UDP
sections.md:
| | TCP | UDP |
|---|---|---|
| Connection | Yes (handshake first) | No; you just send datagrams |
| Delivery | Guaranteed: lost segments are retransmitted | Best effort; may be lost |
| Order | Ordered byte stream | No ordering |
| Extras | Flow control, congestion control | Almost nothing, tiny header |
| Use for | HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, DB connections, almost everything | DNS, voice/video, games, QUIC (HTTP/3) |

- **Three-way handshake:** `SYN` → `SYN-ACK` → `ACK`.
  - It takes three messages because each side must send its starting sequence number **and** hear that the other side
    received it.
  - With only two messages, the server would never know the client got its number.
- **Head-of-line (HOL) blocking:** TCP delivers bytes strictly in order. If one packet is lost, everything behind it
  waits for the retransmit, even data that belongs to a different request.
- "UDP is faster" is a trap. UDP isn't higher bandwidth. It only skips the handshake, the retransmits and the ordering
  waits. Pick it when a late packet is useless anyway (live audio), or when you build your own reliability on top
  (QUIC).
- TCP guarantees delivery to the other machine's **kernel buffer**. It does not guarantee the app processed the data.
  That's why app-level ACKs and idempotency still matter.
- **Closing:** `FIN` → `ACK`, `FIN` → `ACK`, four messages. The side that closes first sits in **TIME_WAIT** for a while.
  A service that opens thousands of short connections piles up TIME_WAIT and can run out of ephemeral ports.
  **Connection reuse** fixes it.

sections.title: TLS: privacy and identity
sections.label: TLS
sections.md:
TLS gives you two things:

1. **Authentication:** you're really talking to `shop.example.com`.
   - The server sends its **certificate chain**.
   - The client checks that each signature chains up to a **trusted root CA** in its trust store, that the hostname
     matches, and that the certificate hasn't expired.
2. **Encryption:** both sides derive the same **symmetric session key** using a key exchange (ECDHE).
   - Asymmetric crypto (public/private keys) is slow, so it's used only for the handshake: identity plus key exchange.
   - Bulk data uses fast symmetric encryption (AES-GCM).

Other details:
- TLS runs **after** TCP and costs **1 RTT** in TLS 1.3 (TLS 1.2 needed 2). Resumed sessions can do **0-RTT**.
- **Forward secrecy** (from ECDHE): a stolen server private key later can't decrypt traffic recorded today, because
  the session keys were ephemeral.
- **TLS termination:** usually the load balancer or reverse proxy in front of your app decrypts (§5 explains those). Traffic inside the VPC may then be plain
  HTTP, or re-encrypted.

So a fresh HTTPS connection costs **DNS + 1 RTT (TCP) + 1 RTT (TLS) before the first byte of HTTP is even sent.**
That's why reusing connections matters so much.

sections.title: HTTP versions: each one fixed the previous one's bottleneck
sections.label: HTTP versions
sections.md:
- **HTTP/1.1:** text protocol, keep-alive connections, but one request at a time per connection. Browsers work around
  it by opening about 6 connections per host.
- **HTTP/2:**
  - Binary framing, with many concurrent **streams multiplexed over one TCP connection**.
  - Header compression (HPACK).
  - Problem left over: it still runs on TCP, so one lost packet stalls every stream (TCP HOL blocking).
- **HTTP/3:**
  - Runs on **QUIC over UDP**. Each stream recovers its own losses, so one lost packet stalls only its own stream.
  - TLS 1.3 is built in, so setup is 1 RTT total (0-RTT on resume).
  - Connection migration: your phone switching from Wi-Fi to 4G keeps the same connection.

sections.title: The server side: CDN → load balancer → reverse proxy → app
sections.label: CDN, proxy, load balancer
sections.md:
**CDN:** caches content at edge locations near users.
- It lowers latency, takes load off the origin, and absorbs traffic spikes and DDoS.
- Caching is controlled by `Cache-Control` and TTLs.
- To invalidate, use **versioned file names** (`app.3f9a.js`, the best option), a purge API, or short TTLs.
- Private files: use **signed URLs** with an expiry, and lock the origin so only the CDN can read it.

**Reverse proxy** (nginx, Envoy, ALB): one front door for many servers. It takes jobs off the app:
- TLS termination
- Compression and caching
- Rate limiting
- Routing (`/api/*` → service A)
- Access logs, timeouts, security headers
- Hiding the internal topology

A *forward* proxy works the other way: it acts for **clients**, like a corporate proxy.

**Load balancer: L4 vs L7.**
- **L4** (AWS NLB) balances **TCP/UDP connections** by IP and port. It never reads the payload, so it's very fast and
  works with any protocol.
- **L7** (AWS ALB, nginx, Envoy) understands **HTTP**:
  - It routes by host, path or header.
  - It terminates TLS.
  - It can retry, rewrite and do sticky sessions.
- Algorithms:
  - **Round robin** and **weighted round robin**
  - **Least connections:** good when request costs vary a lot.
  - **IP hash / consistent hashing:** the same client or key goes to the same server (affinity, cache locality).
- **Health checks** take dead targets out of rotation automatically.

**Keep-alive and connection pools:** reuse connections instead of paying TCP + TLS every time.
- Without reuse you get more latency, more CPU, TIME_WAIT pile-up, port exhaustion, and a DB flooded by connection
  churn.
- A pool also **caps concurrency** toward a dependency, so size it against the DB's connection limit.

sections.title: HTTP semantics you'll be asked about
sections.label: HTTP semantics
sections.md:
**Status codes:**
- `400`/`422`: bad input.
- `401`: not logged in. `403`: logged in, not allowed.
- `404`: not found. `409`: conflict, such as a duplicate or a state clash.
- `429`: rate limited, sent with `Retry-After`.
- `502`/`503`/`504`: upstream trouble. `504` means a gateway's dependency timed out.
- Rule of thumb: on a 4xx, retrying the same request won't help. On a 5xx, retrying later might.

**Safe vs idempotent:**
- Safe means no side effects: `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`.
- Idempotent means doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once: the safe methods, plus `PUT` and `DELETE`.
- **`POST` is neither**, so a retried POST can double-charge. Fix it with an **Idempotency-Key** header that the server
  deduplicates on.

**CORS:**
- The browser blocks scripts from **reading** cross-origin responses (origin = scheme + host + port) unless the server
  opts in with `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers.
- Non-simple requests (JSON body, custom headers, PUT/DELETE) send an `OPTIONS` **preflight** first.
- CORS is enforced by the **browser**, not the server. curl and your React Native app ignore it. It is **not** auth.

sections.title: In the browser: from response to page
sections.label: In the browser
sections.md:
The response has arrived. The browser now builds the page:

1. **Parse the HTML** top to bottom into the DOM.
2. **Fetch the sub-resources** it finds (CSS, JavaScript, images, fonts). These are more HTTP requests, which reuse the
   open connection when they can (keep-alive in HTTP/1.1, many streams on one connection in HTTP/2, §4).
3. **CSS blocks rendering** (the page can't be painted correctly without it). A plain `<script>` **blocks parsing**
   until it downloads and runs; `defer` and `async` stop that.
4. **Layout and paint:** work out sizes and positions, then draw.

Next time, much of this comes from caches: the browser's HTTP cache (`Cache-Control`, `ETag`) and the CDN (§5).

Why a backend engineer cares: put static assets behind a CDN with long cache lifetimes, compress responses, and keep
the number of round trips and connections low.

sections.title: Putting it together: the life of a request
sections.label: Life of a request
sections.md:
Now the whole trip, each step pointing back to its section:

```
you type URL
  │
  ├─ 1. DNS ............ name → IP           (cache everywhere, TTL)                         §1
  ├─ 2. TCP ............ open a connection   (3-way handshake, 1 RTT)                        §2
  ├─ 3. TLS ............ make it private     (cert check + key exchange, 1 RTT in TLS 1.3)   §3
  ├─ 4. HTTP ........... send the request    (CDN → load balancer → reverse proxy → app)     §4 §5
  ├─ 5. Response ....... status + headers + body                                              §6
  └─ 6. Browser ........ parse, fetch sub-resources, render                                   §7
```

- On a cold start, the first byte of HTTP needs **DNS + 1 RTT (TCP) + 1 RTT (TLS)** first. That's why connection reuse,
  CDNs close to the user and HTTP/2–3 matter.
- **Caching happens at every hop:** DNS answers (§1), the CDN (§5), the browser cache (§7), and the app's own cache
  (Redis, week 4).
- In an interview, tell it as one story in this order, and go deep on whichever step they ask about.


---

sections.title: Go core overview
sections.label: Go core overview
sections.md:
*Read before the questions (~25 min)*

Covers week 1:
- **Tue:** interfaces, structs, methods
- **Wed:** errors, wrapping, sentinels
- **Thu:** context, generics, zero values
- **Sat:** explain out loud
- **Sun:** quiz

The ideas here are the ones Grab and Shopee probe. If you come from TypeScript, the traps are where Go *looks* like TS
but isn't.

---

sections.title: Structs, methods, receivers
sections.label: Structs, receivers
sections.md:
```go
type Submission struct {
    ID     string
    UserID string
    Status string
}

func (s Submission) IsFinal() bool { return s.Status == "approved" }   // value receiver: works on a copy
func (s *Submission) Approve()     { s.Status = "approved" }           // pointer receiver: mutates the original
```

**Use a pointer receiver** when any of these is true:
- The method mutates the receiver.
- The struct is large.
- It contains a `sync.Mutex` or anything else that must not be copied.

Otherwise a value receiver is fine. Keep one style per type.

sections.title: Interfaces, and which receivers satisfy them
sections.label: Interfaces, method sets
sections.md:
```go
type Repo interface {                       // declared by the CONSUMER (the service), not the implementation
    Create(ctx context.Context, s Submission) error
    Get(ctx context.Context, userID, id string) (Submission, error)
}

type Service struct{ repo Repo }
func NewService(r Repo) *Service { return &Service{repo: r} }
```

- There's no `implements` keyword. Any type with those methods satisfies `Repo`: the real DynamoDB repo, or a
  `fakeRepo` in tests.
- **"Accept interfaces, return structs."** The consumer declares the small interface it needs. The implementation
  package never imports it, so the packages stay decoupled.
- Keep interfaces small (1–3 methods): `io.Reader`, `error`, `fmt.Stringer`.
- **Method sets** (asked a lot): `T` has only the value-receiver methods from §1, while `*T` has **both**. So if any
  interface method has a pointer receiver, only `*T` satisfies the interface. Passing a plain `T` fails to compile.
- **Embedding** a struct is composition, not inheritance. The embedded type's fields and methods are promoted, but
  there is no virtual dispatch back into the outer type.

**The nil-interface trap.** (`error` is itself an interface with one method, `Error() string`; §4 covers errors.)
An interface value is a pair: (type, value). It equals `nil` only when **both** are nil.

```go
func find() error {
    var e *MyErr = nil
    return e            // interface = (*MyErr, nil)  →  err != nil is TRUE
}
```

Fix: return a literal `nil` when there's no error.

sections.title: Zero values
sections.label: Zero values, maps, slices
sections.md:
Every variable starts at its zero value. Go never leaves memory uninitialised.

| Type | Zero value | Gotcha |
|---|---|---|
| int, float | `0` | |
| string | `""` | |
| bool | `false` | |
| pointer, func, chan, interface | `nil` | |
| slice | `nil` | usable: `len` is 0, `append` works |
| map | `nil` | **reads are fine, writes panic**: `make` it first |
| struct | every field zeroed | |

- **"Make the zero value useful":** `sync.Mutex`, `bytes.Buffer` and `strings.Builder` work without a constructor.
- Downside: is `0` "not set" or a real zero? Use a pointer (`*int`) or the comma-ok idiom when you need to tell them
  apart.
- **Maps:**
  - `v, ok := m[k]` tells a missing key apart from a stored zero.
  - Iteration order is randomised on purpose.
  - Maps are **not safe for concurrent writes**: that's a fatal crash, not just a wrong value.

**Slices** are a header of (pointer, len, cap).
- Copying a slice copies the header, so both copies share the data.
- `append` writes in place if `cap` allows. Otherwise it allocates a bigger array and copies into it.
- Two slices over the same array can overwrite each other. Break the sharing with `slices.Clone` or `s[a:b:b]`.

sections.title: Errors (Wednesday's block)
sections.label: Errors
sections.md:
`error` is just an interface: `type error interface { Error() string }`. Errors are **values**, returned last and
checked explicitly.

```go
var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")            // sentinel: a package-level value

type ValidationError struct{ Field, Reason string }  // custom type: carries data
func (e *ValidationError) Error() string { return e.Field + ": " + e.Reason }

// repo layer
return fmt.Errorf("get submission %s: %w", id, ErrNotFound)   // %w WRAPS: adds context, keeps the original

// edge (handler): translate once
switch {
case errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound):          // walks the wrap chain comparing to the sentinel
    writeError(w, 404, "NOT_FOUND")
case errors.As(err, &ve):                  // var ve *ValidationError — finds a typed error in the chain
    writeError(w, 400, "VALIDATION_ERROR", ve.Field)
default:
    log(err); writeError(w, 500, "INTERNAL") // don't leak internals
}
```

- **`%w` vs `%v`:** `%v` only formats the message and **breaks the chain**, so `errors.Is` stops working.
- **Never compare `err.Error()` strings.**
- **Sentinel or custom type?**
  - Use a sentinel when callers only need to *branch* on the error.
  - Use a custom type when callers need *data* from it: a field name, a retry-after value.
  - Both become part of your package's API, so export only what callers must branch on.
- **The single handling rule:** each layer either **wraps and returns** the error, or **handles** it (logs it, turns it
  into a status). Never both, or you get the same error logged five times. HTTP status codes belong at the edge, not in
  the service.
- `errors.Join(a, b)` combines several errors into one, and `Is`/`As` match any of them. Use it for collecting
  validation failures, or errors from closing many resources.
- **`panic`** is for bugs, impossible states, and broken config at startup. It is **not** try/catch.
  - `recover()` only works inside a `defer`, in the **same goroutine**.
  - A panic in a goroutine you started kills the whole process.
  - `net/http` recovers per request.
- **`defer`:**
  - Runs when the **function** returns (not the block), in LIFO order.
  - Its arguments are evaluated immediately.
  - `defer f.Close()` inside a loop piles up until the function ends.

sections.title: Context (Thursday, briefly; week 2 goes deeper)
sections.label: Context
sections.md:
`context.Context` carries three things down a call chain:
- **cancellation**
- a **deadline**
- **request-scoped values**: request ID, auth subject

Rules:
- It's the **first parameter**, named `ctx`: `func (r *Repo) Get(ctx context.Context, …)`.
- Never store it in a struct. Pass it down every call that does I/O.
- `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(parent, 2*time.Second); defer cancel()`: always call `cancel`, or the timer
  leaks.
- When the client disconnects or the deadline passes, `ctx.Done()` closes. DB and HTTP clients that take `ctx` abort.
- Context values are for request-scoped data only, never for optional parameters. Use a private key type to avoid
  collisions.

sections.title: Generics (Thursday)
sections.label: Generics
sections.md:
```go
func DecodeJSONBody[T any](r *http.Request) (T, error) {
    var v T
    err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&v)
    return v, err
}
req, err := DecodeJSONBody[CreateSubmissionRequest](r)   // typed result, no casts
```

- Type parameters give you one function over many types, **checked at compile time**. Without them you'd use
  `interface{}` plus type assertions.
- Constraints:
  - `any`
  - `comparable` (usable as a map key, supports `==`)
  - type sets like `~int | ~float64`
- Use generics when the **type** varies and the logic is the same (containers, helpers like `Map`/`Filter`, decode).
  Use interfaces when the **behaviour** varies.

sections.title: Packages, visibility, struct tags, DI, tests
sections.label: Packages, tags, DI, tests
sections.md:
**Visibility:** a **Capitalised** identifier is exported from the package. A lowercase one is private to it.
- `encoding/json` only sees exported fields.
- `internal/` restricts who can import a package.
- Import cycles are compile errors.

**Struct tags** are metadata that libraries read through reflection:
- `json:"status,omitempty"` sets the JSON name and skips the field when empty.
- `dynamodbav:"status"` sets the DynamoDB attribute name.
- `validate:"required"` is read by the validator.
- `json:"-"` hides a field from the API.
- A typo in a tag fails **silently**. `go vet` catches some of these.

**Dependency injection without a framework:** `main` is the composition root. It reads config, builds clients, and
passes them into constructors:

```go
repo := dynamo.NewRepo(client)
svc := submission.NewService(repo)
h := api.NewHandler(svc)
```

On Lambda this happens once, at cold start.

**Table-driven tests:**

```go
tests := []struct{ name string; in Req; wantStatus int }{
    {"ok", validReq, 201},
    {"missing field", Req{}, 400},
    {"duplicate", dupReq, 409},
}
for _, tc := range tests {
    t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) { /* call handler via httptest, assert status */ })
}
```

- Fake the dependencies through interfaces. You don't need a mocking framework.
- Useful flags: `go test ./... -race -count=1 -cover`.


---

sections.title: HTTP API overview
sections.label: HTTP API overview
sections.md:
*Read before the questions (~15 min)*

Covers week 1 **Fri** (REST design, status codes, idempotent methods). Also feeds **Sun**: Build M1, which is exactly
this, in Go. Status codes and safe/idempotent methods are also in **Networking** §6.

---

sections.title: Resources, not actions
sections.label: Resources
sections.md:
```
GET    /submissions                 list the caller's submissions   (?status=approved&cursor=…)
POST   /submissions                 create one                       → 201 + Location / body
GET    /submissions/{id}            read one                         → 200 | 404
PATCH  /submissions/{id}            partial update
DELETE /submissions/{id}            remove                           → 204
POST   /submissions/{id}/finalize   an action that isn't CRUD
```

- Use **nouns** and **plural** collections. The HTTP **method** is the verb, so never write `/getSubmission`.
- **Nest** only for real ownership: `/projects/{id}/guideline`. Filter with query params.
- `PUT` **replaces** the whole resource, which makes it idempotent. `PATCH` changes some fields.

sections.title: Status codes: pick by "who's at fault, and can they retry?"
sections.label: Status codes
sections.md:
| Situation | Code |
|---|---|
| Created | `201` (+ the new resource) |
| Accepted, processing later (long job) | `202` + a status URL |
| No body (delete) | `204` |
| Malformed / invalid input | `400` (some teams use `422` for valid JSON that fails rules) |
| No / bad credentials | `401` |
| Authenticated but not allowed | `403` |
| Not found, **or not yours** | `404` (don't reveal it exists) |
| Duplicate / state conflict | `409` |
| Rate limited | `429` + `Retry-After` |
| Bug / unknown error | `500` (log the detail, return a generic message) |
| Overloaded / dependency down | `503` (+ `Retry-After`) |
| Upstream timed out | `504` |

A 4xx means "don't retry this unchanged". A 5xx means "retry later might work".

sections.title: One error contract for the whole API
sections.label: Error contract
sections.md:
```json
{ "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR", "message": "projectId is required", "details": [{ "field": "projectId", "reason": "required" }] }
```

- `code` is **stable and machine-readable**. Clients branch on it, never on `message`.
- Codes are part of the contract: document them in the OpenAPI spec.
- Never leak internals (stack traces, SQL, AWS error text). An unknown error becomes `500 INTERNAL`, and the real
  detail goes to the logs.
- In Go, the **handler** maps errors to this shape with `errors.Is`/`errors.As` (see **Go core** §4).

sections.title: Layers and validation
sections.label: Layers, validation
sections.md:
```
handler   →  decode JSON, read user id from the VERIFIED token, call service, map error → status
service   →  validate DTO, business rules, orchestrate; returns domain errors (ErrNotFound, ErrConflict)
repo      →  storage only; scopes every query by owner (userId + id)
```

- Shape and type checks happen at the edge (decode). **Business rules** go in the service, **before any write**.
- Frontend validation is UX only. The backend never trusts the client.
- **User id comes from the token, never the body or query.** Otherwise you get **IDOR**: change an id in the request,
  and you read or act as someone else.
  - Unguessable UUIDs don't fix this.
  - The fix is to scope by owner: `Get(userID, submissionID)`. Someone else's id then returns 404.

sections.title: Idempotency (retries are normal)
sections.label: Idempotency
sections.md:
- **Safe** methods: `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`.
- **Idempotent** methods: the safe ones, plus `PUT` and `DELETE`.
- **`POST` is neither.** Clients, proxies and mobile networks retry on timeout, so a retried `POST /payments` can
  charge twice.

The fix is an **`Idempotency-Key`** header (a UUID per logical operation):
1. The server stores key → (request hash, status, response) **atomically**, together with the side effect. Use a unique
   constraint or a conditional write. Don't "check, then insert": two requests can both see "not exists".
2. Same key and same body: return the stored response.
3. Same key, different body: `409` or `422`.
4. Handle "first request still running", and expire keys after a retention window.

sections.title: Things that come up in follow-ups
sections.label: Pagination, versioning, more
sections.md:
- **Pagination:**
  - Offset (`?offset=40`) is simple, but slow deep into the list, and pages shift when rows are inserted.
  - Cursor/keyset is stable and index-friendly. It uses an opaque cursor such as `(createdAt, id)` and returns the rows
    after it.
  - DynamoDB only supports cursor style.
- **Versioning:**
  - Put the version in the path: `/api/v1`.
  - Make **additive** changes only: new optional fields, new endpoints. Never rename or repurpose a field.
  - Old mobile apps live for months.
- **Middleware** (`func(next http.Handler) http.Handler`):
  - Request ID, logging, panic recovery, auth, CORS, timeouts, metrics.
  - Order matters: recovery and request ID go outermost.
- **Timeouts:** Go's zero values mean *no timeout*.
  - Set the server's `ReadHeaderTimeout`, `ReadTimeout`, `WriteTimeout` and `IdleTimeout`.
  - Give `http.Client` a `Timeout`. The default client can hang forever.
- **Long jobs:** return `202` with a status resource. The client polls it, or you push (webhook, SSE, push
  notification). Never hold the request open for minutes.

weeks.theme: Concurrency from the real repo + OS essentials

sections.title: OS overview
sections.label: OS overview
sections.md:
*Read before the questions (~25 min)*

Read this part first: goroutines and Go's scheduler (Part 2) are explained in terms of the threads, context switches
and I/O models below.

Covers week 2 **Tue** (processes, threads, memory, scheduler) and **Thu** (file descriptors, syscalls, signals), then
the Saturday quiz and Sunday's Shopee-style fundamentals. Shopee asks this as rapid-fire.

---

sections.title: Processes, threads, context switches
sections.label: Processes, threads
sections.md:
| | Process | Thread |
|---|---|---|
| Owns | its own virtual address space, fd table, resources | its own stack and registers |
| Shares | nothing by default (isolated) | the process's memory and file descriptors |
| Switch cost | higher (address-space switch, TLB flush) | lower |
| A crash | doesn't hurt other processes | can take down the whole process |

- Threads communicate cheaply through shared memory, but need synchronisation.

**Context switch:** the kernel saves one thread's registers, program counter and stack pointer and restores another's.
- Triggers: time slice expires (preemption), blocking on I/O or a lock, a sleeping syscall, an interrupt.
- Direct cost: microseconds of kernel work. Indirect cost: cold CPU caches and TLB (worse across processes).
- Too many runnable threads → time spent switching instead of working. One reason for event loops and goroutines.

**fork, exec, copy-on-write:**
- `fork` creates a child that's a copy of the parent. `exec` replaces the current process image with a new program.
- **Copy-on-write:** after fork both share physical pages marked read-only; a page is copied only when one side writes.
  That makes fork cheap. Redis forks for background RDB snapshots this way.
- **Zombie:** a dead child whose parent hasn't called `wait()`. **Orphan:** a child whose parent died; `init` adopts it.

**IPC on one machine:**
- Pipes and named pipes (byte streams, usually parent-child). **Unix domain sockets** (bidirectional, fast, local).
- **Shared memory** (fastest, needs synchronisation), message queues, signals (tiny notifications only).
- TCP on localhost / HTTP / gRPC when the parts may later move to other machines.
- Files and databases as a shared medium: slow but durable.

sections.title: Memory
sections.label: Memory, GC
sections.md:
**Process layout** (low to high addresses): text (code) → data/BSS (globals) → **heap** (grows up) → memory-mapped
regions → **stack** (grows down).
- **Stack:** function frames, locals, return addresses. Automatic and fast, one per thread, limited (stack overflow).
- **Heap:** objects that outlive a call or have dynamic size; managed by malloc/free or a GC.
- Goroutines (Go's lightweight threads, Part 2) have separate, growable stacks that themselves live in heap memory the
  runtime manages.

**Virtual memory:** each process sees its own contiguous address space.
- The MMU maps virtual pages to physical frames through **page tables**, cached in the **TLB**.
- It gives isolation, lazy allocation, sharing (libraries, copy-on-write) and swapping.
- **Page fault:** touching a page that isn't in RAM. Minor fault: the kernel allocates or maps it. Major fault: it reads
  from disk. Then the instruction retries. An invalid address → **SIGSEGV**.

**CPU caches:** memory is loaded in **cache lines** (usually 64 bytes).
- Sequential access uses every byte of a loaded line, and hardware prefetchers predict it.
- A 2D array is row-major, so row-by-row is sequential; column-by-column jumps a whole row each step and misses.
- **False sharing:** two cores writing different variables on the same line bounce it between caches.

**Go: stack or heap?** The compiler's **escape analysis** decides, not you.
- A value escapes to the heap when it outlives the function: a returned pointer, stored in a heap object, captured by an
  escaping closure, or put in an interface.
- Stack allocation is nearly free; heap allocation costs time plus GC work.
- See decisions with `go build -gcflags=-m`; measure with `-benchmem` and pprof alloc profiles.
- `new(T)` vs `&T{}` doesn't decide it; either can live on the stack.

**Go's GC:** concurrent, tri-colour **mark-and-sweep**, non-generational, non-moving, with short stop-the-world pauses
(usually sub-millisecond).
- `GOGC` (default 100) sets how much the heap may grow before the next cycle. `GOMEMLIMIT` is a soft memory cap.
- GC cost scales with the **live heap and allocation rate**, not with garbage. The real lever is allocating less: reuse
  buffers, avoid pointer-heavy structures.

sections.title: Kernel, syscalls, file descriptors, I/O
sections.label: Syscalls, fds, I/O
sections.md:
**User vs kernel mode:** user mode can't touch hardware or other processes' memory; kernel mode can.
- A **syscall** (`read`, `write`, `open`, `socket`, `mmap`, `futex`…) traps into the kernel, does the privileged work,
  and returns.
- It costs more than a function call (mode switch), so buffering and batching reduce them.
- `strace` shows a process's syscalls: the quickest way to see what it's blocked on.

**File descriptors:** an integer index into the process's table of open things: files, sockets, pipes.
`0/1/2` = stdin/stdout/stderr.
- **Every TCP connection uses one.** Limits exist per process (`ulimit -n`, `RLIMIT_NOFILE`) and system-wide.
- "Too many open files" = leaked descriptors (unclosed files, unclosed `resp.Body`) or a limit too low for the load.
- Debug with `lsof -p PID` or `ls /proc/PID/fd`. Fix leaks with `defer Close()`, then raise the limit if still needed.

**I/O models:**
- **Blocking:** the thread sleeps until data is ready. One thread per connection.
- **Non-blocking:** calls return `EAGAIN` at once; you retry.
- **Multiplexing:** one thread waits on many descriptors. `select`/`poll` are O(n) per call; **epoll** is O(ready),
  with edge or level triggering.
- **Async I/O / io_uring:** submit operations, collect completions later.
- **Go:** the netpoller uses epoll (kqueue on macOS). Your code looks blocking; the runtime parks the goroutine (Part 2)
  and wakes
  it on readiness.

**Inodes and links:**
- An **inode** holds a file's metadata and block pointers, not its name. Directory entries map names → inode numbers.
- **Hard link:** another name for the same inode (same filesystem only). Data lives until the last link and the last
  open handle are gone.
- **Symlink:** a small file containing a path. Can cross filesystems; breaks if the target moves.
- You can run out of **inodes** with disk space left (millions of tiny files).

sections.title: Scheduling and synchronisation
sections.label: Scheduling, locks
sections.md:
**Linux scheduler:** CFS (and EEVDF since kernel 6.6) aims for a fair CPU share: track each thread's virtual runtime
and run the one that has had the least.
- `nice` (-20..19) weights the share. Real-time policies (`SCHED_FIFO`/`RR`) preempt normal threads.
- I/O-bound threads sleep a lot and get scheduled quickly when they wake: good interactivity.
- Containers use **cgroup CPU quotas**. When the quota runs out the container is **throttled**: a classic cause of
  latency spikes.

**Mutex vs semaphore vs spinlock:**
- **Mutex:** exclusive, one holder, released by the owner.
- **Semaphore:** a counter allowing up to N holders. (A binary semaphore is a lock without ownership.)
- **Spinlock:** busy-waits instead of sleeping. Only for very short critical sections on multi-core.
- Go: `sync.Mutex`; a buffered channel or `x/sync/semaphore`; spinning is runtime-internal.

**Deadlock: the four Coffman conditions** (all four must hold):
1. Mutual exclusion
2. Hold and wait
3. No preemption
4. Circular wait

Break one: acquire locks in a **global order** (breaks circular wait), take all locks at once, or use timeouts /
try-lock. Databases detect deadlocks with a **wait-for graph** and abort one transaction.

**Load average:** the average number of tasks **running or waiting to run**, plus tasks in uninterruptible sleep
(D state, usually disk I/O), over 1, 5 and 15 minutes.
- Compare it to the core count: **8.0 on 4 cores ≈ 2× oversubscribed**, or stuck on I/O.
- Check CPU utilisation and `iowait` to tell CPU saturation from I/O blockage.

sections.title: Signals, containers, debugging
sections.label: Signals, containers, tools
sections.md:
**Signals:**
- `SIGINT` = Ctrl+C. `SIGTERM` = a polite termination request (Docker, Kubernetes, ECS and systemd send it on stop).
  Both can be caught.
- `SIGKILL` (`kill -9`) **can't be caught or ignored**: immediate death, no cleanup.
- Orchestrators send SIGTERM, wait a grace period (e.g. 30 s), then SIGKILL.
- So the app must catch SIGTERM, stop taking new work and drain within the grace period. Part 2 §7 shows how a Go server does it.

**Namespaces and cgroups:**
- **Namespaces** isolate what a process *sees*: PID, network, mount, user, UTS.
- **cgroups** limit what it can *use*: CPU, memory, I/O.
- A container is just processes + namespaces + cgroups + a filesystem image. Not a VM.
- Over the memory limit → the kernel **OOM killer** kills it (**exit code 137**). No graceful shutdown.
- Make runtimes respect the limit: `GOMEMLIMIT`, JVM container awareness.

**A slow Linux box: first commands**
- `top`/`htop`: CPU, load and memory per process. `uptime`: load average vs core count.
- `free -h`, `vmstat 1`: memory, swap, run queue, context switches. `iostat`, `df -h`, `du`: disk I/O and space.
- `ss -tanp` (or `netstat`): connections and their states. `lsof`: open files and sockets.
- `journalctl`, log files, `dmesg` (OOM kills, disk errors). Then `strace`, `perf` or pprof on the process itself.


---

sections.title: Go concurrency overview
sections.label: Go concurrency overview
sections.md:
*Read before the questions (~30 min)*

Covers week 2:
- **Mon:** goroutines, channels, select
- **Tue:** mutex vs channel, WaitGroup, errgroup
- **Wed:** context cancellation, leaks, races
- **Fri:** quiz · **Sat:** explain out loud · **Sun:** Build M2 (graceful shutdown + middleware)

Part 1 (OS) comes first because everything here builds on threads, context switches and epoll.

Grab and Shopee both ask concurrency. The bar is not "I know the keywords" but "I can say what blocks, who closes what,
and how it stops". Every section ends with the questions it answers.

---

sections.title: Goroutines and the scheduler
sections.label: Goroutines, scheduler, Lambda
sections.md:
A **goroutine** is a function running concurrently, started with `go f()` and managed by the Go runtime, not the OS.

| | Goroutine | OS thread |
|---|---|---|
| Stack | starts ~2–8 KB, grows and shrinks | fixed ~1–8 MB |
| Created by | the Go runtime | the kernel |
| Switching | in user space, cheap | kernel context switch |
| How many | hundreds of thousands | thousands at most |

- The runtime multiplexes many goroutines onto a few OS threads: **M:N scheduling**.
- **Blocking network I/O parks the goroutine, not the thread.** The netpoller (epoll/kqueue, Part 1 §3) wakes it when data is
  ready. `GOMAXPROCS` threads run Go code in parallel (default: number of cores).

**The G-M-P model** (deep, but a classic):
- **G** = goroutine. **M** = OS thread ("machine"). **P** = processor: a scheduling context with a **local run queue**.
  There are `GOMAXPROCS` Ps.
- An M must hold a P to run Go code. Each P has a local queue; there is also a global queue.
- **Work stealing:** an idle P steals half of another P's queue.
- **Blocking syscall:** the M hands its P to another M so Go code keeps running. Network I/O goes through the netpoller
  instead of blocking threads.
- **Preemption:** since Go 1.14 the runtime can asynchronously preempt a tight loop so it can't hog a P.

**Concurrency on Lambda** (how `submission-feature` runs):
- One execution environment handles **one invocation at a time**. Concurrency comes from AWS starting more
  environments, not from goroutines.
- Everything built in `main` (clients, repo, service, in-memory caches) survives across **warm** invocations, in that
  environment only. Two environments can hold different cached values for up to the TTL.
- Cold start = runtime init + `main`'s setup. Keep `main` lean; use reserved/provisioned concurrency to bound or pre-warm.

sections.title: Channels and select
sections.label: Channels, select
sections.md:
| Operation | Unbuffered | Buffered (cap n) | Closed | nil |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| send | blocks until a receiver takes it | blocks only when full | **panics** | blocks forever |
| receive | blocks until a sender arrives | blocks only when empty | zero value at once, `ok=false` | blocks forever |

- Unbuffered = a **rendezvous**: both sides meet, which also synchronises them.
- **Only the sender closes**, and closing is a **broadcast**: every receiver wakes up.
- A nil channel blocks forever, which is useful to switch off one `select` case.
- `chan struct{}` carries no data: a pure signal.

**The stop/done pattern** (tus-feature's lock: `Unlock` does `close(u.stop)` then `<-u.done`):
- `close(stop)` tells the keep-alive goroutine to stop: its `case <-u.stop` fires.
- The goroutine runs `defer close(u.done)`, so `<-u.done` waits until it has **really exited**.
- Result: no heartbeat can renew the lease after `Unlock` released it. No race between renew and release.

**select + ticker** (the analyzer's `loop`):

```go
svc.Run(ctx)                       // once immediately
ticker := time.NewTicker(every)
defer ticker.Stop()
for {
    select {
    case <-ctx.Done():             // SIGTERM via signal.NotifyContext → exit cleanly
        return
    case <-ticker.C:
        if err := svc.Run(ctx); err != nil && ctx.Err() == nil { log(err) }  // no shutdown noise
    }
}
```

- A tick that fires while `Run` is still busy is **dropped**, not queued (the ticker's channel holds 1). No pile-up.

**Timeouts on a blocking call:**
- `select { case r := <-resultCh: … case <-time.After(d): … }` stops **waiting**, but the work keeps running.
- A `context.WithTimeout` passed into the call is better: the deadline propagates into nested I/O and **cancels** it.
- In loops use `time.NewTimer` + `Stop` (before Go 1.23, `time.After` timers weren't collected until they fired).

sections.title: Mutex, atomics, WaitGroup, errgroup
sections.label: Mutex, atomics, errgroup
sections.md:
**Mutex or channel?**
- **Mutex** for shared state with short critical sections: a cache, a counter, a map.
- **Channel** to hand over ownership of data or to signal events: pipelines, work queues, done signals.
- "Share memory by communicating" is guidance, not a law. A mutex is simpler for plain shared state.
- `RWMutex` only helps with many readers and rare writers. **Atomics** for a single counter or flag.

**sync/atomic:** `atomic.Int64`, `atomic.Bool`, `atomic.Pointer[T]`.
- Lock-free and cheap, but only for **one** variable. Anything multi-field needs a mutex.
- Atomics also give happens-before ordering for that variable.

**WaitGroup vs errgroup:**
- `sync.WaitGroup` waits for a set of goroutines. No errors, no cancellation. (`wg.Go` is the Go 1.25 helper for
  `Add` + `Done`.)
- `errgroup.Group`: `g.Go(func() error)`, and `g.Wait()` returns the **first** non-nil error.
- `errgroup.WithContext` cancels the derived ctx on the first error, so siblings stop early. `SetLimit(n)` bounds
  concurrency.
- In the repo: the analyzer uses a WaitGroup for two long-lived loops; profile/admin use errgroup to fan out independent
  reads and publishes.

**sync.Once and singleflight:**
- `sync.Once` runs an initialisation exactly once, even with concurrent callers. If the function errors or panics it
  still counts as done. (`sync.OnceValue` / `OnceFunc` since 1.21.)
- `singleflight.Group` collapses concurrent calls **with the same key** into one execution; every caller gets the same
  result. It prevents a cache stampede on a miss but caches nothing afterwards.

**Holding a lock during I/O** (`criteriaTemplate` holds `s.mu` while it calls DynamoDB on a miss). Is it a bug?
- Cost: everyone queues behind one slow call.
- Benefit: it **deduplicates** concurrent misses (one fetch per expiry), like singleflight, so no thundering herd.
- On Lambda one environment handles one request at a time, so contention is near zero. In a long-running server it
  would matter.
- Alternatives: `singleflight.Group`, a double-checked read under `RLock`, or serve stale while one goroutine refreshes.
- Catch: the **first caller's ctx** bounds the fetch. If it's cancelled, everyone waiting sees the error.

sections.title: Races, deadlocks, leaks, the memory model
sections.label: Races, deadlocks, leaks
sections.md:
**Data race:** two goroutines touch the same memory at the same time, at least one writes, and there is no
synchronisation.
- The result is **undefined**: torn values, stale reads, crashes on concurrent map writes, heisenbugs.
- "It works on my machine" proves nothing: the bad interleaving may simply not have happened yet.
- Detect with `go test -race` / `go run -race`. It only finds races that actually execute, so run real tests under it.
- Fix: mutex, channel, atomic, or don't share (each goroutine owns its data).

**Happens-before:** if A happens-before B, B is guaranteed to see A's writes. Without it, another goroutine may see
writes late or out of order. Things that create it:
- A channel send happens-before the matching receive completes. Closing happens-before a receive that sees the close.
- `Unlock` happens-before a later `Lock` of the same mutex.
- `wg.Wait` returns after every `Done`'s effects are visible.
- A plain variable gives **no** ordering. Polling `done = true` without sync is broken.

**Deadlocks:**
- Circular wait: two goroutines each hold a lock the other needs (inconsistent lock order).
- Channel deadlocks: an unbuffered send with no receiver, waiting on a channel nobody closes, `Wait` after too many `Add`s.
- `fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!` appears only when **every** goroutine is blocked. A partial
  deadlock (a few stuck) goes undetected: use timeouts, a lock order, and goroutine profiles.

**Goroutine leaks:** a goroutine blocked forever, never collected.
- Causes: sending on a channel nobody reads, receiving from one nobody closes, waiting on a lock, a loop with no exit.
- Classic: a request starts a goroutine, the caller times out and returns, and the goroutine's result send blocks
  forever.
- Prevent: every goroutine has an exit (`ctx.Done()` or a close), use a **buffered result channel of size 1**, and the
  creator owns the lifetime.
- Detect: `runtime.NumGoroutine()` or the pprof goroutine profile growing over time; `goleak` in tests.

**`go sendEmail(user)` in a handler:**
- No error handling, no retry, no bound on how many run, and it may outlive the request's context.
- On deploy or shutdown the process exits and in-flight goroutines are lost.
- **On Lambda it's worse:** the environment freezes once the handler returns, so the goroutine may run during the next
  invocation, or never.
- Side effects that must happen go through something durable: SQS, an outbox, an event.

sections.title: Patterns: worker pools and pipelines
sections.label: Worker pools, pipelines
sections.md:
**Bounding concurrency** (10,000 items, each calling an external API):
- Don't start 10,000 goroutines against one dependency: you hit rate limits, connection limits and memory.
- **Worker pool:** N workers read from a `jobs` channel and write to `results`; close `jobs` when all are queued.
- Or a **semaphore**: a buffered channel of size N, or `errgroup.SetLimit(N)`.
- Pick N from the dependency's limits, pass ctx for cancellation, and decide fail-fast vs collect-all-errors.

**Fan-out / fan-in and pipelines:**
- Fan-out: several goroutines read one channel to parallelise a stage. Fan-in: merge several channels into one.
- Each stage **owns its output channel and closes it** when its input is exhausted. Only the sender closes.
- Downstream `range`s over the channel until it closes.
- Early exit: share a `done` channel or ctx so upstream stops sending when downstream quits. Otherwise upstream leaks.

sections.title: Context in practice
sections.label: Context in practice
sections.md:
Week 1 covered the basics (first param, `defer cancel()`, the tree). Two repo-specific uses:

**`context.WithValue`:**
- Only for **request-scoped** data that crosses API boundaries: request ID, trace ID, the caller's identity or IP.
  Never for optional parameters or dependencies.
- Keys must be **unexported custom types** so packages can't collide: `lib/auth` uses `type clientIPKey struct{}`.
  A string key like `"ip"` could clash.
- A `struct{}` key is zero-size and unique to the package. Expose typed helpers (`WithClientIP`, `ClientIP`) because
  values come back as `any`.

**`context.WithTimeout(context.WithoutCancel(req.Event.Context), hookTimeout)`** (tus-feature's hook):
- `WithoutCancel` keeps the parent's **values** but drops its **cancellation**: if the upload's request ends, the hook
  still finishes.
- `WithTimeout` then adds its own bound, so the detached work can't hang forever.
- Use it for work that must complete once started (recording that an upload finished) even if the client disconnects.
- Risk: detached work outliving shutdown. The explicit timeout is the guard.

sections.title: Graceful shutdown and distributed locks
sections.label: Shutdown, distributed lock
sections.md:
**tus-feature's main on SIGTERM:**
1. `signal.NotifyContext(ctx, SIGINT, SIGTERM)` gives a ctx that's cancelled when the signal arrives.
2. A goroutine waits on `<-ctx.Done()`, then calls `server.Shutdown` with a **30-second** timeout context.
3. `Shutdown` stops accepting connections, closes idle ones, and waits for in-flight requests (up to the timeout).
4. `ListenAndServe` returns `http.ErrServerClosed`: expected, not an error. `main` waits on a `shutdown` channel so it
   doesn't exit before `Shutdown` finishes.
5. `RegisterOnShutdown` cancels the server's `BaseContext` (`WithCancelCause`), so long uploads learn they must stop.

**A distributed lock in DynamoDB** (lease + heartbeat):
- **Acquire** = a conditional write: only if the lock is free or expired. Store the owner and a lease expiry.
- A **heartbeat** goroutine renews the lease while held. If a renewal finds another owner, it asks the handler to unlock.
- Lease expiry frees locks held by crashed instances.
- What still goes wrong: a long GC pause or network partition lets the lease expire while the old holder **still acts**.
  The real fix is a **fencing token** checked on every write.


---

sections.title: Extras overview
sections.label: Extras overview
sections.md:
*Read before the questions (~15 min)*

Covers week 2 **Thu** (pagination, versioning, gRPC basics; pagination and versioning are in week 1 Part 3 §6) plus the
Go-language questions that didn't fit week 1.

sections.title: Strings, init, loop variables, JSON
sections.label: Strings, init, loops, JSON
sections.md:
**Strings, bytes, runes:**
- A string is an immutable sequence of **bytes**, usually UTF-8. `len(s)` counts **bytes**, not characters.
- `s[i]` is a byte. `for i, r := range s` decodes UTF-8 into **runes** (`int32` code points).
- To index by character, convert to `[]rune` (copies). Build strings with `strings.Builder`.
- Vietnamese diacritics are multi-byte, so byte-indexed code breaks on them.

**Package variables and `init()`:**
- Package-level vars initialise in dependency order, then `init()` runs, all before `main`, once per package.
- Hidden work at import time is hard to test and order-dependent, and its errors can only panic.
- Prefer explicit construction in `main` (DI). A package-level singleton is fine for cheap, stateless, safe things like
  a validator instance.

**Loop variables (Go 1.22):**
- Before 1.22 a `for` loop variable was **one variable reused** every iteration, so closures and goroutines captured
  the same one: `for _, v := range xs { go func(){ use(v) }() }` used the last `v`.
- Since 1.22 each iteration gets a **fresh** variable (when the module's `go` line is ≥ 1.22).
- The old fixes: shadow it (`v := v`) or pass it as an argument.

**encoding/json pitfalls:**
- Only exported fields are encoded; tags set names and `omitempty`.
- Unknown fields are **ignored** by default (`DisallowUnknownFields` rejects them); missing fields stay zero values.
- Into `interface{}`, numbers decode as `float64`: precision loss above 2^53. Use typed fields or `json.Number`.
- A nil slice encodes as `null`, an empty slice as `[]`. That difference is part of your API contract.

sections.title: Go vs Node, honestly
sections.label: Go vs Node
sections.md:
| | Go | Node.js |
|---|---|---|
| Concurrency | goroutines on all cores, runtime scheduler | single-threaded event loop + async I/O |
| CPU-bound work | runs in parallel | blocks the loop (needs worker threads) |
| Types, deploy | static types, one static binary, fast start, low memory | huge ecosystem, same language as the frontend |
| Errors | returned values, checked explicitly | exceptions and rejected promises |

Say it as a trade-off, not a verdict: Node lets a JS team move fast and share code with the frontend; Go wins on
CPU-heavy or high-concurrency services and on operational simplicity.

sections.title: gRPC and API contracts
sections.label: gRPC, OpenAPI
sections.md:
**gRPC service definition:** a `.proto` file declares a `service` with `rpc` methods and request/response `message`s
whose fields are **numbered**. Code is generated for the server and every client.
- Four kinds of RPC: **unary**, **server streaming**, **client streaming**, **bidirectional streaming**.
- Errors use gRPC status codes (`NotFound`, `InvalidArgument`, `DeadlineExceeded`, `Unavailable`…), not HTTP statuses.
- **Deadlines propagate** across services. **Interceptors** are the middleware (auth, logging, metrics).

**gRPC vs REST/JSON:**
- gRPC: Protobuf schema + generated clients, compact binary, HTTP/2 multiplexing, streaming, deadlines.
  Great for internal service-to-service calls with strict contracts and high volume.
- Costs: not browser-native (needs gRPC-Web or a gateway), hard to debug by hand, schema-evolution discipline
  (never reuse field numbers), and an L7 load balancer that understands HTTP/2.
- REST/JSON: universal, cacheable with HTTP semantics, easy for public APIs and browsers.

**OpenAPI as the contract:**
- A machine-readable description of endpoints, schemas, errors and auth: the agreement between backend and clients.
- It enables generated clients and types, mock servers so the frontend can start early, contract tests, and reviewing
  an API change **before** writing code.
- The risk is **drift** between spec and code. CI checks or generating code from the spec keep them honest.
- In this repo, spec + explainer + data design + code ship as one deliverable.

weeks.theme: SQL: indexes, transactions, isolation, locking + DynamoDB

sections.title: Transactions overview
sections.label: Transactions overview
sections.md:
*Read before the questions (~25 min)*

Covers week 3 **Tue** (transactions and ACID), **Wed** (isolation levels, MySQL RR vs Postgres RC) and **Thu**
(locking, deadlocks, SELECT FOR UPDATE). Checkpoint 6 asks isolation out loud, so this part matters twice.

---

sections.title: ACID and the logs behind it
sections.label: ACID, logs
sections.md:
| Letter | Promise | What breaks without it |
|---|---|---|
| **A**tomicity | all statements commit, or none | a transfer debits A but never credits B |
| **C**onsistency | constraints and invariants hold before and after (FK, CHECK, UNIQUE, your rules) | an order points at a deleted user |
| **I**solation | concurrent transactions don't see each other's partial work, as far as the level promises | a report reads half of a transfer |
| **D**urability | once commit returns, it survives a crash | the "paid" row vanishes after a restart |

Durability and crash recovery come from logs:
- **WAL / redo log:** every change is appended sequentially and **flushed before commit returns**. Data pages can be
  written later; after a crash the log is replayed.
- **Undo log (InnoDB):** old row versions, used for rollback and for MVCC reads.
- **Binlog (MySQL, server level):** a logical change stream for replication and point-in-time recovery. A two-phase
  commit keeps redo log and binlog consistent.
- These logs also feed **CDC** (Debezium), the same idea as DynamoDB Streams feeding my Go service's relay.

sections.title: Isolation levels and MVCC
sections.label: Isolation, MVCC
sections.md:
**The anomalies:**
- **Dirty read:** you see another transaction's uncommitted write.
- **Non-repeatable read:** you read a row twice and get different values.
- **Phantom:** you run a range query twice and new rows appear.
- **Lost update:** two read-modify-writes; the second overwrites the first.
- **Write skew:** two transactions read the same data, each writes a different row, and together they break an
  invariant (two doctors both go off call).

| Level | Prevents | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Read Uncommitted | nothing | dirty reads allowed |
| Read Committed | dirty reads | new snapshot **per statement**. **Postgres default** |
| Repeatable Read | + non-repeatable reads | one snapshot **per transaction**. **MySQL InnoDB default** (plus gap / next-key locks for locking reads) |
| Serializable | everything | behaves like some serial order |

- **Postgres Repeatable Read = snapshot isolation:** no phantoms, but **write skew is possible**.
- **Postgres Serializable (SSI)** detects dangerous patterns and **aborts** a transaction, so the app must **retry**.

**MVCC** (multi-version concurrency control): writers create new row versions, readers see a snapshot, so **reads
don't block writes**.
- **Postgres** keeps old tuple versions in the table itself (`xmin`/`xmax`). **VACUUM** reclaims dead tuples; if it
  can't keep up you get **bloat**.
- **InnoDB** updates rows in place and keeps old versions in the **undo log**. A long-running transaction stops purge.
- A snapshot = which transactions' changes are visible: taken per statement (RC) or per transaction (RR).

sections.title: Locking, deadlocks, unique constraints
sections.label: Locking, deadlocks, unique
sections.md:
**Pessimistic vs optimistic:**
- **Pessimistic:** lock the row while you work: `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`. Others wait. Good under high contention; risks
  deadlocks and long waits.
- **Optimistic:** read a version, write `… WHERE version = :v` (or a conditional write). On conflict, re-read and retry.
  Good when conflicts are rare. **My Go service's ledger** uses a version attribute with up to 5 retries.
- Often you need neither: one atomic statement does it.
  `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = ? AND balance >= 10`

**Deadlocks in the database:**
- Two transactions lock rows in opposite orders (A then B vs B then A) and wait on each other.
- The DB detects the cycle and **aborts one** with a deadlock error.
- The app catches it and **retries the whole transaction**. Keep transactions short; touch rows in a consistent order
  (sort the ids).
- InnoDB gap / next-key locks under Repeatable Read can deadlock even on inserts into a range.

**Unique constraints as the referee:**
- Two concurrent inserts can't both succeed: the database decides, not your code.
- Check-then-insert in application code **races**. Insert-and-handle-conflict doesn't:
  `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, or catch the unique violation.
- Store idempotency keys under a unique constraint and retries become no-ops.
- My Go service does the same in DynamoDB with `attribute_not_exists` conditions and a fingerprint guard table (Part 4 §3).


---

sections.title: Indexes overview
sections.label: Indexes overview
sections.md:
*Read before the questions (~25 min)*

Covers week 3 **Mon** (indexes) and **Fri** (query plans, N+1, normalization). Checkpoint 6 asks you to justify every
index by a query.

---

sections.title: B-tree, composite and covering indexes
sections.label: B-tree, composite, covering
sections.md:
**B-tree:** a balanced tree of sorted keys. Lookups, range scans and `ORDER BY` in O(log n) instead of a full scan.
- Leaf entries point to rows. Postgres: to the heap tuple. InnoDB secondary index: to the **primary key**, then a second
  lookup.
- Costs: storage, **slower writes** (every insert/update maintains every index), more plans to choose from.
- Only useful when selective enough: for a low-selectivity filter the planner may still scan the table.

**Composite index `(user_id, status, created_at)`, the leftmost-prefix rule:**
- Usable for `user_id`; `user_id + status`; `user_id + status + created_at` (range or order).
- Not efficiently for `status` alone or `created_at` alone: no leading column.
- **Equality columns first, then the range / sort column.**
  `WHERE user_id=? AND status=? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20` is served entirely by the index.
- A range on a middle column stops the columns after it from being used for seeking.

**Covering and clustered:**
- **Covering index:** it contains every column the query needs, so the table isn't touched (index-only scan; Postgres
  `INCLUDE` columns).
- **InnoDB clustered index:** rows live inside the primary key's B-tree. Secondary indexes store the PK, so a
  non-covered lookup descends a second tree.
- So in InnoDB a **short, increasing primary key** keeps inserts cheap and secondary indexes small. Random UUIDs
  fragment it.
- Postgres tables are heaps; index-only scans need an up-to-date visibility map.

sections.title: When an index isn't used, and reading EXPLAIN
sections.label: Unused index, EXPLAIN
sections.md:
**Why your index is ignored:**
- A function or cast on the column (`lower(email) = …`, `created_at::date = …`) unless you build an expression index.
- A leading-wildcard `LIKE '%abc'`; a type mismatch / implicit conversion; `OR` across different columns.
- Not the leftmost prefix of a composite index; low selectivity, so a scan is cheaper.
- Stale statistics, a small table, or the planner's cost model simply prefers a sequential scan.

**EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE:**
- `EXPLAIN` shows the chosen plan and estimates. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` **runs** it and shows actual rows and time per node.
- Look for: Seq Scan on a big table, a big **estimate vs actual** row mismatch (stale stats), sorts or hash joins
  spilling to disk, nested loops over many rows.
- Fix: an index matching filter + order, rewrite the query, refresh stats (`ANALYZE`), cut rows earlier.
- Measure before and after, on realistic data volume.

sections.title: Joins, N+1, pagination, COUNT
sections.label: Joins, N+1, keyset, COUNT
sections.md:
**Joins:**
- `INNER`: only matching rows. `LEFT`: every left row, NULLs where the right doesn't match.
- Anti-join ("rows with no match"): `LEFT JOIN … WHERE right.id IS NULL` or `NOT EXISTS`.
- Algorithms: **nested loop** (few outer rows + index on the inner side), **hash join** (equality, bigger sets),
  **merge join** (both sides already sorted). The planner picks from estimated sizes and available indexes.

**N+1:** one query for a list, then one query **per item** for related data: N+1 round trips.
- Typical with ORM lazy loading (Prisma, TypeORM, GORM relations touched in a loop).
- Fix: a `JOIN`, one `WHERE id IN (…)` batch, the ORM's eager loading (`include` / `preload`), or a dataloader.
- Detect: query logs / APM show the same query shape N times per request.

**Keyset pagination in SQL** (newest first):

```sql
SELECT * FROM submissions
WHERE user_id = $1 AND (created_at, id) < ($2, $3)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;
-- index: (user_id, created_at DESC, id DESC)
```

- `id` is the **tie-breaker**, so the order is total and no row is skipped or repeated.
- The index gives a range scan with constant cost per page. The client gets `(created_at, id)` as an opaque cursor.

**`COUNT(*)` and soft deletes:**
- `COUNT(*)` on a big table is slow because under MVCC each transaction may see a different count, so the DB must scan
  (index-only scan at best). InnoDB too.
- Fixes: an approximate count (`pg_class.reltuples`), a maintained counter table, or a pre-aggregated read model.
- **Soft delete** (`deleted_at`): keeps history and undo, but every query and unique index must filter it (partial
  indexes), and tables grow. Alternatives: archive tables, an event log for audit.

sections.title: Schema design and live migrations
sections.label: Schema, migrations
sections.md:
**Normalize or denormalize:**
- **Normalize (3NF):** each fact stored once, no update anomalies, joins at read time.
- **Denormalize:** copy data to where it's read to skip joins. Faster reads, but writes must update every copy or accept
  staleness.
- **Snapshots are deliberate denormalization:** store the value as of an event (price at order time, project terms at
  submission time).
- Read models, materialized views and caches are *managed* denormalization.

**Changing a schema with no downtime: expand / contract**
1. Add the new column or table (nullable or with a default).
2. Deploy code that writes **both** old and new.
3. Backfill.
4. Switch reads to the new.
5. Drop the old.

- Each step must work with the code version still running: rolling deploys run old and new side by side.
- Beware locking DDL on big tables: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (Postgres), online DDL / gh-ost / pt-online-schema-change
  (MySQL).
- Versioned migrations live in the repo and are applied by CI/CD, reversible where possible.


---

sections.title: Scaling overview
sections.label: Scaling overview
sections.md:
*Read before the questions (~15 min)*

---

sections.title: Connection pools, replication, sharding
sections.label: Pools, replicas, sharding
sections.md:
**Connection pools:**
- Opening a connection is expensive: TCP + TLS + auth + (in Postgres) a whole backend process. A pool reuses a bounded set.
- Postgres is happy with a few hundred connections. **Pool size × instances must stay under `max_connections`.**
- **Lambda + Postgres:** Lambda scales to many environments, each with its own connection → a connection storm. Fix
  with **RDS Proxy / PgBouncer**, or a serverless-friendly store (one reason my Go service uses DynamoDB).
- Set pool max, idle timeout and max lifetime; pass ctx deadlines into queries.

**Primary–replica replication:**
- The primary streams its log (WAL / binlog) to replicas, which replay it. Replicas serve reads.
- Usually **asynchronous**, so replicas **lag**: a user may not see their own write (read-your-writes violation).
- Fixes: read your own recent writes from the primary, session stickiness, wait for an LSN / GTID, or synchronous
  replication (slower writes).
- Failover promotes a replica. With async replication the last committed writes can be lost.

**Sharding:**
- Only when one primary can't take the write volume or data size, **after** indexing, caching, read replicas and
  partitioning.
- Pick a **shard key** that matches the access pattern (`user_id`, `merchant_id`); hash vs range; avoid hot shards.
- What gets hard: cross-shard queries and transactions, resharding, global unique ids, joins.
- Try first: table partitioning, splitting by service, managed distributed SQL (Aurora, Vitess, CockroachDB).


---

sections.title: DynamoDB overview
sections.label: DynamoDB overview
sections.md:
*Read before the questions (~20 min)*

It's on your CV, so expect "defend this choice". Sunday's extra quiz is DynamoDB.

---

sections.title: Keys, access patterns, single-table design
sections.label: Keys, single-table, hot keys
sections.md:
**Access patterns first:** list the queries, then design keys so each one is a `GetItem` or a `Query` on **one
partition**. No scans.
- **Partition key:** hashed; spreads data and load across partitions.
- **Sort key:** orders items inside a partition and enables range queries (`begins_with`, `between`).
- Composite keys like `userId + submissionId`; **overloaded keys** (`PK = USER#id`, `SK = PROJECT#id`) to store several
  entity types together.
- Unlike SQL, a new query later may need a new GSI (a second key over the same items, §2) or a backfill.

**Single-table vs table per entity:**
- Single-table: every entity in one table with overloaded PK/SK; related items come back in one Query (pre-joined);
  fewer tables.
- Costs: harder to read and evolve; analytics and backups mix entities; IAM and streams are per table.
- **My Go service:** per-feature tables (submissions, attachments, ledger…) with overloaded keys inside some
  (`USER#`/`PROJECT#`, `FINGERPRINT#`). Table-per-service fits independent deploys and ownership.

**Hot partitions:**
- All traffic for one partition key hits one partition, which has limits (~3,000 RCU / 1,000 WCU).
- Causes: low-cardinality keys (status, date), a celebrity user, a global counter.
- Fixes: high-cardinality keys, **write sharding** (`key#0..N`, aggregate on read), caching hot reads (DAX / Redis).
- Adaptive capacity helps but doesn't remove the per-partition limit.

sections.title: Indexes, consistency, pagination
sections.label: GSI, reads, pagination
sections.md:
**GSI vs LSI:**

| | GSI | LSI |
|---|---|---|
| Keys | different partition + sort key | same partition key, different sort key |
| When | add any time | only at table creation |
| Consistency | **eventually consistent only** | strong reads supported |
| Limits / cost | own throughput; each write to a projected attribute = an extra GSI write | 10 GB per partition key |

- **Sparse index:** only items that have the key attribute appear. Great for work queues like "pending stage".

**Reads:**
- **Eventually consistent** (default): may miss a write from the last ~second; half the cost.
- **Strongly consistent** (`ConsistentRead: true`): sees every successful write; full cost; not on GSIs, not across
  regions.
- Read-after-write in one request flow: use a strong read, or just return the item you wrote.

**Pagination and Scan:**
- Query/Scan return at most **1 MB per call**. Continue with `ExclusiveStartKey = LastEvaluatedKey` until it's empty.
- **`Limit` applies before `FilterExpression`**, so a page can come back with fewer (even zero) items while more exist.
- **Scan** reads the whole table: cost and latency grow with table size. Parallel scans only for batch jobs.
- API cursor: encode `LastEvaluatedKey` opaquely and hand it to the client.

sections.title: Conditional writes and transactions
sections.label: Conditions, transactions
sections.md:
**Conditional writes:** a `ConditionExpression` is checked **atomically with the write**; if false the write fails with
`ConditionalCheckFailed`.
- `attribute_not_exists(PK)` = insert-only (idempotency, uniqueness).
- `version = :v` = optimistic locking.
- In my Go service: submissions created once, attachments claimed once, video fingerprints unique, ledger transactions
  applied once, ledger balance versioned.
- The alternative, read-then-write, races.

**TransactWriteItems:**
- Up to **100 actions** across tables, all-or-nothing, serializable relative to other transactional operations.
- **2× write cost.** A concurrent write to the same items cancels it (`TransactionConflict`).
- Cancellation reasons are **positional**, one per action: that's how my Go service maps a failure back to its cause.
- **No interactive transactions:** you can't read, decide and write inside one. Conditions encode the decisions.

sections.title: Streams, TTL, cost
sections.label: Streams, TTL, cost
sections.md:
**DynamoDB Streams:** an ordered (per item) **24-hour** log of item changes. With `NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES` consumers can
compare before and after.
- Lambda consumes it via an event source mapping: **at-least-once**, ordered per shard; `ReportBatchItemFailures`
  resumes from the failed record.
- Why my Go service publishes events from the stream: it's **CDC instead of an outbox**. The write itself is the event, so
  there's no dual-write problem, and it catches changes written by other services too.
- Limit: about **two consumers per shard**. A third needs Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB.

**TTL and capacity:**
- **TTL:** an epoch-seconds attribute; expired items are deleted in the background (can lag by days). Deletes are free
  and show up in the stream.
- **On-demand:** pay per request, no planning. **Provisioned + auto scaling:** cheaper for steady load.
- Cost grows with item size (1 KB write units, 4 KB read units), GSIs (extra writes), scans, and transactions (2×).
- Keep items small, project only what GSIs need, avoid scans.

sections.title: Putting it together: CAP and choosing a store
sections.label: Choosing a store
sections.md:
You now know both sides: SQL (Parts 1–3) and DynamoDB (§1–§4). This is where they meet.

**CAP:** during a **network partition**, a distributed store must choose **consistency** (refuse or block) or
**availability** (answer, possibly stale).
- It only talks about partitions. "CA" isn't a real option for a distributed system.
- **PACELC** is more useful: if **P**artition → **A** or **C**; **E**lse → **L**atency or **C**onsistency.
  Synchronous replication, for example, buys consistency with latency.
- Example: DynamoDB reads are eventually consistent by default and strongly consistent on request (§2: costs more, not
  on GSIs).

**Postgres or DynamoDB? Use your own project as evidence.**

| Pick Postgres when | Pick DynamoDB when |
|---|---|
| queries are ad hoc or still evolving | access patterns are known up front |
| you need joins, constraints, real transactions | you need predictable single-digit ms at any scale |
| rich indexing and analytics matter | you want serverless pay-per-request and no connection management (Lambda) |

- DynamoDB's costs: design keys and GSIs around the queries first; ad-hoc analytics is hard; transactions are limited
  (100 items, 2× cost).
- Honest evidence from my Go service: a GSI per query, stream consumers to build aggregates, and a guard table to emulate a
  unique constraint.

sections.title: Redis overview
sections.label: Redis overview
sections.md:
*Read before the questions (~30 min)*

Covers week 4 **Mon** (cache-aside, TTL, eviction), **Tue** (invalidation, stampede, distributed locks) and **Thu**
(persistence, single-threaded model), then Friday's quiz and Sunday's Build M4 (Redis cache + docker-compose).
Checkpoint 6 asks caching out loud: cache-aside, invalidation on write, stampede, TTL trade-offs.

---

sections.title: Caching patterns and invalidation
sections.label: Caching patterns
sections.md:
| Pattern | Read | Write | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cache-aside** (lazy loading) | cache → on miss read DB, fill cache with a TTL | update DB, then **delete** the key | only hot data cached; cache can die without data loss. **The default** |
| Write-through | always warm | write cache and DB together | every write pays both |
| Write-behind | always warm | write cache, flush to DB later | fast writes, risk of loss |

**Invalidation: update the DB first, then delete the cache key** (delete, don't set). The TTL is a safety net that
bounds staleness.

The race that remains:
1. A reader misses and reads the **old** value from the DB.
2. A writer updates the DB and deletes the key.
3. The reader now writes the old value into the cache → stale until the TTL.

Mitigations: short TTLs, a **delayed double delete**, versioned values / compare-and-set, or invalidate from **CDC**
(binlog, DynamoDB stream). Decide per data how stale is acceptable: prices are not avatars.

**Three ways a cache hurts the DB:**
- **Stampede** (thundering herd, breakdown): a hot key expires and many requests hit the DB at once.
  Fix: a mutex / singleflight on refill, early probabilistic refresh, serve stale while one request refreshes.
- **Penetration:** requests for keys that exist nowhere skip the cache every time.
  Fix: cache "not found" with a short TTL, a Bloom filter, validate input.
- **Avalanche:** many keys expire together (or the cache restarts).
  Fix: **random jitter** on TTLs, warm-up, rate-limit the DB, a highly available cache.

**HTTP caching for APIs:**
- `Cache-Control`: `max-age`, `no-store`, `private` (browser only) vs `public` (shared caches), `s-maxage` for CDNs.
- `ETag` + `If-None-Match` lets a client revalidate: **304 Not Modified** skips the body.
- Good for public, slow-changing data (legal documents, config). Per-user data must be `private` or `no-store`.
- Never let a shared cache store authenticated responses without varying on auth.

sections.title: Data structures and the single thread
sections.label: Data types, single thread
sections.md:
| Type | Use it for |
|---|---|
| String | cached values, counters (`INCR`), flags, simple locks |
| Hash | an object's fields (session, profile) without serialising the whole thing |
| List | queues (`LPUSH` / `BRPOP`), recent items |
| Set | unique members, tags, membership tests |
| **Sorted set** | leaderboards, priority queues, sliding-window rate limits, time-ordered feeds |
| Stream, bitmap, HyperLogLog, geo | a log with consumer groups; compact counts; locations |

**Why one thread is still fast:**
- Data is in memory; operations are simple, O(1) or O(log n); no locks, no switching between commands.
- One event loop with **epoll** serves many clients. Redis 6+ can use I/O threads for network reads/writes, but
  **commands stay single-threaded**.
- So **every command is atomic**, and Lua scripts and `MULTI/EXEC` run without interleaving.
- The flip side: one slow command blocks everyone. Avoid `KEYS *`, a huge `DEL`, an unbounded `ZRANGE`. Use `SCAN`,
  `UNLINK`, bounded ranges.

**MULTI/EXEC, WATCH, Lua:**
- `MULTI/EXEC` queues commands and runs them together without interleaving. **No rollback** if one fails.
- `WATCH key` = optimistic check-and-set: `EXEC` aborts if the key changed.
- **Lua (`EVAL`)** runs atomically on the server: read-decide-write in one round trip (rate limiters, lock release,
  stock decrement). Keep scripts short; they block the server.

sections.title: Memory, persistence, scaling
sections.label: Memory, persistence, scaling
sections.md:
**Eviction:** `maxmemory` sets the limit; `maxmemory-policy` decides what happens at the limit.
- `noeviction`: writes fail.
- `allkeys-lru` / `allkeys-lfu`: evict any key. **Use one of these for a cache.**
- `volatile-lru` / `volatile-ttl`: only keys that have a TTL. Plus random variants.
- LRU/LFU are approximate (sampling). Mixing cache and real data in one instance is risky.

**Persistence:**
- **RDB:** periodic snapshots via **fork + copy-on-write**. Compact, fast restart, loses writes since the last snapshot.
- **AOF:** append every write; `fsync` always / everysec / no. More durable, bigger, rewritten in the background.
- Often both. Memory can spike during fork under heavy writes (COW copies pages).
- As a pure cache you can turn persistence off. As a primary store you need AOF + replication.

**Replication, Sentinel, Cluster:**
- Replication is **asynchronous**; replicas can serve (possibly stale) reads.
- **Sentinel** monitors, fails over automatically and tells clients the new primary. Acknowledged writes can be lost
  on failover.
- **Cluster** shards across **16,384 hash slots** by `CRC16(key)`; each shard has replicas; clients follow
  `MOVED`/`ASK` redirects.
- Multi-key operations need keys in one slot: **hash tags** `{user:1}:cart`, `{user:1}:profile`.

**Hot keys and big keys:**
- **Hot key:** one key takes a huge share of traffic and overloads one shard (flash-sale item, celebrity profile).
  Fix: a local in-process cache in front, replicate the key (`key#1..N`), read from replicas.
- **Big key:** a value or collection so large that reading or deleting it blocks (millions of members, MB strings).
  Fix: split it, page with `HSCAN`/`ZSCAN`, delete with `UNLINK`. Find them with `--bigkeys` / `MEMORY USAGE`.

sections.title: Locks, rate limits, sessions, pub/sub
sections.label: Locks, limits, sessions
sections.md:
**A Redis lock:**
1. Acquire: `SET lock:key <unique-token> NX PX <ttl>`: only if absent, with an expiry so a crashed holder can't block
   forever.
2. Release with a **Lua script that deletes only if the value is your token**, so you never release someone else's
   lock.
3. Extend while working (watchdog / heartbeat) if the work may outlast the TTL.
- Limits: a pause or a failover can leave **two holders**. For correctness the resource must check a **fencing token**
  (the Redlock debate). Same lesson as week 2's DynamoDB lease lock.

**Rate limiters:**

| Algorithm | How | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed window | `INCR key:user:minute`, `EXPIRE` on first hit | simple; allows 2× bursts at window edges |
| Sliding log | `ZADD` timestamps, `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` old, `ZCARD` | exact; memory per request |
| Sliding window counter | weight the previous window's count by overlap | close to exact, cheap. **My Go service's auth limiter** |
| Token bucket | tokens refill at rate r up to capacity b | controlled bursts; do it atomically in Lua |

**Sessions for a scaled-out app:**
- Sessions in server memory break with more than one instance, or need sticky sessions (bad balancing, painful deploys).
- Shared store: **Redis** (fast, a TTL per session, easy revocation) or the database.
- Stateless JWTs skip the store but make revocation hard (short expiry + refresh tokens, Part 2).
- Sessions in Redis need persistence/replication decisions: losing them logs everyone out.

**Pub/Sub vs Streams vs a broker:**
- **Pub/Sub:** fire-and-forget fan-out to *connected* subscribers. Offline subscribers miss messages. No persistence.
  Fits ephemeral signals: cache-invalidation broadcasts, live presence.
- **Streams:** an append-only log with IDs, consumer groups, acks and pending lists: at-least-once.
- **Brokers** (Kafka, SQS, RabbitMQ): durability, retention, DLQs, scaling and tooling. Week 5.


---

sections.title: Auth overview
sections.label: Auth overview
sections.md:
