cards.k: type params = one func over many types, compile-time checked · constraints: any · comparable · ~int | ~float64 · DecodeJSONBody[T] → typed DTO, no casts · generics when the type varies, interfaces when behaviour varies
keys: Type parameters let one function or type work over many types with compile-time checking (no interface{} + type assertions)
Constraints describe allowed types: any, comparable, or interfaces with type sets (~int | ~float64)
DecodeJSONBody[T] returns a typed T, so every handler decodes its own DTO without casts
Use generics for containers and algorithms; prefer interfaces when behaviour, not type, varies
wrong: Generics replace interfaces
follow: Why can't a method have its own type parameters in Go?
When would you not reach for a generic helper?
cards.answer: Before generics, a helper that worked for any type took interface{} and the caller had to type-assert, losing compile-time checks. Now a function declares a type parameter with a constraint. DecodeJSONBody[T any] decodes a request body into whatever DTO the handler names, and gives back a T, so handleCreate gets a CreateSubmissionRequest directly. I use generics for algorithms and containers; when what changes is behaviour, an interface is still the better tool.

cards.q: How do packages, visibility and modules work in Go? Why is the repo laid out as one module with many feature packages?
cards.k: Capitalised = exported, lowercase = private · go.mod module, import paths start with it · internal/ limits importers · no import cycles · one module: shared lib/, one binary per feature from cmd/
keys: Capitalised identifiers are exported from a package; lowercase stay package-private
A module (go.mod) versions a tree of packages; import paths start with the module path
internal/ directories restrict who can import; no cyclic imports allowed between packages
One module here means shared lib/ packages and one dependency set; each feature compiles to its own binary from cmd/
wrong: Each directory needs its own go.mod
follow: How would you stop features from importing each other's repository packages?
What does `go build ./...` from go-app build?
cards.answer: Visibility is just capitalisation: Service is exported, criteriaTemplate isn't. A module, defined by go.mod, is the versioned unit, and every package inside is imported by module path plus directory, like example.com/go-app/lib/auth. Packages can't import each other in a cycle, and an internal/ directory limits who may import it. This repo is one module so features share lib/ and one set of dependency versions, while each feature's cmd/ builds its own Lambda binary.

cards.q: What are struct tags, and how does this repo use them for JSON, DynamoDB and validation?
cards.k: metadata read by reflection: json, dynamodbav, validate · only exported fields are seen · json:"-" hides from the API · typos fail silently → go vet / tests
keys: String metadata on fields read via reflection by libraries: `json:"name,omitempty"`, `dynamodbav:"..."`, `validate:"required"`
Only exported (capitalised) fields are seen by encoding/json and similar packages
`json:"-"` hides a field from the API while it is still stored (dynamodbav keeps it)
Typos in tags fail silently at runtime: tests or linters (go vet's structtag) catch them
wrong: Tags are checked by the compiler
Lowercase fields are serialised if tagged
follow: Why does the Submission entity carry both dynamodbav and json tags with different visibility?
How does the validator report a field's JSON name instead of its Go name?
cards.answer: Tags are strings attached to struct fields that libraries read through reflection. Here entities carry json tags for the API and dynamodbav tags for storage, so one struct maps to both, and json:"-" keeps internal fields like the S3 key out of responses while they're still saved to DynamoDB. Request DTOs carry validate tags. Only exported fields are visible to these packages, and a typo in a tag compiles fine, which is why go vet checks them.

cards.q: How is dependency injection done in Go without a framework? Walk through this repo's main.go.
cards.k: constructors take deps (NewService(repo)) · main = composition root: config → clients → wire · depend on consumer interfaces → fakes in tests · Lambda: build once at cold start
keys: Constructor functions take dependencies as parameters (NewService(repo), NewHandler(svc)); no container needed
main is the composition root: read config, build clients, wire concrete types into constructors
Depend on interfaces declared by the consumer so tests can substitute fakes
Lambda: build once at cold start, reuse across warm invocations
wrong: You need wire or fx to do DI in Go
follow: What would you lose if service.go created its own DynamoDB client?
When might a DI library start to pay off?
cards.answer: Plain constructors are the DI. main reads the env vars and fails fast if one is missing, builds the DynamoDB client, passes it to repository.New, passes the repository to NewService, the service to NewHandler, and hands Handle to lambda.Start. Because the service only knows the Repo interface, a test can pass a fake instead. All of that runs once per cold start, and warm invocations reuse it. A DI library only pays off when the graph gets big.

cards.q: How do you write tests in Go the idiomatic way, and how does this repo test services without DynamoDB?
cards.k: TestXxx(t) in _test.go · table = []struct{name, in, want} + t.Run · fake deps via interfaces, no mock framework · -race -count=1 -cover · t.Helper, t.Cleanup, t.Parallel
keys: go test runs TestXxx(t *testing.T) functions in _test.go files; t.Run gives named subtests
Table-driven: a slice of cases {name, input, want} looped with t.Run
Dependencies are faked through interfaces: the service takes a Repo interface; tests pass a fake struct
Useful flags: -race, -run, -count=1, -cover; t.Helper, t.Cleanup, t.Parallel
wrong: You need a mocking framework to test Go code
follow: What can't the fakeRepo tests catch (hint: the DynamoDB condition expressions)? How would you test those?
When is a hand-written fake better than a generated mock?
cards.answer: Tests are functions in _test.go files run by go test. The idiom is a table of cases looped with t.Run, so each case has a name in the output. Because the service depends on an interface, the tests hand it a fakeRepo struct that returns canned values and records what it was called with, so no AWS is needed. The gap is that the DynamoDB condition expressions in the repository never run in those tests; you'd need integration tests against DynamoDB Local for that.

cards.q: How do you design REST endpoints for a resource like submissions? Show the routes and the methods.
cards.k: plural nouns: /submissions, /submissions/{id} · method = verb: GET read, POST create, PUT replace, PATCH partial, DELETE remove · nest only for ownership · filter with query params · non-CRUD → POST /{id}/finalize
keys: Nouns for resources, plural collections: GET /submissions, POST /submissions, GET /submissions/{id}
Methods carry the verb: GET read, POST create, PUT replace, PATCH partial update, DELETE remove
Nest only for true ownership (/projects/{id}/guideline); filter collections with query params (?status=approved)
Actions that aren't CRUD become sub-resources or explicit action endpoints (POST /submissions/{id}/finalize)
wrong: Verbs in paths for everything: /getSubmission, /createSubmission
follow: Why does this API take the user from the JWT instead of /users/{userId}/submissions?
How would you model the admin pipeline transitions (preprocessing, qc-analyze, finalize)?
cards.answer: Resources are nouns in plural, and the HTTP method is the verb: GET /submissions lists, POST creates, GET /submissions/{id} reads one. Filters go in the query string, like ?status=approved. State transitions that aren't plain updates are modelled as explicit actions, which is what the admin feature does with /admin/submissions/{id}/finalize. Here the user isn't in the path at all, because the caller's identity comes from the token, so nobody can ask for someone else's submissions by changing a URL.

cards.q: Which HTTP status codes do you use for: validation failure, not logged in, logged in but not allowed, not found, conflict, rate limited, and a dependency timing out?
cards.k: 400 / 422 bad input · 401 not logged in · 403 not allowed · 404 · 409 conflict · 429 + Retry-After · 503 overloaded · 504 upstream timeout · 4xx don't retry, 5xx retry later
keys: 400 (or 422) for invalid input; 401 when unauthenticated; 403 when authenticated but not permitted
404 not found; 409 conflict (e.g. duplicate / state clash); 429 too many requests (with Retry-After)
502 / 503 / 504 for upstream failures: 504 when a gateway's dependency timed out, 503 when overloaded / unavailable
5xx means the client may retry later; 4xx means retrying the same request won't help
wrong: Returning 200 with an error field in the body
Mixing up 401 and 403
follow: Why does the retry behaviour of clients depend on 4xx vs 5xx?
Look at this repo's errorResponse: which domain error maps to 409 and why?
cards.answer: Bad input is 400, or 422 if the team distinguishes syntactically valid but semantically wrong input. 401 means we don't know who you are, 403 means we know and the answer is no. 404 for missing resources, 409 when the request clashes with current state, like submitting a video that's already used, and 429 with Retry-After when rate limited. If our dependency timed out, a gateway answers 504; 503 when we're shedding load. The split matters because clients and proxies retry 5xx but should not retry 4xx unchanged.

cards.q: What should an API error response look like? Critique this repo's error envelope.
cards.k: {code, message, details} · stable machine code, clients branch on code, not message · codes documented in the spec · never leak internals → 500 INTERNAL + log the detail
keys: A consistent machine-readable shape: stable code, human message, optional details (field + reason)
Clients branch on the code, not on message text; codes are part of the contract (documented in the spec)
Don't leak internals (stack traces, SQL, AWS errors): map unknown errors to a generic 500 and log the detail
Repo: {code, message, details} with stable codes like VALIDATION_ERROR, NOT_FOUND, CONFLICT; feature-specific codes like DUPLICATE_VIDEO
wrong: Return the raw exception message to the client
follow: Why does routing log the full error but return 'unexpected server error'?
RFC 7807 problem+json: what does it add?
cards.answer: Every error should have the same shape: a stable code clients can switch on, a readable message, and details such as which field failed and why. Clients must never parse message text. Internal failures become a generic 500 with the details only in logs, so you don't leak table names or AWS errors. This repo does that with httpapi.Error: codes like VALIDATION_ERROR and CONFLICT, plus specific ones like DUPLICATE_VIDEO where the app needs to react differently.

cards.q: Where should input validation live in a layered backend, and what does this repo do?
cards.k: shape / types at the edge (decode) · business rules in the service, before any write · frontend validation = UX only · validate tags → ErrValidation → 400 · data-dependent rules after reads
keys: Syntax/shape at the edge (JSON decode, types); business rules in the service layer, before any side effects
Never trust the client: the frontend's validation is UX only
Repo: DTOs carry `validate` tags; the service calls validate.Struct first and wraps failures in ErrValidation → 400
Some rules need data (attachment exists, belongs to user, right kind): checked in the service after reads
wrong: The frontend already validates, so the backend doesn't need to
follow: Why is the user id never a field in the request DTO?
Which validation in CreateSubmission can only happen inside the database transaction?
cards.answer: Shape problems are caught at the edge, when the JSON doesn't decode; business rules belong in the service, before any write. The client's validation is only for a nicer UX. In this repo request DTOs carry validate tags and every service method starts with validate.Struct, wrapping failures in ErrValidation, which routing maps to 400. Rules that depend on data, like 'this attachment is yours and uploaded', are checked after reading it, and the truly racy ones, like 'not already used', are enforced by the transaction's conditions.

cards.q: Why must a handler take the user id from the verified token and never from the body or query?
cards.k: body + query = attacker-controlled → IDOR · gateway verified the JWT → trust sub · repo scopes by owner: Get(userID, id) · someone else's id → 404 · UUIDs don't fix it
keys: The body and query are attacker-controlled; trusting them = IDOR (insecure direct object reference): read/act as another user
The gateway verified the JWT signature; claims like `sub` are trustworthy, client fields are not
Repositories should also scope queries by the owner (key = userId + resourceId) so a guessed id finds nothing
Repo: auth.Subject(req) reads the sub claim; GetSubmission(userID, submissionID) keys by both
wrong: Using unguessable UUIDs is enough protection
follow: How do admin endpoints authorise differently (groups → permissions)?
What would a pen tester try first against GET /submissions/{id}?
cards.answer: Anything in the body or query string is chosen by the caller, so if the handler took userId from there, anyone could read or act as anyone else: an IDOR bug. The token's sub claim was verified by the gateway, so that's the only trustworthy identity. This repo reads it with auth.Subject and passes it down, and the repository keys lookups by user and resource id together, so guessing someone's submission id returns not-found. Random UUIDs help but are not access control.

cards.q: Design idempotency for POST /payments so a client retry never charges twice.
cards.k: client sends a key per operation · store key → (hash, status, response) atomically with the side effect · same key + body → stored response · different body → 409 / 422 · handle in-flight + expiry
keys: Client sends an Idempotency-Key header (UUID) per logical operation
Server stores key → (request hash, status, response) atomically before/with the side effect (unique constraint or conditional write)
Repeat with the same key: return the stored response; same key with a different body: 409 / 422
Handle the in-flight case (first request still running) and expire keys after a retention window
wrong: Check if the payment exists, then insert (race: two requests both see 'not exists')
follow: Why must the check and the write be one atomic operation?
How do this repo's events carry idempotency, and who uses the key?
cards.answer: The client generates a key per logical payment and sends it with every retry. The server records the key in the same atomic step as the payment, using a unique constraint or a conditional write, along with the response. A retry with the same key gets the stored response; the same key with a different body is rejected. A separate check-then-insert would race. This repo's events carry an IdempotencyKey, and the ledger writes it with attribute_not_exists so a redelivered event can't credit twice.

cards.q: Offset pagination versus cursor (keyset) pagination: how do they work and which would you choose?
cards.k: offset = simple, page N, but slow deep + pages shift · cursor / keyset = (createdAt, id) < cursor, stable, index-friendly · opaque base64 cursor · DynamoDB = cursor only
keys: Offset: ?limit=20&offset=40; simple, jump to page N; but the DB still scans skipped rows (slow at depth) and results shift when rows are inserted
Cursor/keyset: return an opaque cursor (e.g. last createdAt+id); next page = WHERE (created_at, id) < cursor; stable and index-friendly
DynamoDB only supports cursor style (LastEvaluatedKey / ExclusiveStartKey)
Cursors should be opaque (base64) so clients can't depend on internals
wrong: Offset pagination is fine at any scale
follow: How would you paginate GET /submissions if a user had 10,000 submissions?
Why include the id as a tie-breaker in the cursor?
cards.answer: Offset pagination skips N rows, which is simple and lets you jump to a page, but the database still reads the skipped rows and new inserts shift what each page shows. Keyset pagination remembers where you stopped, say the last created-at and id, and asks for rows after that, which uses the index and stays stable. DynamoDB only does it that way, with LastEvaluatedKey. I'd hand clients an opaque base64 cursor so the internal key can change.

cards.q: How do you version an API, and how do you change it without breaking mobile apps that can't be force-updated?
cards.k: path /api/v1 (or header / media type) · additive only: new optional fields, new endpoints · never rename or repurpose · old mobile apps live for months · deprecate → measure → remove · force-update last
keys: Options: path (/api/v1/), header, or media type; path is the most common and visible (this repo uses /api/v1)
Prefer additive, backward-compatible changes: new optional fields, new endpoints; never remove or repurpose fields within a version
Mobile: old app versions live for months; keep old behaviour until usage drops; a minimum-version gate / force-update screen as last resort
Deprecate with notice, telemetry on version usage, then remove
wrong: Bump the version for every change
follow: This repo has a toggle feature: how could it support a forced app update?
Is adding an enum value a breaking change?
cards.answer: The usual way is a version in the path, like this repo's /api/v1. But the real skill is not needing v2: make changes additive, so new optional fields and new endpoints are fine, while removing or renaming a field isn't. Mobile makes this strict, because old app versions stay installed for months. For truly breaking changes you run both versions, track who still calls the old one, and as a last resort gate old clients with a forced-update screen.

cards.q: What is HTTP middleware in Go's net/http, and what typically goes there?
cards.k: func(next http.Handler) http.Handler · request ID, logging, recovery, auth, CORS, timeouts, metrics · order: recovery + request ID outermost, auth before handlers · values via r.Context()
keys: A function that wraps an http.Handler and returns a new Handler: func(next http.Handler) http.Handler
Cross-cutting concerns: request IDs, logging, panic recovery, auth, CORS, timeouts, metrics, rate limiting
Order matters: recovery and request ID outermost; auth before business handlers
Pass request-scoped values via r.Context(); wrap ResponseWriter to capture the status code
wrong: Middleware must be a framework feature
follow: How do you capture the response status code for logging?
In Lambda + API Gateway, which of these jobs moved out of your Go code (the JWT authorizer, CORS)?
cards.answer: Middleware in Go is just a function that takes a handler and returns a handler that does something before or after calling the inner one. That's where request IDs, access logs, panic recovery, auth, CORS and metrics go. Order matters: recovery and request IDs wrap everything, auth comes before your business handlers. To log the status you wrap the ResponseWriter. In this repo some of that moved to API Gateway, which verifies the JWT and handles CORS before the Lambda runs.

cards.q: Which timeouts should a Go HTTP server and client set, and why is the default http.Client dangerous?
cards.k: zero value = no timeout · server: ReadHeader (slowloris), Read, Write, Idle · client: http.Client{Timeout} or ctx deadline, the default hangs forever · deeper calls get shorter deadlines
keys: Server: ReadHeaderTimeout (slowloris), ReadTimeout, WriteTimeout, IdleTimeout; the zero value means no timeout
Client: http.Client{Timeout: …} or per-request context deadlines; the default client has no timeout and can hang forever
Timeouts should shrink as you go deeper (caller's deadline > callee's) so the caller can still respond
tus-feature sets ReadHeaderTimeout and IdleTimeout to its network timeout
wrong: Go's defaults are safe for production
follow: Why can't a resumable-upload server use a short WriteTimeout / ReadTimeout?
What's a slowloris attack?
cards.answer: An http.Server with zero timeouts will wait forever, so a client that sends headers one byte a minute can tie up connections: always set ReadHeaderTimeout and IdleTimeout, plus read and write timeouts that fit the workload. On the client side, http.DefaultClient has no timeout at all, so one stuck dependency can hang a request forever; set Client.Timeout or a context deadline. tus-feature sets header and idle timeouts but not a short overall read timeout, because a big upload legitimately takes minutes.

cards.q: How do you design an API for a long-running job (video analysis taking minutes)?
cards.k: don't hold the request → 202 + status URL · client polls or server pushes (webhook, SSE, push) · job state durable with stages, a worker / queue does the work · idempotent submit · progress + failure reason
keys: Don't hold the request open: accept with 202 (or 201 for the resource) and return a resource id / status URL
Client polls the status resource, or the server pushes (webhook, WebSocket/SSE, push notification) when done
The job state lives in durable storage with explicit stages; a worker / queue does the processing
Make submission idempotent; expose progress and failure reasons
wrong: Keep the HTTP request open until the video is analysed
follow: How does this system do it: who processes, and how does the app learn the result?
Polling vs push for a mobile app: trade-offs?
cards.answer: Never block a request for minutes. Create the job, return immediately with its id and status, and let a worker process it from a queue while the state lives in the database with explicit stages. The client either polls the status endpoint or gets pushed a notification. This system works that way: POST /submissions returns right away with status processing, the analyzer daemon picks pending submissions up and writes results back, and the notification pipeline tells the user when it's approved or rejected.

cards.q: Process versus thread: what does each own, and what do threads share?
cards.k: process = own address space, fd table, isolated · threads share memory + fds, own stack + registers · thread switch cheaper (no TLB flush) · thread crash kills the process, process crash doesn't spread
keys: A process has its own virtual address space, file descriptor table, and resources; isolation between processes
Threads live inside a process and share its memory and file descriptors; each has its own stack and registers
Thread switches are cheaper than process switches (no address-space switch / TLB flush); communication is cheaper but needs synchronisation
A crash in one thread can take down the whole process; a crashed process doesn't corrupt others
wrong: Threads have separate heaps
follow: Where do goroutines fit in this picture?
Why do browsers run tabs in separate processes?
cards.answer: A process is an isolated program instance: its own address space, open files and resources. Threads are units of execution inside one process; they share its memory and file descriptors but each has its own stack and registers. Switching threads is cheaper because the address space stays the same, and sharing memory makes communication cheap but needs locking. Isolation is the price: one bad thread can crash the whole process. Goroutines sit one level up, multiplexed by the Go runtime onto a few threads.

cards.q: What is a context switch, what does it cost, and what triggers one?
cards.k: save registers / PC / SP → restore another · triggers: time slice, blocking I/O or lock, sleeping syscall, interrupt · µs direct + cold caches / TLB · too many runnable threads → switching, not working
keys: The kernel saves one thread's registers/program counter/stack pointer and restores another's
Triggers: time slice expiry (preemption), blocking on I/O or a lock, a syscall that sleeps, an interrupt
Direct cost: microseconds of kernel work; indirect cost: cold CPU caches / TLB (bigger for process switches)
Too many runnable threads → time spent switching instead of working (one reason for event loops / goroutines)
wrong: Context switches are free
follow: Why is a goroutine switch cheaper than an OS thread switch?
How would you see context switches on Linux (vmstat cs, pidstat -w)?
cards.answer: A context switch is the kernel parking one thread, saving its registers and stack pointer, and resuming another. It happens when a time slice runs out, when a thread blocks on I/O or a lock, or on interrupts. The direct cost is small, a few microseconds, but caches and the TLB go cold afterwards, especially when switching processes. With thousands of busy threads you burn real CPU just switching, which is part of why Go schedules goroutines in user space.

cards.q: What do fork and exec do, and what is copy-on-write?
cards.k: fork = copy of parent · exec = replace with a new program · COW: share read-only pages, copy on write → cheap fork, Redis RDB · zombie = not wait()ed · orphan = adopted by init
keys: fork creates a child process that's a copy of the parent; exec replaces the current process image with a new program
Copy-on-write: after fork, parent and child share physical pages marked read-only; a page is copied only when one writes
Makes fork cheap; Redis uses fork + COW for background snapshots (RDB)
Zombie: a dead child whose parent hasn't wait()ed for it; orphan: a child whose parent died (adopted by init)
wrong: fork copies all memory immediately
follow: Why can Redis's memory use spike during a snapshot under heavy writes?
Why do containers need an init process to reap zombies?
cards.answer: fork duplicates a process; exec swaps the program running in a process for another, which is how shells launch commands. Copy-on-write is what makes fork cheap: the child shares the parent's pages until one of them writes, and only then is that page copied. Redis relies on it to snapshot memory in a forked child while the parent keeps serving, which is why heavy writes during a snapshot can nearly double memory use.

cards.q: Name the ways processes communicate on one machine and their trade-offs.
cards.k: pipes / named pipes · Unix domain sockets (fast, local, bidirectional) · shared memory (fastest, needs sync) · message queues · signals (tiny) · localhost TCP / HTTP / gRPC if it may move · files / DB (slow, durable)
keys: Pipes / named pipes (byte streams, parent-child), Unix domain sockets (bidirectional, fast, local)
Shared memory (fastest, needs synchronisation), message queues, signals (tiny notifications only)
TCP on localhost / HTTP / gRPC when components may later move to other machines
Files and databases as a shared medium (slow, durable)
wrong: Signals can carry data payloads
follow: How does the tus hook-client talk to the hook Lambda (it's not local IPC)?
Why do Docker and Postgres use Unix sockets locally?
cards.answer: Locally you have pipes, which is how shell pipelines work; Unix domain sockets, which behave like network sockets but skip the network stack; shared memory, the fastest but you need your own locking; and signals, which can only say 'something happened'. If the pieces might ever run on different machines you just use TCP or HTTP. In this repo tusd runs a small hook-client per hook, and that client calls the hook Lambda over AWS's API, not local IPC.

cards.q: Describe a process's memory layout. What lives on the stack versus the heap?
cards.k: text → data/BSS → heap ↑ → mmap → stack ↓ · stack = frames, locals, per thread, fast, overflow · heap = outlives call / dynamic size, malloc or GC · goroutine stacks live in runtime-managed heap memory
keys: Text (code), data/BSS (globals), heap (dynamic allocations, grows up), memory-mapped regions, stack (grows down)
Stack: function frames, local variables, return addresses; automatic and fast; per thread; limited size → stack overflow
Heap: objects that outlive a call or have dynamic size; managed by malloc/free or a GC
Go's goroutine stacks are separate, growable and themselves live in heap memory managed by the runtime
wrong: The heap is faster than the stack
follow: What causes a stack overflow, and why does recursion depth matter more in Python than Go?
Why is allocating on the stack cheaper than on the heap?
cards.answer: From the bottom: the program's code, then initialised and uninitialised globals, then the heap growing upward, mapped regions like shared libraries, and the stack growing down from the top. The stack holds each call's frame, locals and return address; it's automatic and fast but limited, so deep recursion overflows it. The heap holds anything that outlives a call or whose size isn't known in advance. Go is unusual: each goroutine has its own small stack that the runtime grows by copying.

cards.q: What is virtual memory, and what happens on a page fault?
cards.k: own address space per process · MMU + page tables, cached in TLB · isolation, lazy alloc, sharing, COW, swap · page fault: minor = map / allocate, major = read disk, then retry · invalid → SIGSEGV
keys: Each process sees its own contiguous virtual address space; the MMU maps virtual pages to physical frames via page tables (cached in the TLB)
Gives isolation, lets memory be lazily allocated, shared (libraries, copy-on-write) and swapped
Page fault: access to a page not mapped in RAM; the kernel loads/allocates it (minor fault) or reads it from disk (major fault) and retries
Invalid access → segmentation fault (SIGSEGV)
wrong: Virtual memory means using disk as RAM
follow: Why can a process's virtual size (VSZ) be far larger than its resident size (RSS)?
What is thrashing?
cards.answer: Every process gets its own virtual address space, and the CPU's MMU translates virtual pages to physical memory through page tables, caching translations in the TLB. That gives isolation, lets the kernel hand out memory only when it's touched, share pages between processes, and push cold pages to swap. A page fault is touching a page that isn't currently mapped: the kernel allocates it or reads it in and resumes the instruction. Touching an address you're not allowed to is a segfault.

cards.q: Why does iterating a 2D array row by row run faster than column by column?
cards.k: 64-byte cache lines · sequential uses the whole line + prefetch · row-major → row-wise sequential, column-wise jumps a row → misses · false sharing: two cores, same line, ping-pong
keys: CPU caches load memory in cache lines (typically 64 bytes); sequential access uses every byte of a loaded line
Row-major layout: row-wise iteration is sequential; column-wise jumps by a whole row each step, missing the cache
Hardware prefetchers predict sequential patterns
False sharing: two cores writing different variables on the same line ping-pong it between caches
wrong: Both orders are equally fast because RAM is random access
follow: How can false sharing slow down a per-goroutine counter array?
Why are arrays of structs vs structs of arrays a performance choice?
cards.answer: The CPU doesn't fetch single bytes; it pulls a 64-byte cache line. A row in a row-major array is contiguous, so walking it uses every byte of every line it loads, and the prefetcher stays ahead. Walking a column jumps a whole row each step, so nearly every access misses the cache. The same effect shows up as false sharing when two cores write neighbouring variables on the same line.

cards.q: Stack versus heap in Go: who decides, and why does it matter for performance?
cards.k: compiler decides · escapes when it outlives the func: returned pointer, stored in heap object, escaping closure, interface · stack ≈ free, heap = alloc + GC · -gcflags=-m, -benchmem, pprof · new vs &T{} doesn't decide
keys: The compiler's escape analysis decides: values that outlive the function (returned pointers, stored in heap objects, captured by escaping closures, put in interfaces) go to the heap
Stack allocation is nearly free; heap allocation costs allocation time and GC work
See decisions with `go build -gcflags=-m`; measure with benchmarks and pprof (-benchmem, alloc profiles)
You don't choose with `new` vs `&T{}`; both may be stack or heap
wrong: new() always allocates on the heap
Pointers are always faster than values
follow: How would you find the allocation hot spot in a slow endpoint?
What is sync.Pool for, and when does it backfire?
cards.answer: Go decides for you: escape analysis keeps a value on the stack unless it might outlive the function, for example when you return a pointer to it, store it somewhere long-lived, or put it in an interface. Heap allocations cost more and create work for the garbage collector, so hot paths try to allocate less. You can see the compiler's decisions with -gcflags=-m, but the right workflow is benchmark, profile allocations with pprof, then fix the top offender.

cards.q: How does Go's garbage collector work at a high level, and what can you tune?
cards.k: concurrent tri-colour mark-and-sweep, non-generational, non-moving, sub-ms STW · GOGC=100 heap growth · GOMEMLIMIT soft cap · cost ∝ live heap + allocation rate · real lever: allocate less
keys: Concurrent, tri-colour mark-and-sweep, non-generational, non-moving; short stop-the-world pauses (sub-millisecond typically)
GOGC (default 100) sets how much the heap may grow before the next cycle; GOMEMLIMIT gives a soft memory cap
The real lever is allocating less (reuse buffers, avoid pointer-heavy structures)
GC cost scales with live heap and allocation rate, not with garbage
wrong: Go uses reference counting
Go's GC stops the world for the whole collection
follow: A container OOM-kills a Go service near its limit: which setting helps?
Why can a service with a small live heap but a huge allocation rate still spend a lot of CPU in GC?
cards.answer: Go's collector marks live objects concurrently with your program, using a tri-colour algorithm and a write barrier, then sweeps; pauses are usually well under a millisecond. It doesn't move or compact memory and isn't generational. GOGC controls how much the heap can grow between collections and GOMEMLIMIT sets a soft ceiling, which is the useful one in containers. Most real wins come from allocating less rather than tuning.

cards.q: What is a system call, and what's the difference between user mode and kernel mode?
cards.k: user mode can't touch hardware / others' memory · syscall traps to kernel (read, write, socket, mmap, futex) → returns · costs a mode switch → buffer / batch · strace shows where it blocks
keys: User mode can't touch hardware or other processes' memory; kernel mode can
A syscall (read, write, open, socket, mmap, futex…) traps into the kernel to perform a privileged operation, then returns
Syscalls cost more than function calls (mode switch); batching / buffering reduces them
strace shows a process's syscalls; useful to see where it's blocked
wrong: Every Go function call is a system call
follow: Why does bufio make many small writes faster?
How would strace help with a hung process?
cards.answer: Normal code runs in user mode, which can't touch devices or other processes' memory. To read a file, open a socket or allocate pages it makes a system call, a controlled jump into the kernel, which does the privileged work and returns. That jump is much more expensive than a function call, which is why buffered I/O batches small writes. strace lists the syscalls a process makes, which quickly shows what a stuck process is waiting on.

cards.q: What is a file descriptor, and why do servers hit 'too many open files'?
cards.k: int index into open files / sockets / pipes, 0/1/2 std · every TCP connection = 1 fd · ulimit -n per process + system-wide · 'too many open files' = leak (resp.Body) or low limit · lsof, /proc/PID/fd
keys: An integer index into the process's table of open resources: files, sockets, pipes (0/1/2 = stdin/stdout/stderr)
Every TCP connection uses one; limits per process (ulimit -n / RLIMIT_NOFILE) and system-wide
'Too many open files' = leaked descriptors (unclosed files/response bodies) or a limit too low for the connection count
Debug with lsof -p PID / ls /proc/PID/fd; fix leaks (defer Close, close resp.Body) and raise limits
wrong: File descriptors are only for files on disk
follow: What Go mistake with http.Client leaks descriptors?
Why does a load test fail at exactly ~1024 connections on some machines?
cards.answer: A file descriptor is a small integer the kernel gives you for anything you've opened: a file, a socket, a pipe. Every network connection costs one, and there's a per-process limit, often 1024 by default. 'Too many open files' means either you leak them, classically by not closing an HTTP response body in Go, or the limit is too low for your connection count. lsof or /proc/PID/fd shows what's open.

cards.q: Blocking I/O, non-blocking I/O, I/O multiplexing (select/poll/epoll), and async I/O: how do they differ, and which does Go use?
cards.k: blocking = thread sleeps, thread per conn · non-blocking = EAGAIN, retry · multiplexing: select/poll O(n), epoll O(ready), edge/level · io_uring = submit + completions · Go netpoller: looks blocking, parks goroutines
keys: Blocking: the thread sleeps until data is ready; one thread per connection
Non-blocking: calls return EAGAIN immediately; you must retry
Multiplexing: one thread waits on many descriptors; epoll scales O(ready) vs select/poll O(n), with edge/level triggering
Go's netpoller uses epoll (kqueue on macOS): goroutines look blocking, the runtime parks them and wakes them on readiness
io_uring / true async I/O: submit and get completions
wrong: Go creates a thread per network connection
follow: Why can Node and Go both handle 10k connections but in different styles?
Why does disk I/O still block an OS thread in Go?
cards.answer: With blocking I/O a thread just waits, so you need a thread per connection. Non-blocking calls return immediately with 'try again'. Multiplexing lets one thread wait on thousands of sockets at once, and epoll does it efficiently because it only reports the ready ones. Go hides this: your goroutine calls conn.Read as if it blocked, but the runtime registers the socket with epoll, parks the goroutine and wakes it when data arrives. Node does the same with an explicit event loop and callbacks.

cards.q: What is an inode, and what's the difference between a hard link and a symbolic link?
cards.k: inode = metadata + block pointers, no name · dir entry: name → inode · hard link = same inode, same FS, data lives till last link + handle · symlink = path file, crosses FS, breaks on move · inodes can run out
keys: An inode stores a file's metadata and block pointers (not its name); directory entries map names to inode numbers
Hard link: another name for the same inode (same filesystem only); the data lives until the last link and open handle are gone
Symlink: a small file containing a path; can cross filesystems; breaks if the target moves
You can run out of inodes with free space left (millions of tiny files)
wrong: Deleting a file always frees its space immediately (not while a process holds it open)
follow: df says the disk is full but du can't find the files: why (deleted-but-open logs)?
Why are the skills in ~/.claude/skills symlinks?
cards.answer: An inode is the filesystem's record for a file: permissions, size, timestamps and where its data blocks are, but not its name. Names live in directories and point at inode numbers. A hard link is a second name for the same inode, so the data survives until every name and every open handle is gone. A symlink is a tiny file holding a path, so it can point anywhere, even across filesystems, and it breaks if the target moves, which is exactly what happened to the old iOS skill links.

cards.q: How does the Linux scheduler decide which thread runs next? What are nice values and CPU-bound vs I/O-bound tasks?
cards.k: CFS / EEVDF: fair share by virtual runtime, least-run goes next · nice -20..19 weights · SCHED_FIFO/RR preempt · I/O-bound wakes fast · cgroup CPU quota → throttling → latency spikes
keys: CFS (and EEVDF since 6.6) aim for fair CPU share: track virtual runtime, run the thread that has had the least
nice values (-20..19) weight the share; real-time policies (SCHED_FIFO/RR) preempt normal ones
I/O-bound threads sleep often and get scheduled quickly when they wake: good interactivity
Containers use cgroups CPU quotas: throttling when the quota is exhausted causes latency spikes
wrong: Linux uses plain round robin for everything
follow: Why can a Go service in a container with a 1-CPU limit see latency spikes (CFS throttling, GOMAXPROCS)?
What does load average actually measure?
cards.answer: Linux's default scheduler tries to give each runnable thread a fair share: it tracks how much CPU each has used, weighted by its nice value, and runs the one that's furthest behind. Threads that mostly wait on I/O get picked quickly when they wake, which keeps things responsive. Real-time policies sit above all that. In containers, cgroup quotas throttle you once you use your share in a period, which shows up as latency spikes if GOMAXPROCS is higher than the CPU limit.

cards.q: Mutex versus semaphore versus spinlock?
cards.k: mutex = one owner, owner releases · semaphore = up to N holders · spinlock = busy-wait, tiny sections on multi-core only · Go: sync.Mutex, buffered chan / x/sync/semaphore
keys: Mutex: exclusive ownership, one holder at a time, released by the owner
Semaphore: a counter allowing up to N concurrent holders (binary semaphore ≈ lock without ownership)
Spinlock: busy-waits instead of sleeping: good only for very short critical sections on multi-core, wasteful otherwise
Go equivalents: sync.Mutex, a buffered channel / x/sync/semaphore, runtime-internal spinning
wrong: A semaphore with N=1 is identical to a mutex in every respect (ownership differs)
follow: Where would you use a semaphore in a backend (bounding calls to a dependency)?
Why is spinning bad when there are more threads than cores?
cards.answer: A mutex gives one holder exclusive access, and the holder releases it. A semaphore is a counter that lets up to N holders in, which is perfect for limiting concurrent calls to a dependency. A spinlock loops instead of sleeping, which only makes sense when the wait is shorter than a context switch. In Go, sync.Mutex, a buffered channel or x/sync/semaphore, and the runtime spins briefly inside Mutex for you.

cards.q: What are the four conditions for deadlock, and how do you prevent one?
cards.k: mutual exclusion · hold and wait · no preemption · circular wait → all four · break one: global lock order, take all at once, timeouts / try-lock · DBs: wait-for graph, abort one
keys: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait (Coffman conditions): all four must hold
Break one: acquire locks in a global order (breaks circular wait), take all locks at once, use timeouts / try-lock
Databases detect deadlocks with a wait-for graph and abort one transaction
wrong: Deadlock needs at least three threads
follow: Two transactions update rows A then B and B then A: what happens in Postgres?
How does lock ordering apply to Go mutexes?
cards.answer: A deadlock needs four things at once: resources that only one holder can use, holders waiting for more while keeping what they have, no way to take a resource away, and a cycle of waiting. Remove any one and it can't happen; in practice you impose a lock order so cycles can't form, or use timeouts. Databases detect cycles themselves and kill one transaction, so the application has to retry.

cards.q: What does load average mean on Linux, and how do you interpret 8.0 on a 4-core machine?
cards.k: running + runnable + D-state (disk) tasks, 1 / 5 / 15 min · compare to cores: 8.0 on 4 ≈ 2× oversubscribed or I/O stuck · check CPU % and iowait to tell which
keys: Average number of tasks running or waiting to run, plus tasks in uninterruptible sleep (D state, usually disk I/O), over 1/5/15 minutes
Compare to the core count: 8.0 on 4 cores means roughly 2× oversubscribed (or stuck on I/O)
Check CPU utilisation and iowait to tell CPU saturation from I/O blockage
wrong: Load average is CPU percent
follow: Load is high but CPU is idle: what would you check next?
Why do the 1/5/15-minute numbers together show a trend?
cards.answer: Load average is how many tasks were running or waiting for a CPU, plus, on Linux, those stuck waiting on disk, averaged over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. On a 4-core box, 8 means about twice as much demand as CPUs, or a pile of processes blocked on I/O. To know which, look at CPU usage and iowait: high load with idle CPU points at storage or a network filesystem.

cards.q: SIGTERM versus SIGKILL versus SIGINT: what are they, and why does graceful shutdown depend on the difference?
cards.k: SIGINT Ctrl+C · SIGTERM polite stop from Docker / k8s / ECS / systemd, catchable · SIGKILL uncatchable, no cleanup · SIGTERM → grace period (~30 s) → SIGKILL · so catch it, stop taking work, drain
keys: SIGINT: Ctrl+C; SIGTERM: polite termination request (sent by Docker/Kubernetes/ECS/systemd on stop); both can be caught
SIGKILL (kill -9) can't be caught or ignored: the process dies immediately, no cleanup
Orchestrators send SIGTERM, wait a grace period (e.g. 30 s), then SIGKILL
So the app must catch SIGTERM, stop accepting work and drain within the grace period
wrong: kill -9 lets the program flush its buffers
follow: What happens to tus-feature's in-flight uploads if the grace period is shorter than its 30-second shutdown timeout?
Why is PID 1 in a container special for signals?
cards.answer: SIGINT is what Ctrl+C sends; SIGTERM is the standard 'please stop' that Docker, ECS, Kubernetes and systemd send. A program can catch both and clean up. SIGKILL can't be caught: the kernel just removes the process. Platforms send SIGTERM, wait a grace period, then SIGKILL, so a service catches SIGTERM, stops taking new work and drains before the deadline. tus-feature does exactly that with NotifyContext and a 30-second Shutdown, which only works if the platform's grace period is longer.

cards.q: What are cgroups and namespaces, and what happens when a container exceeds its memory limit?
cards.k: namespaces = what it sees (PID, net, mount, user, UTS) · cgroups = what it uses (CPU, mem, I/O) · container = processes + both + image, not a VM · over memory → OOM kill, exit 137 · GOMEMLIMIT
keys: Namespaces isolate what a process sees (PID, network, mount, user, UTS); cgroups limit what it can use (CPU, memory, I/O)
A container is just processes with namespaces + cgroups + a filesystem image, not a VM
Exceeding the memory limit → the kernel OOM killer kills a process (exit code 137); no graceful shutdown
Set language runtimes to respect limits (GOMEMLIMIT, JVM container awareness)
wrong: Containers have their own kernel
follow: How do you tell an OOM kill from a crash in ECS / Kubernetes?
Why is a container not a security boundary as strong as a VM?
cards.answer: Namespaces control what a process can see: its own process tree, network interfaces, filesystem mounts. Cgroups control what it can use: CPU, memory, I/O. A container is just a process with both applied and an image as its root filesystem, sharing the host kernel. If it goes over its memory limit the kernel's OOM killer kills it immediately, exit code 137, with no chance to shut down cleanly, so runtimes need to know the limit, like GOMEMLIMIT for Go.

cards.q: A Linux server is slow. Which commands do you reach for first, and what does each tell you?
cards.k: top / htop + uptime load vs cores · free, vmstat: memory, swap, run queue · iostat, df, du: disk · ss -tanp, lsof: connections, fds · journalctl, dmesg (OOM) · strace, perf, pprof
keys: top/htop: CPU, load, memory per process; `uptime` load average vs core count
free -h / vmstat: memory, swap, run queue, context switches; iostat / df -h / du: disk I/O and space
ss -tanp / netstat: connections and their states; lsof: open files and sockets
journalctl / log files, dmesg (OOM kills, disk errors); strace / perf / pprof for the process itself
wrong: Restarting first, investigating later, with no data captured
follow: Load average is 16 on a 4-core box but CPU is 20% busy: what's going on (I/O wait / D state)?
How would you find which process is filling the disk?
cards.answer: I start broad: uptime for load against the core count, top to see which process eats CPU or memory, free and vmstat for swapping and the run queue, iostat and df for disk. Then the network: ss to count connections by state. dmesg tells me about OOM kills or disk errors. Once I know which process, I go into it: logs, strace for what it's waiting on, and for a Go service, pprof. High load with idle CPU usually means threads stuck in I/O wait.

cards.q: What is a goroutine, and how is it different from an OS thread?
cards.k: go f() → runtime-managed · ~2–8 KB growable stack vs ~1–8 MB thread · M:N onto few threads, switch in user space · blocking I/O parks the goroutine, not the thread (netpoller) · GOMAXPROCS run in parallel
keys: A function running concurrently, managed by the Go runtime, started with the `go` keyword
Cheap: starts with a small (~2–8 KB) growable stack vs ~1–8 MB fixed thread stacks; you can run hundreds of thousands
The runtime multiplexes many goroutines onto a few OS threads (M:N scheduling); switching is done in user space
Blocking I/O parks the goroutine, not the thread (netpoller); GOMAXPROCS threads run Go code in parallel
wrong: A goroutine is a thread
Goroutines are free so you never need to limit them
follow: What happens when a goroutine makes a blocking syscall?
Why must the analyzer's main wait for its goroutines before returning?
cards.answer: A goroutine is a function the Go runtime runs concurrently. It starts with a tiny stack that grows as needed, so you can have hundreds of thousands, whereas threads reserve megabytes each and are expensive to create and switch. The runtime schedules goroutines onto a small pool of OS threads; when one waits on the network it's parked and the thread runs something else. When main returns the process exits and every goroutine dies with it, which is why the analyzer waits on its WaitGroup.

cards.q: Explain the Go scheduler's G, M and P model.
cards.k: G goroutine · M thread · P scheduling context + local queue, GOMAXPROCS of them · M needs a P to run Go · idle P steals half a queue · blocking syscall hands off the P · async preemption since 1.14
keys: G = goroutine, M = OS thread (machine), P = processor: a scheduling context with a local run queue; there are GOMAXPROCS Ps
An M must hold a P to run Go code; each P has a local queue plus there's a global queue
Work stealing: an idle P steals half of another P's queue
Blocking syscall: the M detaches its P so another M can run it; network I/O uses the netpoller instead of blocking threads
Preemption: asynchronous preemption (since 1.14) stops tight loops from hogging a P
wrong: GOMAXPROCS limits the number of goroutines
follow: Why does GOMAXPROCS matter in containers with CPU limits (Go 1.25 made it cgroup-aware)?
What happened before async preemption to a goroutine stuck in `for {}`?
cards.answer: G is a goroutine, M an OS thread, P a processor slot; there are GOMAXPROCS Ps, usually one per core. A thread needs a P to run Go code, and each P has its own run queue, with a global queue as overflow. Idle Ps steal work from busy ones. If a goroutine enters a blocking syscall, its thread gives up the P so another thread can keep running goroutines; network waits go through the netpoller and don't block a thread at all. Since 1.14 the runtime can preempt a goroutine in a tight loop.

cards.q: How does concurrency work for a Go Lambda like submission-feature? What's shared across invocations, and what isn't?
cards.k: one invocation per environment at a time · concurrency = more environments · main's clients + caches survive warm invocations, per environment only · caches differ between instances · cold start = init + main
keys: One execution environment processes one invocation at a time; concurrency comes from AWS starting more environments
Anything built in main (clients, repository, service, in-memory caches) survives across warm invocations in that environment only
In-memory caches are per environment, so different instances can hold different values for up to the TTL
Cold start cost = runtime init + main's setup; keep main lean; reserved/provisioned concurrency bound or pre-warm
wrong: One Lambda instance handles many requests in parallel like a web server
In-memory caches are shared across all instances
follow: Two users hit different instances right after an admin changes the criteria config: what do they see, and for how long?
What would you need if the cache had to be consistent everywhere?
cards.answer: Each Lambda execution environment runs one request at a time; more traffic means more environments. Whatever main builds, like clients and the service with its five-minute criteria cache, lives as long as that environment and is reused by warm invocations, but it isn't shared with other environments. So after a config change, different instances can serve the old value for up to five minutes. If that mattered, you'd use a shared cache or explicit invalidation.

cards.q: Unbuffered versus buffered channels: what are the semantics of send and receive for each?
cards.k: unbuffered send waits for a receiver (rendezvous) · buffered blocks only when full / empty · closed: receive zero + ok=false, send panics · nil channel blocks forever (switch off a select case)
keys: Unbuffered: send blocks until a receiver takes it (a rendezvous / synchronisation point)
Buffered (cap n): send blocks only when the buffer is full; receive blocks only when empty
Receiving from a closed channel returns the zero value immediately (`v, ok` gives ok=false); sending on a closed channel panics
A nil channel blocks forever on send and receive (useful to disable a select case)
wrong: Buffered channels are always faster and better
Closing a channel discards buffered values (they can still be received)
follow: When does a buffer hide a bug instead of fixing it?
Who should close a channel?
cards.answer: An unbuffered channel is a handshake: the sender waits until a receiver takes the value, so it synchronises the two goroutines. A buffered channel lets senders run ahead until the buffer is full. Receiving from a closed channel never blocks; you get the zero value and ok is false, while sending to a closed channel panics. A nil channel blocks forever, which is a handy way to switch off a case in a select.

cards.q: In tus-feature's lock, `Unlock` does `close(u.stop)` then `<-u.done`. Explain this stop/done pattern.
cards.k: close(stop) broadcasts → keepAlive's case fires · goroutine defer close(done) · <-done waits until it really exited → no renew after release · chan struct{} = pure signal
keys: close(stop) broadcasts to every receiver at once: the keepAlive goroutine's `case <-u.stop` fires
done is closed by the goroutine itself (`defer close(u.done)`), so `<-u.done` waits until it has really exited
This guarantees no heartbeat renews the lease after Unlock releases it (no race between renew and release)
Channels of struct{} carry no data: pure signals
wrong: Sending one value on stop would be equivalent (only if exactly one receiver, and it would block if nobody listens)
follow: What would go wrong if Unlock released the lock without waiting on done?
Why struct{} rather than bool?
cards.answer: stop is how Unlock tells the heartbeat goroutine to quit: closing a channel wakes every receiver, so the select in keepAlive returns. done goes the other way: the goroutine closes it on exit, so Unlock blocks on <-u.done until the heartbeat has definitely stopped. Only then does it release the lock in DynamoDB. Without that wait, a renew already in flight could re-extend a lease we just released. struct{} channels carry no data; they're pure signals.

cards.q: Walk through the analyzer's `loop` function: how does it run work periodically and stop cleanly?
cards.k: run once → select on ctx.Done() or ticker.C · SIGTERM cancels ctx → return · defer ticker.Stop() · skip logging if ctx is done · a tick during Run is dropped (buffer 1), no pile-up
keys: Runs svc.Run once immediately, then waits in a select on `ctx.Done()` or `ticker.C`
When ctx is cancelled (SIGTERM via signal.NotifyContext), the select returns and the goroutine exits
defer ticker.Stop() releases the ticker; errors are logged only if ctx isn't already cancelled (shutdown noise)
A tick that fires while Run is still working is dropped, not queued (ticker channel buffer is 1): no pile-up
wrong: time.Sleep in a loop is equivalent (it can't be interrupted by cancellation)
follow: What happens if one Run takes longer than the interval?
Why is the error check `err != nil && ctx.Err() == nil`?
cards.answer: Each loop calls Run right away, then blocks in a select on two channels: the context's Done channel and the ticker. A tick starts the next round; a cancelled context ends the goroutine. Using select instead of Sleep is what makes shutdown immediate. If a run overruns the interval, the ticker drops missed ticks rather than queueing them, so work doesn't pile up. Errors are only logged when we aren't shutting down, because a cancelled context makes in-flight calls fail on purpose.

cards.q: How do you put a timeout on a blocking operation in Go? What's the trade-off between select + time.After and context?
cards.k: select on result or time.After · ctx.WithTimeout preferred: propagates and cancels nested I/O · time.After only stops waiting, work keeps running · loops: NewTimer + Stop
keys: select { case r := <-resultCh: ... case <-time.After(d): ... } or a context with WithTimeout
Context is preferred for calls into libraries: the timeout propagates into nested I/O and cancels it
time.After only stops waiting; the underlying work keeps running unless it is cancelled too
Use time.NewTimer + Stop for repeated timeouts in loops (pre-1.23 time.After timers weren't collected until they fired)
wrong: time.After cancels the operation
follow: Lambda has its own deadline: how do you leave time to clean up before it hits?
If you time out waiting on a goroutine's result channel, how do you stop that goroutine from leaking?
cards.answer: Either select between the result and time.After, or pass a context with a timeout. Context is better for real calls, because the deadline travels into the HTTP or DynamoDB call and actually stops it; time.After only stops you waiting while the work carries on. In loops, a reusable Timer with Stop avoids piling up timers, a leak that only went away in Go 1.23.

cards.q: Mutex or channel: how do you decide?
cards.k: mutex = shared state, short critical sections · channel = hand over ownership / signal events · 'share by communicating' is guidance · RWMutex for read-heavy · atomics for one counter
keys: Mutex: protecting shared state (a cache, a counter, a map) with short critical sections
Channel: transferring ownership of data or signalling events between goroutines (pipelines, work queues, done signals)
'Share memory by communicating' is guidance, not a rule; a mutex is simpler for plain shared state
RWMutex helps only with many readers and rare writers; atomics for single counters/flags
wrong: Channels are always more idiomatic than mutexes
follow: Why is the submission service's criteria cache a mutex and not a channel-based owner goroutine?
What's the cost of holding a mutex across a network call?
cards.answer: If several goroutines need to read and update the same data, a mutex around short critical sections is the simplest correct answer; the submission service's criteria cache is exactly that. Channels are for handing work or data from one goroutine to another and for signals, like the lock's stop and done channels. For a single counter or flag, atomics. RWMutex only pays off with lots of readers and rare writes.

cards.q: When would you use sync/atomic instead of a mutex?
cards.k: single-word state: atomic.Int64, Bool, Pointer[T] · lock-free, cheap · one variable only, multi-field → mutex · gives happens-before for that variable
keys: For single-word state: counters, flags, a pointer swap (atomic.Int64, atomic.Bool, atomic.Pointer[T])
Lock-free and cheap, but only for one variable; anything multi-field needs a mutex
Atomics also give memory-ordering guarantees (happens-before) for that variable
wrong: Atomics make a whole struct thread-safe
follow: How would you count requests in a hot path without contention?
Why can't you check-then-act with two atomic operations?
cards.answer: Atomics are for one value: a request counter, a ready flag, swapping a pointer to an immutable config. They avoid lock overhead and are safe across goroutines. The moment the invariant spans two fields, or you need check-then-act, you need a mutex, because two atomic operations aren't atomic together.

cards.q: sync.WaitGroup versus errgroup: what does each give you, and where does this repo use them?
cards.k: WaitGroup = wait, no errors, no cancel (wg.Go in 1.25) · errgroup: g.Go(func() error), Wait → first error · WithContext cancels siblings · SetLimit bounds concurrency · analyzer WG, profile/admin errgroup
keys: WaitGroup waits for a set of goroutines to finish; no error handling, no cancellation (wg.Go is the Go 1.25 helper for Add+Done)
errgroup.Group: g.Go(func() error), g.Wait() returns the first non-nil error
errgroup.WithContext cancels the derived ctx on the first error, so siblings can stop early; SetLimit bounds concurrency
Repo: analyzer uses WaitGroup for two long-lived loops; profile/admin use errgroup to fan out independent reads/publishes
wrong: errgroup cancels running goroutines by itself (they must watch gctx)
WaitGroup returns errors
follow: In GetDashboard, why must every g.Go use gctx, not ctx?
What does SetLimit add when fanning out over 10,000 users?
cards.answer: A WaitGroup only counts goroutines and waits for them; the analyzer uses one to run its submit and poll loops and wait until both stop. errgroup adds error handling: Wait returns the first error, and WithContext gives a context that's cancelled as soon as one goroutine fails, so the others can give up early if they pass that context into their calls. profile's GetDashboard fetches four independent things in parallel that way, and admin fans out notification publishing over batches. SetLimit caps how many run at once.

cards.q: What are sync.Once and singleflight for?
cards.k: Once = init exactly once, done even on error/panic (OnceValue 1.21) · singleflight = collapse same-key concurrent calls, share the result · stops a stampede, caches nothing after
keys: sync.Once runs an initialisation exactly once, even with concurrent callers (lazy singletons)
singleflight.Group collapses concurrent calls with the same key into one execution; all callers share the result
singleflight prevents cache stampedes on a miss; it doesn't cache afterwards
Errors/panics in Once.Do: the function is still considered done (OnceValue/OnceFunc in Go 1.21+)
wrong: singleflight caches results
follow: How would singleflight replace the mutex in criteriaTemplate?
If the first caller's ctx is cancelled inside singleflight, what do the waiting callers get?
cards.answer: sync.Once guarantees a piece of initialisation runs exactly once no matter how many goroutines race to call it. singleflight is for repeated work: if 100 goroutines ask for the same key at once, one does the call and the other 99 wait and get the same answer, which stops a cache stampede on a miss. It doesn't remember the answer afterwards; you still need the cache.

cards.q: criteriaTemplate holds s.mu while it calls DynamoDB on a cache miss. Is that a bug? What are the trade-offs?
cards.k: serialises callers behind one slow call · but dedupes misses (like singleflight), no herd · Lambda: 1 request per env → no contention · alternatives: singleflight, RLock double-check, serve stale · first caller's ctx bounds it
keys: Holding the lock during I/O serialises everyone behind one slow call: all callers wait for the miss to finish
But it also deduplicates concurrent misses (only one fetch per expiry), like singleflight, and avoids a thundering herd
In Lambda one execution environment handles one request at a time, so contention there is near zero; it would matter in a long-running server
Alternatives: singleflight.Group, double-checked read under RLock, serve stale while one goroutine refreshes
Also note: the context of the first caller bounds the fetch; if it's cancelled, others see the error
wrong: It's always a bug to hold a lock across I/O
It's fine in every environment
follow: How would you rewrite it for an HTTP server with 1,000 concurrent requests?
What does singleflight do with errors and context cancellation?
cards.answer: In a busy server it would be a real problem: every request that needs the template waits for one slow DynamoDB call. On the other hand it guarantees one fetch per expiry instead of a stampede, which is what singleflight gives you. Here it runs in Lambda, where an execution environment handles one request at a time, so there's no contention and the simple version is fine. In a long-running server I'd use singleflight, or serve the stale value while one goroutine refreshes.

cards.q: What is a data race, how do you detect one, and why is 'it works on my machine' not evidence?
cards.k: same memory, concurrent, ≥1 write, no sync · undefined: torn values, stale reads, map crash · 'works on my machine' = interleaving not hit yet · go test -race (only executed paths) · mutex / channel / atomic / don't share
keys: Two goroutines access the same memory concurrently, at least one writes, with no synchronisation (happens-before)
Effects are undefined: torn values, stale reads, map crashes, heisenbugs
Detect with `go test -race` / `go run -race` (instrumented; only finds races that actually execute)
Fix with a mutex, channel, atomic, or by not sharing (each goroutine owns distinct data)
wrong: Races are only a problem on multi-core machines
Reads never race
follow: admin-feature's usersWithoutSubmissions has goroutines writing into one shared slice: race or not? Why?
Why should CI run the tests with -race?
cards.answer: A data race is two goroutines touching the same memory at the same time, at least one writing, with nothing ordering them. The result isn't just a wrong number: the compiler and CPU may reorder things, so behaviour is undefined. The race detector, -race, instruments memory accesses and reports races that actually happen while tests run, so it needs tests that exercise the concurrency. Writing distinct elements of one slice, like submitted[offset+j], isn't a race, and errgroup's Wait makes the results visible afterwards.

cards.q: What does 'happens-before' mean in the Go memory model? Give two operations that establish it.
cards.k: A hb B → B sees A's writes · send hb receive completes · close hb receive of the close · Unlock hb next Lock · wg.Wait after all Done · plain variable = no ordering, polling done=true is broken
keys: If A happens-before B, B is guaranteed to see A's writes; without it, goroutines may observe writes late or out of order
A send on a channel happens-before the corresponding receive completes; closing a channel happens-before a receive that sees the close
Unlock happens-before a later Lock of the same mutex; wg.Wait returns after all Done calls' effects are visible
Plain shared variables give no ordering: that's why 'done = true' polling without sync is broken
wrong: Writes are always visible immediately to other goroutines
follow: Why can GetDashboard read `profile` after g.Wait() without a mutex?
Why is `for !done {}` polling a plain bool from another goroutine broken even if it 'works' in testing?
cards.answer: Happens-before is the guarantee that one goroutine's writes are visible to another. Without it, the compiler and CPU may reorder or cache values, so a flag another goroutine sets may never appear to change. Channel operations, mutex unlock-then-lock and WaitGroup or errgroup Wait all create that ordering. That's why GetDashboard can read the variables its goroutines filled in right after g.Wait returns, without a mutex.

cards.q: What causes deadlocks in Go programs, and what does 'all goroutines are asleep' mean?
cards.k: circular lock order · unbuffered send with no receiver · channel nobody closes · too many Add · 'all goroutines are asleep' only if ALL block · partial = undetected → timeouts, lock order, profiles
keys: Circular waits: two goroutines each holding a lock the other needs (inconsistent lock order)
Channel deadlocks: unbuffered send with no receiver, waiting on a channel nobody closes, Wait with too many Adds
The runtime detects a global deadlock only when every goroutine is blocked ('fatal error: all goroutines are asleep')
Partial deadlocks (some goroutines stuck) go undetected: use timeouts, lock ordering, goroutine profiles
wrong: Go detects all deadlocks
follow: Recursive locking: what happens if a method holding s.mu calls another method that locks s.mu?
How would you debug a production service that stopped responding?
cards.answer: Deadlocks come from cycles of waiting: two goroutines taking two mutexes in opposite orders, or a send on an unbuffered channel that nobody will ever receive. Go's mutexes aren't re-entrant, so locking s.mu twice in the same goroutine deadlocks. The runtime only notices when every goroutine is blocked; a deadlock involving a few goroutines in a server goes unnoticed, so you need a goroutine dump via pprof to see who waits on what.

cards.q: What causes goroutine leaks, and how do you find and prevent them?
cards.k: blocked forever: send nobody reads, receive nobody closes, lock, no exit · caller times out, result send blocks · exit via ctx / close · result chan buffer 1 · creator owns lifetime · NumGoroutine, pprof, goleak
keys: A goroutine blocked forever: sending on a channel nobody reads, receiving from one nobody closes, waiting on a lock, or a loop with no exit
Typical case: a request starts a goroutine, the caller returns early on timeout, the goroutine's result send blocks forever
Prevent: every goroutine has an exit (ctx.Done / close), buffered result channel of size 1, the creator owns the lifetime
Detect: runtime.NumGoroutine / pprof goroutine profile growing over time; goleak in tests
wrong: Leaked goroutines are garbage-collected
follow: How does a buffer of 1 fix the 'timed-out caller' leak?
Which goroutines in tus-feature could leak, and what stops them?
cards.answer: A goroutine leaks when it blocks forever, and the GC never reclaims it or anything it references. The classic one is a worker sending its result on an unbuffered channel after the caller already gave up on a timeout. Every goroutine needs a way out, usually ctx.Done or a closed channel, and the code that starts it should own when it ends, like the lock's stop/done pair. In production you watch the goroutine count and the pprof goroutine profile; in tests, goleak.

cards.q: A handler starts `go sendEmail(user)` and returns immediately. What's wrong with this in a server, and what's worse about it in Lambda?
cards.k: no error, no retry, no bound, outlives the request · lost on deploy / shutdown · Lambda freezes after return → may never run · must-happen side effects → SQS / outbox / event
keys: No error handling or retry; no bound on how many run; the goroutine may outlive the request's context
On shutdown/deploy the process exits and in-flight goroutines are lost
In Lambda, the environment freezes after the handler returns: the goroutine may never run until the next invocation, or never
Better: a durable queue (SQS / outbox / event) for side effects that must happen
wrong: Background goroutines are a fine fire-and-forget mechanism everywhere
follow: How does this repo deliver notifications instead?
If you must do it in-process, what would you add (bounded worker, WithoutCancel + timeout, WaitGroup on shutdown)?
cards.answer: A bare goroutine for a side effect has no retries, no limit and no owner: if it fails nobody knows, and a deploy kills it mid-flight. In Lambda it's worse, because the environment is frozen as soon as the handler returns, so the goroutine might run during the next invocation or never. Anything that must happen goes through something durable; this repo publishes events and lets the notification feature deliver from an SQS queue with retries and a dead-letter queue.

cards.q: How do you bound concurrency when processing 10,000 items that each call an external API?
cards.k: don't start 10k goroutines → rate limits, connections, memory · worker pool: N workers on a jobs channel · or semaphore / errgroup.SetLimit · N from the dependency's limits · ctx · fail-fast vs collect
keys: Don't start 10,000 goroutines against a dependency: you'll hit rate limits, connection limits and memory
Worker pool: N workers reading from a jobs channel, results on another channel, close jobs when done
Or a semaphore (buffered channel of size N) / errgroup.SetLimit(N)
Choose N from the dependency's limits; propagate ctx for cancellation; decide fail-fast vs collect-errors
wrong: Goroutines are cheap so start one per item
follow: admin-feature splits user IDs into batches with lo.Chunk: how does that bound concurrency?
How do you keep results in input order?
cards.answer: The goroutines are cheap but the dependency isn't: 10,000 parallel calls will trip rate limits or exhaust connections. So I bound it: a fixed number of workers pulling from a jobs channel, or simply errgroup with SetLimit, or a buffered channel used as a semaphore. N comes from the dependency's limits. admin-feature does a variant: it chunks the users into batches and runs one goroutine per batch, which bounds concurrency by the number of batches.

cards.q: Explain fan-out / fan-in and a pipeline of stages connected by channels. How do you shut a pipeline down?
cards.k: fan-out = many readers on one channel · fan-in = merge into one · each stage owns + closes its output · downstream ranges until closed · shared done / ctx so upstream stops, else leaks
keys: Fan-out: several goroutines read from one channel to parallelise a stage; fan-in: merge several channels into one
Each stage owns its output channel and closes it when its input is exhausted (only the sender closes)
Downstream ranges over the channel until it's closed
Early exit: a shared done/ctx so upstream stages stop sending when downstream quits, else they leak
wrong: Receivers should close channels
follow: How do you know when to close a merged output channel (WaitGroup over the senders)?
When is a pipeline over-engineering compared with errgroup?
cards.answer: A pipeline is stages connected by channels. Fan-out means several goroutines read from the same input channel; fan-in merges several outputs into one, closing the merged channel after a WaitGroup sees every sender finish. The rule that keeps it sane: the stage that sends on a channel is the one that closes it. And every stage selects on a done context while sending, so if the consumer stops early, upstream stops too instead of leaking.

cards.q: When is context.WithValue appropriate, and why does lib/auth use `type clientIPKey struct{}` as the key?
cards.k: request-scoped only: request ID, trace ID, caller identity / IP · never options or deps · unexported key type (type clientIPKey struct{}) → no collisions · typed getters because values are any
keys: Only for request-scoped data that crosses API boundaries: request IDs, trace IDs, the caller's identity/IP; not for optional parameters or dependencies
Keys must be unexported custom types to avoid collisions between packages (a string key 'ip' could clash)
A struct{} key type is zero-size and unique to the package; expose typed getters/setters (WithClientIP / ClientIP)
Values are untyped (any): wrap access in functions that type-assert safely
wrong: Put the database connection in the context
follow: Why does ClientIP use the two-value type assertion?
Should the user ID travel in ctx or as a parameter here? Why does this repo pass userID explicitly?
cards.answer: Context values are for data that belongs to the request and has to cross layers without every signature changing, like a request ID or the client's IP for audit logs. They're not for dependencies or optional arguments, because they're invisible in signatures. Keys should be an unexported type, so no other package can collide with yours; lib/auth uses an empty struct type and exposes WithClientIP and ClientIP, which does a safe type assertion. Important inputs like the user ID are passed explicitly in this repo.

cards.q: tus-feature's hook does `context.WithTimeout(context.WithoutCancel(req.Event.Context), hookTimeout)`. Why both?
cards.k: WithoutCancel keeps values, drops cancellation → hook finishes if the client leaves · WithTimeout adds its own bound · for must-finish work · risk: outliving shutdown, the timeout guards it
keys: WithoutCancel keeps the parent's values but detaches from its cancellation: if the upload's request context ends, the hook still finishes
WithTimeout then adds its own bound so the detached work can't hang forever
Use case: work that must complete once started (recording that an upload finished) even if the client disconnects
Risk: detached work outliving shutdown; the explicit timeout is the guard
wrong: WithoutCancel removes the values too
It's the same as context.Background()
follow: What would happen to the post-finish hook if the client disconnected right after the last byte and the ctx were not detached?
Where else would you want WithoutCancel (e.g. audit logs, async side effects)?
cards.answer: The hook runs on behalf of an upload request, and that request's context is cancelled the moment the client goes away. Some hook work must finish anyway, like marking the attachment uploaded after the final byte arrived. WithoutCancel keeps the parent's values but ignores its cancellation, and WithTimeout puts a fresh 30-second bound on it so it can't run forever. Unlike context.Background, you keep the trace and request values.

cards.q: Walk through tus-feature's main: how does the server shut down gracefully on SIGTERM?
cards.k: NotifyContext(SIGINT, SIGTERM) → <-ctx.Done() → server.Shutdown(30 s ctx) → stop accepting, close idle, wait in-flight · ErrServerClosed is expected · main waits on shutdown channel · RegisterOnShutdown cancels BaseContext
keys: signal.NotifyContext(ctx, SIGINT, SIGTERM) gives a ctx cancelled when the signal arrives
A goroutine waits on <-ctx.Done(), then calls server.Shutdown with a 30-second timeout context
Shutdown stops accepting new connections, closes idle ones, and waits for in-flight requests (up to the timeout)
ListenAndServe returns http.ErrServerClosed (expected, not an error); main waits on the `shutdown` channel so it doesn't exit before Shutdown finishes
RegisterOnShutdown cancels the server's BaseContext (WithCancelCause), so long uploads learn they must stop
wrong: Calling os.Exit on SIGTERM is graceful enough
Shutdown kills active requests immediately
follow: Why can't main just return after ListenAndServe returns?
What does the load balancer need to do during a deploy for this to be lossless (deregistration delay)?
Why is a 30-second timeout needed at all?
cards.answer: NotifyContext turns SIGTERM into a cancelled context.
