cards.answer: Memory on one server only works with one server; with several, a user's next request may land elsewhere, and sticky sessions just move the problem to deploys and uneven load. A shared store like Redis gives every instance the same view, per-session TTLs and instant revocation. Stateless JWTs avoid the store entirely but you can't revoke an issued access token, which is why my Go service relies on short-lived tokens and Cognito refresh tokens.

cards.q: Redis Pub/Sub versus Redis Streams versus a real message broker: when is each appropriate?
cards.k: Pub/Sub = fire-and-forget to connected subscribers, offline miss it · Streams = log + consumer groups + acks, at-least-once · Kafka / SQS / RabbitMQ = durable, retention, DLQ, tooling · Pub/Sub for invalidation, presence
keys: Pub/Sub: fire-and-forget fan-out to connected subscribers; offline subscribers miss messages; no persistence
Streams: an append-only log with IDs, consumer groups, acknowledgements and pending lists: at-least-once
Brokers (Kafka, SQS, RabbitMQ): durability, retention, DLQs, scaling and operational tooling
Pub/Sub fits ephemeral signals (cache invalidation broadcasts, live presence)
wrong: Pub/Sub guarantees delivery
follow: How would you broadcast cache invalidations to 20 app instances?
Why didn't my Go service use Redis for notifications delivery?
cards.answer: Pub/Sub pushes a message to whoever is subscribed right now; anyone offline misses it, so it suits signals like 'invalidate this key' or live presence. Streams keep messages in a log with consumer groups and acks, so you get at-least-once processing. For business-critical messaging you usually want a managed broker with retention, retries and dead-letter queues, which is why my Go service uses EventBridge and SQS instead.

cards.q: What is a JWT, how is it verified, and what are the classic JWT mistakes?
cards.k: header.payload.signature, base64url · payload readable: signed, not encrypted · verify sig (RS256 via JWKS) → exp / nbf → iss → aud · mistakes: alg none, skip aud/iss, long expiry, PII inside, localStorage · can't revoke
keys: header.payload.signature, base64url; payload claims (sub, exp, iss, aud, iat, custom) are readable by anyone: signed, not encrypted
Verify: signature with the issuer's key (RS256 public key from JWKS), then exp/nbf, iss and aud
Mistakes: accepting alg=none / algorithm confusion, not checking aud/iss, long expiry, putting secrets/PII in the payload, storing in localStorage
Statelessness means the server can't revoke an issued token before exp
wrong: JWTs are encrypted so the payload is private
follow: Why does Cognito sign with RS256 (asymmetric) rather than HS256?
How would a service verify tokens without calling Cognito on every request (JWKS caching)?
cards.answer: A JWT is three base64url parts: a header, a payload of claims, and a signature over both. Anyone can decode the payload, so it's signed, not secret. Verifying means checking the signature with the issuer's public key, usually fetched from its JWKS endpoint and cached, then expiry, issuer and audience. The classic mistakes are accepting alg none, skipping the audience check, long-lived tokens and putting sensitive data in the claims. Because nothing is stored server-side, you can't take a token back before it expires.

cards.q: Server-side sessions versus JWT access tokens with refresh tokens: trade-offs, and how do you log a user out?
cards.k: session = opaque id + server state, easy revoke, needs store · JWT = self-contained, no store, no revoke before exp · short access + long revocable rotating refresh · logout = revoke refresh, access lives till exp
keys: Sessions: an opaque id → server-side state; easy revocation and logout; needs a shared store and a lookup per request
JWT: self-contained, verified locally, scales without a store; can't be revoked before exp
So: short-lived access tokens (minutes–1h) + long-lived refresh tokens that can be revoked and rotated
Logout: revoke the refresh token; existing access tokens stay valid until expiry (my Go service's idp comment says exactly this)
wrong: Deleting the JWT on the client invalidates it
follow: When would you need a token denylist, and what does it cost you?
What does refresh-token rotation detect?
cards.answer: A session is a random id pointing at server-side state, so logging out is just deleting it, at the cost of a store lookup on every request. A JWT is verified on its own, so it scales without a store but can't be revoked before it expires. The standard compromise is short-lived access tokens plus a refresh token you can revoke. That's how logout works here: RevokeToken kills the refresh token, and as the code comment says, access tokens already issued stay valid until they expire.

cards.q: Session cookies versus bearer tokens in an Authorization header: how do they travel and what attacks does each invite?
cards.k: cookies sent automatically → CSRF unless SameSite / token · HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite → XSS can't read · bearer added by code → no CSRF, but localStorage → XSS steals · mobile bearer, browser HttpOnly cookie
keys: Cookies are sent automatically by the browser to their domain: convenient, but invite CSRF unless SameSite / CSRF tokens are used
HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookies keep tokens away from JavaScript (XSS can't read them)
Bearer tokens in headers are added by code: no CSRF by default, but if stored in localStorage XSS can steal them
Mobile apps typically use bearer tokens; browser apps often prefer HttpOnly cookies
wrong: Tokens are always more secure than cookies
HttpOnly prevents CSRF
follow: Which does this backend use, and why does that suit a mobile app?
How would you add a web portal to the same backend safely?
cards.answer: The browser attaches cookies automatically, which is convenient but means another site can trigger requests that carry them, so you need SameSite or CSRF tokens. Marking them HttpOnly and Secure keeps scripts from reading them. A bearer token in the Authorization header is only sent when your code adds it, so CSRF isn't a problem, but wherever the code can read it, an XSS bug can too. This backend uses Cognito JWTs as bearer tokens, which fits a mobile client.

cards.q: Explain OAuth2's authorization code flow with PKCE. When would you use client credentials instead?
cards.k: owner · client · auth server · resource server · redirect → login + consent → short code → exchange at token endpoint · PKCE: hash of verifier first, verifier at exchange → stolen code useless · client credentials = M2M
keys: Roles: resource owner (user), client (app), authorization server, resource server (API)
Auth code: app redirects to the auth server, user logs in and consents, app gets a short-lived code, exchanges it at the token endpoint for tokens
PKCE: the app sends a hash of a random code_verifier first and the verifier at exchange, so a stolen code is useless (required for mobile/SPA public clients)
Client credentials: machine-to-machine, no user (e.g. the analyzer authenticating to the data platform)
Implicit flow and password grant are deprecated
wrong: OAuth2 is an authentication protocol by itself
follow: Where does the analyzer get a token for the data platform, and which flow is that?
Why can't a mobile app keep a client secret?
cards.answer: The app sends the user to the authorization server, the user signs in there, and the app receives a short-lived code that it exchanges for tokens. PKCE protects public clients like mobile apps and SPAs: the app first sends a hash of a random secret and later proves it knows the secret, so an intercepted code can't be redeemed. With no user involved, like one service calling another, you use client credentials; the analyzer reads a client id and secret from Secrets Manager to get its data-platform token that way.

cards.q: How is OpenID Connect different from OAuth2?
cards.k: OAuth2 = delegated authorisation · OIDC adds authentication: ID token (sub, email, iss, aud, nonce), userinfo, discovery + JWKS · access token → API, ID token → client only · Cognito is an OIDC provider
keys: OAuth2 is delegated authorisation (access to an API); OIDC adds authentication on top
OIDC adds the ID token (a JWT about the user: sub, email, iss, aud, nonce), the userinfo endpoint and discovery (.well-known/openid-configuration, JWKS)
Access tokens are for APIs; ID tokens are for the client to know who logged in; don't send ID tokens to APIs as access tokens
Cognito is an OIDC provider; the API Gateway authorizer validates against its issuer
wrong: OIDC is a replacement for OAuth2 unrelated to it
follow: What is the nonce in an ID token for?
Which token should the mobile app send to API Gateway here, and why?
cards.answer: OAuth2 only answers 'may this app call that API on the user's behalf'. OpenID Connect layers identity on top: an ID token describing who logged in, a userinfo endpoint and a discovery document with the provider's keys. The ID token is for the client; APIs should receive access tokens. Cognito is an OIDC provider, and the JWT authorizer is configured with its issuer and the app client as the audience.

cards.q: How should passwords be stored, and why not with SHA-256?
cards.k: never plaintext / reversible · slow salted hash: bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2id · SHA-256 too fast, GPUs billions/s · salt beats rainbow tables, pepper if DB leaks · best: identity provider (Cognito)
keys: Never store plaintext or reversible encryption for verification; store a slow, salted hash: bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2id
SHA-256 is fast: GPUs try billions per second; slowness and memory-hardness make brute force expensive
A unique salt per password defeats rainbow tables; a pepper (server-side secret) adds defence if the DB leaks
Better still: delegate to an identity provider (my Go service uses Cognito, so the app never stores passwords)
wrong: Hash with MD5 plus a salt and you're fine
follow: auth-feature encrypts the pending password with AES-GCM until the OTP is verified: why encryption here and not hashing?
Why is the OTP stored as an HMAC with a pepper instead of plaintext?
cards.answer: You store a deliberately slow, salted hash like bcrypt or Argon2id, never plaintext. Fast hashes like SHA-256 let an attacker with the database try billions of guesses a second; a slow, memory-hard function makes that expensive, and a per-user salt kills precomputed tables. Here the app delegates passwords to Cognito. The one place it holds a password is between sign-up and OTP verification, where it must be recovered to create the Cognito user, so it's encrypted with AES-GCM rather than hashed, and the OTP itself is stored only as a peppered HMAC.

cards.q: Design an email OTP verification flow that resists brute force and abuse.
cards.k: CSPRNG 6 digits, minutes, single use · store HMAC hash with pepper · limit attempts per code / account, rate-limit sends per email + IP, resend cooldown · constant-time compare · generic responses, no enumeration
keys: Random 6-digit code from a CSPRNG, short expiry (minutes), single use
Store only a hash (HMAC with a server-side pepper) so a DB leak doesn't reveal live codes
Limit attempts per code / per account, rate-limit sends per email and per IP, cooldown between resends
Compare in constant time; generic responses so attackers can't enumerate accounts
wrong: A 6-digit code is safe because guessing is hard
follow: With 6 digits and 5 attempts per code, what's an attacker's chance per code?
How does auth-feature's guard combine email and IP limits?
cards.answer: Generate the code with a cryptographic random source, give it a short expiry and make it single-use. Store only a keyed hash so a leaked table is useless. The real defence is limits: a few attempts per code, a cap on sends per email and per IP, and a cooldown before resending, and the responses shouldn't reveal whether an account exists. auth-feature does this: OTPs are peppered HMACs and the guard checks sliding-window limits per email and IP.

cards.q: What is an HMAC, how does my Go service use it for uploads, and why compare signatures with hmac.Equal?
cards.k: keyed hash: proves sender has the secret + no tampering · attachment-feature signs kind, size, type, expiry → hook-feature recomputes + verifies · hmac.Equal constant-time, == leaks via timing · expiry inside the signed data
keys: HMAC = a keyed hash: proves the message was produced by someone with the secret and wasn't altered
attachment-feature signs the upload metadata (kind, size, type, expiry) with a shared secret; hook-feature recomputes and verifies before accepting the upload
hmac.Equal is constant-time: a byte-by-byte == leaks how many leading bytes matched through timing
Include an expiry in the signed data so a signature can't be replayed forever
wrong: Base64-encoding the metadata is enough to stop tampering
follow: What could a client do if the size limit weren't inside the signed data?
HMAC vs digital signature (RSA/ECDSA): when do you need the asymmetric one?
cards.answer: An HMAC is a hash computed with a secret key, so only someone with the key can produce a valid one, and any change to the message breaks it. attachment-feature signs the upload's metadata, including size, type and an expiry, and the tusd pre-create hook recomputes the HMAC and rejects the upload if it doesn't match, so a client can't raise its own size limit. The comparison uses hmac.Equal because a normal comparison returns early, and that timing difference can let an attacker guess the signature byte by byte.

cards.q: Authentication versus authorisation: where does each happen in my Go service?
cards.k: AuthN = who you are, AuthZ = what you may do · Cognito JWT → API Gateway authorizer checks sig, iss, aud, exp before Lambda · Lambda scopes by sub (owner) · admin: groups → actions via auth.Can · server-side, every request
keys: Authentication = who you are (verify credentials / token); authorisation = what you may do
AuthN: Cognito issues JWTs; API Gateway's JWT authorizer verifies signature, issuer, audience, expiry before the Lambda runs
AuthZ: the Lambda takes the user from the `sub` claim and scopes data by it (owner checks); admin routes map Cognito groups → actions with auth.Can
Both must be enforced server-side on every request
wrong: If the token is valid, the request is authorised
follow: Where would an IDOR bug live in this architecture?
Why check permissions in the Lambda even though the gateway verified the token?
cards.answer: Authentication establishes identity; authorisation decides what that identity may do. Here Cognito issues the JWT and API Gateway's JWT authorizer verifies it before any code runs, so authentication is done at the edge. Authorisation happens in Go: the handler takes the user id only from the verified sub claim and every query is scoped to it, and admin endpoints check the user's Cognito groups against an action with auth.Can. A valid token alone proves nothing about whether you may touch a given submission.

cards.q: RBAC versus ABAC: which does my Go service's admin side use, and where would RBAC alone not be enough?
cards.k: RBAC = roles → permissions (Cognito groups → permissions.go) · ABAC = user / resource / context attributes · 'only assigned submissions', 'only my project' need ABAC · one place, default deny, tested
keys: RBAC: permissions attached to roles, users get roles (Cognito groups → actions in permissions.go)
ABAC: decisions use attributes of user, resource and context (owner, region, project, time)
RBAC alone can't express 'a QC may only analyse submissions assigned to them' or 'reporters see only their project': that needs resource attributes
Keep authorisation checks in one place, default deny, test them
wrong: Checking the role in the frontend is enough
follow: How would you add 'QC can only decide their own assigned submissions' to this design?
Why is default-deny the safe default?
cards.answer: RBAC gives permissions to roles and roles to users; here Cognito groups like admins, qc-leaders and reporters map to allowed actions, and handlers call auth.Can. ABAC decides from attributes of the user, the resource and the context, which you need as soon as a rule says 'only the submissions assigned to you'. You'd keep the group check and add an ownership or assignment check against the resource in the service, defaulting to deny.

cards.q: How do SQL injection and XSS happen, and how do you prevent them?
cards.k: SQLi = input concatenated into query → parameterised queries, least-privilege DB user · NoSQL injection too, DynamoDB expression values = parameters · XSS = input rendered as HTML / JS → encode output, CSP, HttpOnly
keys: SQL injection: user input concatenated into a query string; prevent with parameterised queries / prepared statements, least-privilege DB users
NoSQL injection exists too (operator objects in Mongo filters); DynamoDB's expression attribute values play the role of parameters
XSS: untrusted input rendered as HTML/JS; prevent with output encoding (React escapes by default; beware dangerouslySetInnerHTML), Content-Security-Policy, HttpOnly cookies
Validate input, but encoding/parameterisation is the actual defence
wrong: Escaping quotes manually is enough to stop SQL injection
follow: Find the equivalent of a parameterised query in the submission repository's UpdateExpression.
As a React developer, where could XSS still creep in?
cards.answer: SQL injection happens when input is glued into a query string, so input like ' OR 1=1 -- changes the query itself; parameterised queries keep data and code separate, which is the fix. DynamoDB's ExpressionAttributeValues serve the same purpose. XSS is the same mistake in HTML: untrusted data rendered as markup or script. React escapes text by default, so the risks are dangerouslySetInnerHTML, unsafe URLs and third-party HTML; a Content-Security-Policy adds a second layer.

cards.q: What are CSRF and SSRF, and how do you defend against each?
cards.k: CSRF = other site uses victim's cookies → SameSite, CSRF token, check Origin, bearer immune · SSRF = server fetches attacker URL (169.254.169.254) → allow-list, block private ranges after DNS, IMDSv2 · webhooks, avatar-by-URL
keys: CSRF: another site makes the victim's browser send an authenticated request (cookies attach automatically); defend with SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens, checking Origin; bearer tokens in headers are immune
SSRF: the server is tricked into fetching an attacker-chosen URL (cloud metadata 169.254.169.254, internal services)
SSRF defence: allow-list destinations, block private/link-local ranges after DNS resolution, IMDSv2, no raw redirects
Any feature that fetches user-supplied URLs (avatars by URL, webhooks) is an SSRF risk
wrong: CORS prevents CSRF
follow: Why is a mobile API using bearer tokens not exposed to CSRF?
If you added 'upload avatar from URL', what would you check before fetching?
cards.answer: CSRF abuses the browser: a malicious page submits a request to your site and the browser attaches the user's cookies. SameSite cookies, anti-CSRF tokens and Origin checks stop it, and APIs that use bearer tokens in a header, like this one, aren't exposed because nothing is attached automatically. SSRF abuses your server: it fetches a URL the attacker chose, such as the cloud metadata endpoint. Any 'fetch this URL' feature needs an allow-list and blocking of private IP ranges, checked after DNS resolution.

cards.q: Where should secrets live, and how does my Go service handle them?
cards.k: never in code, images, config, logs · Secrets Manager / SSM / Vault: IAM, rotation, audit · my Go service: template declares shells, values set outside CloudFormation · read once at cold start, keep in memory
keys: Never in code, images, or committed config; not in logs
A secret store (AWS Secrets Manager / SSM Parameter Store / Vault) with IAM-controlled access, rotation, audit
My Go service: secret/template.yaml declares only the secret shells; values are set outside CloudFormation so deploys never overwrite them
Read once at cold start and keep in memory (analyzer reads its data-platform credentials; auth-feature its keys)
wrong: Environment variables in the CloudFormation template are a fine place for API keys
follow: Why would adding SecretString to the template be dangerous here?
How would you rotate the CDN signing key without downtime?
cards.answer: Secrets belong in a managed store like Secrets Manager, where IAM controls who can read them, access is audited and rotation is possible, never in code, images or committed config. My Go service's secret template only declares empty secret shells; the values are put in from the console, so a redeploy can never overwrite or leak them. Services read their secrets once at cold start, like the analyzer reading its data-platform credentials.

cards.q: Encryption at rest versus in transit, symmetric versus asymmetric, and what envelope encryption with KMS is.
cards.k: in transit = TLS · at rest = disk / DB / S3 · symmetric AES-GCM fast · asymmetric for key exchange + signatures · envelope: data key encrypts data, KMS master key encrypts data key, rotate cheaply · unique nonce per GCM call
keys: In transit: TLS between clients and services (and service-to-service); at rest: disk/database/S3 encryption
Symmetric (AES-GCM): fast, same key both ways; asymmetric (RSA/ECC): key exchange, signatures
Envelope encryption: data encrypted with a data key; the data key encrypted by a KMS master key that never leaves KMS; rotate master keys without re-encrypting data
AES-GCM needs a unique nonce per encryption (auth-feature uses a random nonce each time) and authenticates the ciphertext
wrong: Encrypting at rest protects you from an application-level SQL injection
follow: What happens if a GCM nonce is ever reused with the same key?
Who can decrypt data encrypted with a KMS key (IAM + key policy)?
cards.answer: In transit means TLS on every hop; at rest means the stored bytes are encrypted, which protects stolen disks and snapshots but not an application that's tricked into reading data. Symmetric ciphers like AES-GCM do the bulk work; asymmetric keys handle key exchange and signatures. With envelope encryption, each piece of data gets its own data key, and only that small key is encrypted by a KMS master key that never leaves KMS. GCM also requires a fresh nonce every time, which is why auth-feature generates a random one per encryption.

cards.q: What must never appear in logs, and how do you keep it out?
cards.k: never: passwords, JWTs, refresh tokens, API keys, OTPs, card numbers · minimise PII · log ids + outcomes + error class · redact in the logging layer · structured slog key/values
keys: Passwords, tokens (JWTs, refresh tokens, API keys), OTPs, secrets, full card numbers; minimise PII (emails, phones, IPs) per policy
Log ids and outcomes instead (userId, submissionId, error class); redact at the logging layer
Structured logging makes it easy to see what each field contains and to filter
My Go service's rule: no secrets, tokens or PII in logs; slog with explicit key/values
wrong: Logging the full request body helps debugging, so it's worth it
follow: auth-feature has a WithExposedOTP option: what is that for, and why must it never be on in production?
How would you retroactively deal with a token that was logged?
cards.answer: Credentials of any kind, passwords, OTPs, tokens, API keys, never go into logs, and personal data is kept to what's needed. Log identifiers and outcomes, user id, submission id, error, not request bodies. Structured logging with explicit fields, like slog here, makes it obvious what's being written. auth-feature has an option to expose the OTP for test environments, exactly the kind of switch that must be impossible to enable in production.

cards.q: What does least privilege mean on AWS, and how is it applied to my Go service's Lambdas?
cards.k: only needed actions on needed resources, no dynamodb:* on * · one role per Lambda, exact actions + table / index ARNs · limits blast radius · import ARNs, resource policies close the other side
keys: Each workload gets only the actions on the resources it needs; no wildcards like dynamodb:* on *
One IAM execution role per Lambda; policies list exact actions (GetItem, PutItem, UpdateItem, Query) and exact table / index ARNs
Limits the blast radius of a bug or a compromised function
Cross-stack ARNs are imported, not hard-coded; resource policies (Lambda permissions, S3 bucket policies) close the other side
wrong: Admin access during development is fine if you remember to remove it
follow: Why does the submission Lambda only get PutItem on the guard table, not GetItem?
What's the difference between an IAM role policy and a resource policy?
cards.answer: Every function gets a role with only the actions on the exact resources it needs. In my Go service each Lambda has its own execution role; the submission function, for example, can GetItem, PutItem, UpdateItem and Query on its table and named indexes, but only PutItem on the guard table, because that's all it does there. If that function had a bug or were compromised, the damage would stay inside those permissions.

cards.q: How do VPCs, security groups and private subnets protect a backend? Where does my Go service use them?
cards.k: DBs + internal services in private subnets · security groups = stateful allow-lists (LB → app 8080 → DB 5432), NACLs stateless · VPC endpoints to S3 / DynamoDB · my Go service: analyzer on EC2 in data-platform VPC, tusd behind ALB
keys: Put databases and internal services in private subnets with no inbound internet route
Security groups are stateful allow-lists between components (LB → app on 8080, app → DB on 5432); NACLs are stateless subnet filters
VPC endpoints let private resources reach AWS services (S3, DynamoDB) without the internet
My Go service: a shared VPC; the analyzer runs on EC2 inside the data-platform VPC; tusd runs on EC2 behind an ALB
wrong: Being in a VPC makes a service secure by itself
follow: Why is a DynamoDB/S3 VPC endpoint both a security and a cost win?
What does tusd's security group need to allow, and from where?
cards.answer: Network boundaries limit who can even reach a component: databases and internal services sit in private subnets with no inbound route from the internet, and security groups allow only the specific hops you need, like load balancer to app and app to database. VPC endpoints let private machines talk to S3 or DynamoDB without going through the internet. Here tusd sits behind an ALB and the analyzer runs on EC2 inside the data-platform VPC.

cards.q: Name the API vulnerabilities you check for first (OWASP API Top 10 style) in an endpoint review.
cards.k: IDOR: change an id, see someone else's? · broken auth · excessive data exposure · mass assignment · missing rate / size / page limits · injection · misconfig: verbose errors, open CORS, no TLS
keys: Broken object-level authorisation (IDOR): can I access another user's object by changing an id?
Broken authentication; excessive data exposure (returning internal fields); mass assignment (client sets fields it shouldn't)
Missing rate limiting / resource limits (payload size, page size); injection (SQL, NoSQL, command)
Security misconfiguration: verbose errors, permissive CORS, missing TLS
wrong: Authentication alone prevents IDOR
follow: How does `json:"-"` on entity fields relate to excessive data exposure?
How would mass assignment happen if a handler decoded the body straight into the stored entity?
cards.answer: First, object-level authorisation: change the id in the URL and see if you get someone else's data. Then authentication flaws, responses that expose internal fields, and mass assignment, where the client sets fields like status or credit amount that only the server should set. Then limits: rate limits, page sizes, upload sizes. Then injection and misconfiguration. This repo defends against exposure and mass assignment by decoding into request DTOs and hiding internal fields with json:"-".

cards.q: Why put a queue or event bus between services? What do you gain and what does it cost?
cards.k: decouple: producer doesn't know consumers · buffer spikes, slow work off the request, retries without the user · costs: eventual consistency, duplicates, reordering, harder tracing · submission → ledger, notification, referral
keys: Decoupling: producers don't know consumers; new consumers subscribe without changing the producer
Absorbs spikes (buffering), lets slow work happen outside the request, and retries failures without the user waiting
Costs: eventual consistency, duplicates and reordering, harder debugging/tracing, more infrastructure
My Go service: a submission write fans out to ledger, notification and referral via EventBridge without the submission service knowing them
wrong: Async makes the system faster for the user in every case
follow: When would you keep a call synchronous even though a queue is available?
How does a user learn the result of async work in this app?
cards.answer: A queue or bus lets the producer hand off work and move on: consumers can be added without touching it, spikes are buffered, and failures are retried without a user waiting. The price is that everything downstream is eventually consistent, messages can arrive twice or out of order, and a request's story is spread across services, so tracing matters. In my Go service the submission write becomes an event that the ledger, notifications and referrals each consume independently.

cards.q: At-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once: what do they mean, and what do real systems give you?
cards.k: at-most-once = ack before work, crash loses · at-least-once = ack after, crash → duplicates (SQS, EventBridge, Streams, Kafka) · exactly-once delivery isn't real → exactly-once effects = at-least-once + idempotent consumer
keys: At-most-once: ack before processing; a crash loses the message
At-least-once: ack after processing; a crash means redelivery → duplicates (SQS, EventBridge, DynamoDB Streams, Kafka by default)

Exactly-once delivery isn't achievable end to end in general; you get exactly-once *effects* with at-least-once + idempotent consumers (or transactional processing inside one system, e.g. Kafka transactions)
Design every consumer to tolerate duplicates
wrong: SQS FIFO means exactly-once processing
follow: Where exactly can a duplicate push notification happen in my Go service's sender?
What does Kafka's 'exactly-once semantics' actually cover?
cards.answer: At-most-once acknowledges before working, so a crash loses the message. At-least-once acknowledges after, so a crash means it's delivered again, which is what SQS, EventBridge, DynamoDB Streams and Kafka give you by default. True exactly-once delivery across systems doesn't exist; what you build is exactly-once effect: at-least-once delivery plus consumers that make a repeat harmless. FIFO dedup only covers a five-minute window on send, not your processing.

cards.q: Explain Kafka's model: topics, partitions, offsets, consumer groups. How is it different from SQS?
cards.k: topic → partitions = append-only logs, offsets · retention by time / size, not consumption · key → partition → order · group: one consumer per partition, parallelism ≤ partitions, commit offsets · many groups + replay vs SQS
keys: A topic is split into partitions: append-only logs; each record has an offset; retention by time/size, not by consumption
Producers choose a partition by key (same key → same partition → ordered)
A consumer group shares partitions: each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group; parallelism ≤ partition count; consumers commit offsets
Many groups can read the same data independently and replay from old offsets; SQS deletes on ack and has no replay
wrong: Adding consumers beyond the partition count increases throughput
Kafka deletes messages when they are consumed
follow: What happens during a consumer group rebalance?
When would you pick Kafka over SQS + EventBridge for my Go service?
cards.answer: A Kafka topic is a set of partitions, each an append-only log where records keep an offset and stay for the retention period whether or not anyone read them. Producers pick the partition by key, which is what gives per-key order. A consumer group divides the partitions among its members, one consumer per partition, so you can't usefully have more consumers than partitions, and each group tracks its own offsets. That's the big difference from SQS: many independent readers and the ability to replay history, versus a queue that deletes on acknowledgement.

cards.q: How does Kafka avoid losing messages? Explain replication, acks and ISR.
cards.k: leader + followers, in-sync = ISR · acks=all + min.insync.replicas=2 · unclean.leader.election=false · enable.idempotence stops producer duplicates · commit offsets after processing
keys: Each partition has a leader and followers (replication factor, e.g. 3); followers in sync form the ISR
Producer acks=all + min.insync.replicas=2: a write is acknowledged only when enough replicas have it
unclean.leader.election=false: don't promote an out-of-sync replica (avoids losing acknowledged data)
Producer idempotence (enable.idempotence) prevents duplicates from producer retries; consumers commit offsets after processing for at-least-once
wrong: acks=1 is safe because the leader wrote it to disk
follow: What's the latency cost of acks=all?
Commit the offset before or after processing: what does each give you?
cards.answer: Each partition is replicated, typically three times; one replica leads and the in-sync followers form the ISR. With acks=all and min.insync.replicas of 2, the producer only gets a success once at least two replicas have the record, so losing one broker loses nothing. Disabling unclean leader election stops a lagging replica from taking over and silently dropping acknowledged records. On the producer, idempotence stops retries from writing duplicates; on the consumer, committing offsets after processing gives at-least-once.

cards.q: Kafka versus RabbitMQ (or SQS): how do you choose?
cards.k: Kafka = log: throughput, retention, replay, many groups, per-partition order, heavy ops · RabbitMQ = routing, per-message acks, priorities, delays · SQS = managed, simple, no replay · streaming → Kafka, tasks → Rabbit / SQS
keys: Kafka: a distributed log; high throughput, retention and replay, many consumer groups, per-partition order; operationally heavier
RabbitMQ: a broker with exchanges and routing, per-message acks, priorities, delays; messages removed when acked
SQS: fully managed queue; simple, scales automatically, no replay, FIFO with limits
Event streaming / analytics / replay → Kafka; task queues and routing → RabbitMQ / SQS
wrong: They are interchangeable
follow: Which would you use for a payment event stream that analytics also needs to replay?
Which for a simple background email queue?
cards.answer: Kafka is a replicated log: huge throughput, data kept for days, any number of consumer groups that can replay, and order per partition, but it's more to run. RabbitMQ is a classic broker: flexible routing through exchanges, acknowledgement per message, priorities and delayed delivery, and messages disappear once handled. SQS is the managed, no-operations queue. I'd use Kafka when several systems need the same stream or replay, and a queue for plain background tasks.

cards.q: How does EventBridge routing work, and why would a team choose it over direct SQS queues per consumer?
cards.k: PutEvents (source, detail-type, detail) → rules match → targets · consumers own their rule, producer unchanged · retries per target + DLQ · at-least-once, unordered · check FailedEntryCount on partial failure
keys: Producers PutEvents to a bus with source + detail-type + detail; rules match patterns and send to targets
Each consumer owns its rule and target; the producer is unchanged when consumers are added
Built-in retries per target and DLQs; but delivery is at-least-once and order isn't guaranteed
PutEvents can partially fail: check FailedEntryCount (my Go service's Publisher does)
wrong: EventBridge preserves ordering
follow: Which detail-types does the ledger's rule subscribe to?
Why does the Publisher treat FailedEntryCount > 0 as an error?
cards.answer: Producers put events on a bus, each with a source, a detail-type and a JSON detail, and every consumer defines a rule that matches the events it cares about and routes them to its target. Adding a consumer is a new rule, with no change to the producer. Delivery is at least once and unordered, with retries and a DLQ per target. PutEvents can succeed overall while individual entries fail, which is why my Go service's Publisher checks FailedEntryCount.

cards.q: How do you make a consumer idempotent? Show how my Go service's ledger does it.
cards.k: stable key from the business fact (submissionId + action) · record key atomically with the effect · ledger: TRANSACTION#key + attribute_not_exists in the same TransactWriteItems as balance · set is safe, increment isn't
keys: Every message carries a stable idempotency key derived from the business fact (submissionId + action), not a random per-send id
The consumer records the key atomically with its side effect (unique constraint / conditional write); a repeat finds it and becomes a no-op
Ledger: transaction item keyed TRANSACTION#<idemKey> with attribute_not_exists(PK) in the same TransactWriteItems as the balance update; on conflict it returns the existing transaction
Natural idempotency: set status = 'pushed' is safe to repeat; increment is not
wrong: Keep a list of processed ids in memory
Check whether it was processed, then process (two steps)
follow: Why is the key derived from submissionId and the action rather than a UUID generated at publish time?
Which side effects can't be made idempotent (sending an email), and what do you do then?
cards.answer: The message needs a key that identifies the business fact, like 'submission X approved', so every redelivery has the same key. The consumer writes that key in the same atomic step as its effect, so the second delivery hits the uniqueness check and does nothing. That's exactly the ledger: the transaction row is keyed by the event's idempotency key with attribute_not_exists, inside the same DynamoDB transaction as the balance update, and a replay just returns the stored transaction.

cards.q: What is a dead-letter queue, when should a message go there, and what do you do with it?
cards.k: after maxReceiveCount or poison message · stops one bad message blocking / burning retries · alarm on depth > 0, long retention, redrive after fix · transient → retry, permanent → drop / DLQ now
keys: A side queue for messages that failed processing N times (maxReceiveCount) or are poison (malformed, invalid)
Prevents one bad message from blocking or burning retries forever
Needs an alarm (depth > 0), retention long enough to investigate, and a redrive process after the fix
Distinguish: transient errors → retry; permanent/invalid → drop with a log or DLQ immediately
wrong: A DLQ means messages are safely handled
follow: My Go service's notification queue: what's maxReceiveCount, retention and the alarm?
Why does the ledger consumer return nil on a malformed event instead of an error?
cards.answer: A dead-letter queue is where messages go after failing a set number of times, so one poison message can't retry forever or block the rest. It's only useful with an alarm and someone who looks: the notification queue here moves a message to its DLQ after five receives, keeps it for 14 days and alarms as soon as anything is in it, so you can fix the bug and redrive. Messages that can never succeed, like malformed events, shouldn't even retry; the ledger consumer logs and drops them.

cards.q: How should retries be configured across a pipeline: EventBridge → Lambda → SQS → Lambda? Where can retries multiply?
cards.k: each hop retries: EventBridge (185 / 24 h) + DLQ, async Lambda, SQS maxReceiveCount · layers multiply → retry storm · exponential backoff + jitter, cap attempts, max event age, DLQ · every hop idempotent
keys: Each hop has its own retry policy: EventBridge target retries (up to 185 attempts / 24 h here) with a DLQ; async Lambda retries; SQS redelivery up to maxReceiveCount
Retries multiply across layers (retry storms) and amplify load on a struggling dependency
Use exponential backoff with jitter, cap attempts, set maximum event age, send exhausted messages to a DLQ
Make every hop idempotent because each retry layer can create duplicates
wrong: More retries are always safer
follow: If FCM is down for an hour, which layer absorbs it in my Go service?
Why does the notification ingestion Lambda set MaximumEventAgeInSeconds?
cards.answer: Every hop retries on its own: EventBridge retries delivering to the target, here up to 185 times over a day before its DLQ; an asynchronously invoked Lambda retries a couple of times; SQS redelivers until maxReceiveCount. Stack them carelessly and one failure turns into dozens of attempts hammering a dependency that is already down. So each layer gets capped attempts, backoff with jitter, an age limit and a DLQ, and every consumer is idempotent.

cards.q: A Lambda consumer receives a batch of 100 records and one fails. What should happen, and how does my Go service handle it?
cards.k: no partial response → whole batch retried, 99 duplicates, shard blocks · ReportBatchItemFailures: failed ids / first failed sequence number · bisect-on-error, max retries, on-failure destination · relay returns seq + stops
keys: Without partial batch responses, the whole batch is retried, reprocessing 99 successes (duplicates) and possibly blocking the shard
ReportBatchItemFailures: return the failed item ids; for streams return the first failed sequence number so processing resumes from there
Stream mappings also set bisect-on-error, max retry attempts and an on-failure destination so a poison record doesn't block the shard for 24 hours
The relay returns the failed record's sequence number and stops
wrong: Return an error so everything retries; consumers are idempotent anyway
follow: Why must a stream consumer stop at the first failure rather than continue?
What does bisect-batch-on-function-error do?
cards.answer: If the function just errors, the whole batch comes back, so the 99 that worked run again, and on a stream the shard stops moving. With partial batch responses the function reports exactly what failed; for a stream that's the first failed sequence number, and processing resumes from there, keeping order. The relay does that and stops at the first failure. The stats consumer's mapping also bisects failing batches, caps retries and sends what's left to a failure destination, so one poison record can't stall the shard for its full 24-hour retention.

cards.q: How do you get ordering in a messaging system, and why is global ordering usually a bad idea?
cards.k: order per entity only, via partition / group key · SQS FIFO MessageGroupId · Kafka key · Streams per item · global order = one partition = no parallelism · retries break order unless the key stops on failure
keys: Order only where it matters: per entity (per user, per order), via a partition / message group key
SQS FIFO MessageGroupId; Kafka partition key; DynamoDB Streams order per item (shard)
Global order = one partition = no parallelism; per-key order scales by having many keys
Retries can break order unless processing of a key stops on failure (FIFO + partial batch failure semantics)
wrong: Standard SQS preserves order
follow: My Go service groups notifications by userId: what does that guarantee and what not?
What happens to ordering if a consumer processes message 2 while message 1 is being retried?
cards.answer: You ask for ordering per entity, not globally: all messages for one user or one order go to the same partition or message group, so they're processed in order while different keys run in parallel. A global order means one lane and no scaling. The notification queue groups by userId for exactly that. The subtle part is retries: if a consumer carries on with later messages of a group after one fails, the order breaks anyway.

cards.q: A consumer can't keep up and the queue keeps growing. What do you do?
cards.k: measure depth + oldest message age + throughput + errors · scale consumers within partition / downstream limits, batch, fix the slow step · cap concurrency to protect downstream · shed low priority · alert on age
keys: Measure first: queue depth and age of the oldest message, consumer throughput and error rate
Scale consumers (within partition / downstream limits), batch work, optimise the slow step
Protect the downstream dependency: concurrency limits (reserved concurrency), backpressure instead of scaling into it
Shed or defer low-priority work; alert on message age, not only depth
wrong: Increase the consumer count without limit
follow: Why is 'age of oldest message' a better alarm than queue depth?
How does Lambda's maximum concurrency on an SQS mapping protect the database?
cards.answer: First find out why: is it volume, a slow dependency, or errors causing retries? Watch the oldest message's age, because that's what users feel. If the dependency has headroom, scale consumers or batch more; if it doesn't, adding consumers just knocks it over, so you cap concurrency and let the queue absorb the backlog, deferring low-priority work. The queue exists exactly so the producer doesn't have to slow down when this happens.

cards.q: What's the dual-write problem, and how do the outbox pattern and change data capture solve it? Why did my Go service choose CDC?
cards.k: dual write: DB then broker, crash between → lost or phantom event · outbox = event row in same tx + relay · CDC = read the change log (binlog / WAL / Streams) · my Go service: CDC, stage changes + other team's writer emit no events
keys: Dual write: save to the DB and publish to the broker as two steps; a crash between them loses or invents events
Outbox: write the event to an outbox table in the same DB transaction; a relay publishes from it and marks it sent
CDC: read the DB's change log (binlog / WAL / DynamoDB Streams) and turn changes into events; no outbox table
My Go service: the submissions stream is the source, because stage transitions publish no domain events and one writer is another team's service; the stream checkpoint is the delivery record
wrong: Publish first, then write to the DB
follow: What does CDC cost: coupling consumers to the table's shape, and how does the relay limit that?
Why is a third stream consumer a problem here, and what's the fix?
cards.answer: If a service writes to its database and then publishes an event, a crash in between leaves them disagreeing. The outbox pattern writes the event into a table in the same transaction and a relay publishes it afterwards. CDC skips the table and reads the database's own change log. My Go service uses CDC: the submissions table's stream feeds a relay that turns status changes into SubmissionCreated, Approved and so on, which also catches writes made by the analyzer and another team's service that never publish anything. The relay translates rows into domain events, so consumers don't depend on the table layout.

cards.q: What is a saga? Compare orchestration and choreography.
cards.k: long transaction = local tx steps + compensations · choreography: react to events, no coordinator, hard to follow as it grows · orchestration: coordinator (Step Functions, Temporal) · compensation = business undo · idempotent steps
keys: A long business transaction across services as a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action on failure
Choreography: services react to each other's events (no central coordinator); simple at first, hard to follow as steps grow
Orchestration: a coordinator (workflow engine, Step Functions, Temporal) tells each service what to do and handles compensation
Compensations are business undo (refund, release stock), not rollbacks; every step must be idempotent
wrong: A saga gives you ACID across services
follow: Is my Go service's approved → credit → notify chain choreography or orchestration?
What's the compensation if the credit succeeded but a revoke arrives later?
cards.answer: A saga breaks a cross-service transaction into local steps, each committing on its own, and defines a compensating action to undo earlier steps if a later one fails, like releasing stock if payment fails. With choreography each service listens for events and reacts, which is what my Go service does: approval emits an event, the ledger credits, notifications send. With orchestration a coordinator drives the steps and compensations, which is easier to reason about once the flow has many branches.

cards.q: Containers versus virtual machines: what's the difference, and why did containers win for app deployment?
cards.k: VM = guest OS on hypervisor, strong isolation, GBs, slow boot · container = host-kernel processes + namespaces + cgroups, MBs, ms–s start · same image laptop → CI → prod, dense, fast rollback · shared kernel → Firecracker
keys: VM: a full guest OS on a hypervisor; strong isolation; heavy (GBs, slow boot)
Container: processes on the host kernel isolated with namespaces + cgroups; image = app + its userland dependencies; MBs, starts in ms–s
Wins: the same image runs on a laptop, CI and production; dense packing; fast scaling and rollbacks
Weaker isolation than VMs (shared kernel); Fargate / Firecracker run containers inside micro-VMs for that reason
wrong: A container includes its own kernel
follow: Why does Lambda use Firecracker micro-VMs rather than plain containers?
What is 'works on my machine' and how do images fix it?
cards.answer: A VM virtualises hardware and runs a whole operating system per instance, which isolates strongly but is heavy. A container is just a process tree on the host's kernel, fenced off with namespaces and limited with cgroups, and its image carries the app and its libraries. That makes images small and fast to start, and the same image runs everywhere, which is what killed 'works on my machine'. The shared kernel is the trade-off, which is why Lambda and Fargate run workloads in lightweight VMs underneath.

cards.q: Write down what a good production Dockerfile for a Go service looks like, and why.
cards.k: multi-stage: build in golang, ship static binary (CGO_ENABLED=0) on distroless / scratch · go.mod + download before source for cache · non-root, no secrets, pinned base · one process, env config, stdout logs, healthcheck
keys: Multi-stage: build in a golang image, copy only the static binary (CGO_ENABLED=0) into a tiny final image (distroless / scratch / alpine)
Order layers for cache hits: copy go.mod/go.sum and download modules before copying the source
Run as a non-root user; no secrets in the image or build args; pin base image versions
One process per container; config via env; log to stdout/stderr; EXPOSE and a HEALTHCHECK where the platform uses it
wrong: Ship the golang:latest image with the source inside
follow: Why does copying go.mod before the source speed up rebuilds?
My Go service builds `GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 CGO_ENABLED=0`: what does each flag do, and how does that carry over to a container?
cards.answer: Two stages: build the binary in a Go image, then copy only that static binary into a minimal base like distroless, so the final image is a few megabytes with almost nothing to attack. Copy go.mod and go.sum and download modules before copying the code, so dependency layers stay cached. Run as non-root, keep secrets out of the image, pin versions, and log to stdout. It's the same build my Go service already does for Lambda: a static arm64 binary with CGO off.

cards.q: What is a Lambda cold start, what makes it slow, and how do you reduce it?
cards.k: new environment: download code → start runtime → run init (main) · slower: big package, JVM, heavy init, low memory · fix: small Go binary on provided.al2023, light init, more memory, provisioned concurrency · warm reuses init
keys: First invocation on a new execution environment: download code, start the runtime, run init (main: clients, config)
Grows with package size, runtime (JVM slow, Go fast), init work, VPC attachment (much improved), memory size (more CPU)
Reduce: small static binaries (Go provided.al2023), lazy/light init, more memory, provisioned concurrency for latency-critical paths
Warm invocations reuse everything built in init
wrong: Cold starts happen on every request
follow: Why is reading Secrets Manager once at init a good trade-off?
What does provisioned concurrency cost you?
cards.answer: A cold start is AWS creating a new execution environment: fetch the code, start the runtime, run your init code, which for these Go Lambdas is main building the clients and reading config. Go on provided.al2023 with a small static binary is about as fast as it gets; Java is the slow end. You keep init light, give the function more memory, which also gives more CPU, and for latency-critical paths pay for provisioned concurrency. Everything built in init is reused by warm invocations.

cards.q: Vertical versus horizontal scaling, and what does a service need to be horizontally scalable?
cards.k: vertical = bigger box, simple, capped, downtime · horizontal = more instances behind an LB · needs stateless servers, state in shared stores · idempotency + graceful shutdown · then the DB is the bottleneck
keys: Vertical: a bigger machine; simple, limited, often downtime; horizontal: more instances behind a load balancer
Horizontal needs stateless app servers: sessions/state in shared stores, no local files the next request relies on
Idempotent request handling and graceful shutdown make adding/removing instances safe
The database usually becomes the bottleneck: read replicas, caching, then partitioning
wrong: Any service scales horizontally by adding instances
follow: What state does tusd keep that makes horizontal scaling harder, and how does the DynamoDB lock help?
Why are Lambdas horizontally scalable by construction?
cards.answer: Vertical scaling buys a bigger machine, which is easy until it isn't. Horizontal scaling adds instances behind a load balancer, and it only works if any instance can serve any request: no sessions in memory, no files on local disk that the next request needs. Lambdas are stateless by construction. tusd is the interesting case: an upload spans many requests and is buffered locally, which is why it uses a DynamoDB lock so only one instance works on an upload at a time.

cards.q: Explain the basic Kubernetes objects: Pod, Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap/Secret, HPA.
cards.k: Pod = containers scheduled together · Deployment = N replicas + rolling update · Service = stable IP / DNS LB · Ingress = HTTP from outside · ConfigMap / Secret · HPA scales · probes + requests / limits
keys: Pod: one or more containers scheduled together (shared network); the unit of scheduling
Deployment: desired number of identical pods, rolling updates and rollbacks (via ReplicaSets)
Service: a stable virtual IP / DNS name load-balancing across pods; Ingress: HTTP routing from outside
ConfigMap / Secret: configuration injected as env or files; HPA: scales replicas on CPU/custom metrics
Probes (liveness/readiness) and resource requests/limits matter for scheduling and stability
wrong: You deploy containers directly without pods
follow: What happens to traffic during a rolling update if readiness probes are missing?
Requests vs limits: what happens when a pod exceeds its memory limit?
cards.answer: A pod is the smallest thing Kubernetes runs: one or more containers sharing a network. A Deployment keeps a set number of identical pods running and rolls out new versions gradually. A Service gives those pods one stable name and load-balances across them, and an Ingress routes outside HTTP traffic in. ConfigMaps and Secrets inject configuration, and the HorizontalPodAutoscaler adds pods when CPU or a custom metric rises. Probes and resource requests and limits are what keep it stable.

cards.q: Lambda, ECS Fargate, EC2 or Kubernetes: how would you choose for a new service? Why does my Go service use both Lambda and EC2?
cards.term: Lambda vs Fargate vs EC2 vs k8s
cards.k: Lambda = spiky events, low ops, 15 min, cold starts · Fargate = long-running containers, no servers · EC2 = full control, you run it · k8s = portable, needs a platform team · my Go service: Lambda handlers, EC2 tusd + analyzer
keys: Lambda: event-driven / spiky / low ops; limits (15-minute max, payload sizes, cold starts, connection storms to SQL)
Fargate/ECS: long-running containers without managing servers; good for HTTP services, workers, steady load
EC2: full control, long-lived processes, special needs (local disk, custom networking); you manage OS and scaling
Kubernetes: portable orchestration and a rich ecosystem; worth it at scale with a platform team, heavy otherwise
My Go service: Lambdas for request/event handlers; EC2 for tusd (long uploads, local buffer) and the analyzer (long-running polling daemon in a VPC)
wrong: Kubernetes is always the professional choice
follow: Why can't tusd be a Lambda?
What would move you from Lambda to Fargate for the API?
cards.answer: Lambda is my default for request handlers and event consumers: no servers, scales to zero, pay per use, but each run is capped at 15 minutes and payloads are limited. Fargate runs long-lived containers without servers to manage, good for steady HTTP services and workers. EC2 is for when I need the machine itself. Kubernetes pays off with many services and a platform team. My Go service mixes them for exactly those reasons: Lambdas for the API and consumers, EC2 for tusd, which streams multi-gigabyte uploads with a local buffer, and for the analyzer daemon.

cards.q: What is infrastructure as code, and how does my Go service's CloudFormation setup compare with Terraform?
cards.k: versioned, reviewed, repeatable, no click-ops · CloudFormation: AWS-native, exports / ImportValue, drift detection · Terraform: multi-cloud, state, plan / apply · my Go service: stack per concern · gap: ESMs via CLI in deploy.sh
keys: Infrastructure declared in versioned files, reviewed and applied repeatably (no click-ops); environments become reproducible
CloudFormation: AWS-native, stacks with exports/imports (Fn::ImportValue), drift detection; Terraform: multi-cloud, state file, plan/apply, modules
My Go service: one stack per concern, shared stacks exported and imported by features, params.json per feature
Gap: event source mappings are created with AWS CLI calls in deploy.sh, outside IaC (drift risk)
wrong: IaC is only for big companies
follow: What's the risk of creating the event source mappings with the CLI instead of CloudFormation?
How does Terraform's plan step help code review?
cards.answer: IaC means the infrastructure lives in versioned files that are reviewed and applied the same way every time, so you can recreate an environment and see every change in a diff. CloudFormation is AWS-native and organises things into stacks that export and import values; Terraform works across clouds, keeps a state file and shows a plan before applying. My Go service uses one CloudFormation stack per concern, wired with imports, but creates its stream and queue event source mappings with CLI calls in deploy.sh, which can drift from what's in the repo.

cards.q: What should a CI/CD pipeline for a Go backend do, from push to production?
cards.k: PR: build, vet / lint, tests -race, integration (DB container), govulncheck · merge: one immutable artifact tagged by commit, promoted · staging + smoke → progressive prod + auto rollback · secrets via store / OIDC
keys: On every PR: build, go vet / lint, unit tests with -race, integration tests (DB in a container), security scans (govulncheck)
On merge: build an immutable artifact (image or binary) once, tag it with the commit, promote the same artifact through environments
Deploy automatically to staging, run smoke tests, then production with a progressive strategy and automatic rollback on alarms
Secrets from the CI's secret store / OIDC role, never in the repo
wrong: Build separately for each environment
follow: My Go service has no CI pipeline in the repo: what's the first job you'd add, and why?
Why use OIDC federation from GitHub Actions to AWS instead of stored access keys?
cards.answer: Every pull request should build, vet and lint, run the tests with the race detector and an integration suite against a real database in a container, and scan dependencies. After merge, build the artifact once, tag it with the commit, and promote that exact artifact through staging and production, with smoke tests and a canary or rolling deploy that rolls back on alarms. My Go service deploys by running deploy.sh by hand, so the first job I'd add is a CI check running go build, vet and test on every merge request.

cards.q: How should a service get its configuration in different environments? What does my Go service do?
cards.k: config from env (12-factor), same artifact everywhere · validate at start, fail fast · secrets from a store · flags / remote config for runtime · my Go service: CloudFormation env vars, log.Fatal in main, DynamoDB config table
keys: Config from the environment (12-factor), not compiled in; the same artifact runs everywhere
Validate at startup and fail fast on missing or invalid values
Secrets from a secret store, not plain env vars in templates; feature flags / remote config for runtime changes
My Go service: env vars set by CloudFormation per stack, checked in main with log.Fatal; runtime config in a DynamoDB config table
wrong: Use a different build per environment
follow: Why fail fast at startup instead of failing on the first request?
Which settings belong in the config table instead of env vars, and why?
cards.answer: The same build should run in every environment, with differences coming from configuration: environment variables for wiring like table names, a secret store for credentials, and a runtime config store for things product people change without a deploy. Validate everything at startup and refuse to start if something's missing. My Go service does both: main checks each required env var and exits, and settings like the criteria template and duplicate-check mode live in a DynamoDB config table read at runtime.

cards.q: How would you design large file uploads (videos, hundreds of MB) from a mobile app?
cards.k: never through API / Lambda (limits, timeouts, cost) · direct to S3: pre-signed multipart or resumable tus · authorise up front (signed expiring metadata) → record key → complete via hook · validate type + size server-side
keys: Don't stream through your API servers / Lambda (payload limits, timeouts, cost)
Upload directly to object storage with pre-signed URLs (S3 multipart) or a resumable protocol (tus) for flaky mobile networks
Authorise the upload up front (signed, expiring metadata), record the object key, mark complete via a callback/hook
Validate type/size server-side, scan if needed, and never trust the client-reported size
wrong: Base64 the video into a JSON POST
follow: Why did this team choose tus over plain pre-signed S3 uploads?
How does hook-feature stop someone uploading a 10 GB file with forged metadata?
cards.answer: Big files shouldn't pass through your API at all: Lambda has payload limits and timeouts, and you pay for the transfer time. Either give the client a pre-signed URL to S3, using multipart for large files, or run a resumable upload server like tus, which matters on mobile networks that drop. This repo uses tus: attachment-feature signs upload metadata with an expiry, the pre-create hook verifies the signature, file type and size before accepting, and the post-finish hook marks the attachment uploaded.

cards.q: What is a backend-for-frontend (BFF), and how do you design endpoints that are efficient for a mobile app?
cards.k: API layer shaped for one client, aggregates → one call per screen · mobile: few round trips, small payloads, offline / retry, careful versioning · screen-shaped endpoints (/profile/me/dashboard) · cost: duplication, UI coupling
keys: A BFF is an API layer shaped for one client: aggregates several services so the app makes one call per screen
Mobile: minimise round trips (high latency), keep payloads small, support offline/retry, version carefully
Screen-shaped endpoints (e.g. GET /profile/me/dashboard, /profile/me/state) vs generic CRUD
Trade-off: duplication and coupling to the UI vs fewer calls and simpler clients
wrong: The app should call every microservice directly
follow: profile-feature's dashboard fans out four reads in parallel: why do that on the server rather than the app?
When would GraphQL be a better fit?
cards.answer: A BFF is an API made for one client, usually aggregating data so the app can render a screen with one request. On mobile that matters because each round trip is expensive on a slow network. This repo has screen-shaped endpoints like the dashboard and the app-state endpoint, which fan out reads in parallel on the server and return one payload. The cost is coupling those endpoints to the UI; GraphQL is the alternative when many screens need different shapes of the same data.

cards.q: Why does every network call need a timeout, and how do you choose it?
cards.k: no timeout → hung dependency holds goroutines, connections, spreads upstream · set just above its p99 + within the caller's budget, deeper = shorter · propagate ctx deadlines · split by work: analyzer 30 s API, 2 h video
keys: Without one, a hung dependency holds goroutines/threads/connections forever and the failure spreads upstream
Choose from the dependency's latency distribution (a bit above its p99) and the caller's own budget; deeper calls get shorter timeouts
Propagate deadlines (context) so work stops when the caller has given up
Separate connect/request/transfer timeouts where the work differs (the analyzer uses 30 s for API calls and 2 h for video transfers)
wrong: Use the same 30-second timeout everywhere
follow: Why does the analyzer need two different HTTP clients?
A Lambda has a 15-second timeout and calls a service with a 20-second timeout: what's wrong?
cards.answer: A call with no timeout can wait forever, and while it waits it holds a goroutine, a connection and maybe a lock, so one stuck dependency drags its callers down too. Set the timeout a little above the dependency's normal p99, and inside your own budget, so a caller always has time to respond; pass deadlines down with context. Different kinds of calls get different limits: the analyzer gives API calls 30 seconds but video transfers two hours, with a separate client for each.

cards.q: How should a client retry a failed call? Explain exponential backoff with jitter.
cards.k: retry only transient (timeout, 5xx, throttle) + idempotent ops · base × 2^attempt, capped · jitter breaks lockstep · cap attempts + total time, respect Retry-After · retry at one layer, layers multiply
keys: Retry only transient failures (timeouts, 5xx, throttling) and only idempotent (or idempotency-keyed) operations
Exponential backoff: wait base × 2^attempt, capped; jitter (random spread) stops clients retrying in lockstep
Cap attempts and total time; respect Retry-After
Retries at several layers multiply: retry at one layer, ideally the one closest to the user's intent
wrong: Retry immediately in a tight loop until it works
Retry every error including 400s
follow: Why does jitter matter when 10,000 clients fail at the same second?
The AWS SDK already retries: what happens if you wrap it in your own retry loop too?
cards.answer: Retry only what might succeed next time, like timeouts, 5xx and throttling, and only operations that are safe to repeat. Wait longer after each failure, doubling up to a cap, and add random jitter so thousands of clients don't retry at the same instant and knock the service over again. Cap attempts and honour Retry-After. And pick one layer to retry; the AWS SDK already retries, so wrapping it in another loop multiplies the attempts.

cards.q: Why are retries and idempotency two halves of one design? Use a payment or a submission as the example.
cards.k: timeout = unknown outcome → must retry · no idempotency → double charge / two submissions · keys + conditional writes make retry safe everywhere · external provider: query status by your key first
keys: Retries are needed because timeouts leave the outcome unknown (did it succeed?)
Without idempotency, a retry after an unknown outcome can duplicate the effect (double charge, two submissions)
Idempotency keys / conditional writes make 'try again' safe, so clients and infrastructure can retry freely
For unknown outcomes at external providers, query status by your key before retrying
wrong: Make the timeout long enough and retries won't be needed
follow: The app's POST /submissions times out. What happens if it retries, given the transaction's conditions?
The payment provider timed out: what do you do before charging again?
cards.answer: A timeout doesn't tell you whether the call worked, so clients have to retry, and a retry is only safe if doing it twice has the same effect as once. That's why the two always come together. If the app's create-submission call times out and it retries, the transaction's condition that the attachment hasn't been claimed yet makes the second attempt fail cleanly instead of creating a duplicate. With an external payment provider you look the payment up by your idempotency key before trying again.

cards.q: What is a circuit breaker, what are its states, and when does it help more than retries?
cards.k: trips open after failure rate / N failures · open = fail fast, protect both sides · half-open = few trial calls → closed on success · beats retries for a dependency down for a while · pair with a fallback
keys: Wraps calls to a dependency; trips open after a failure rate/consecutive failures threshold
Open: fail fast without calling (protects the dependency and the caller's resources); half-open: let a few trial calls through; closed again on success
Helps when a dependency is down or overloaded for a while: retries would add load and latency
Pair with a fallback (cached data, default, degrade the feature)
wrong: A circuit breaker fixes the dependency
follow: What would a sensible fallback be if the data-platform API is down for the analyzer?
How do you tune the thresholds without flapping?
cards.answer: A circuit breaker watches calls to a dependency. When failures pass a threshold it opens and fails calls immediately instead of waiting on timeouts, which saves your threads and gives the dependency room to recover. After a cool-down it goes half-open, lets a few calls through, and closes again if they succeed. It beats retries when an outage lasts more than a moment, and it's best with a fallback, like serving cached data or degrading the feature.

cards.q: What does graceful degradation mean? Give an example from my Go service.
cards.k: dependency fails → core flow keeps working with less · stale cache, hide widget, queue for later, manual path · analyzer: after maxExternalFailures → manual QC per pipeline config · decide core vs optional up front
keys: When a dependency fails, keep the core flow working with reduced functionality instead of failing entirely
Examples: serve stale cache, hide a non-essential widget, queue work for later, fall back to a manual path
My Go service's analyzer: after maxExternalFailures it stops retrying the external ML stage and, depending on the pipeline config, hands the submission to manual QC
Decide in advance which features are core and which can degrade
wrong: Degradation means returning 500 politely
follow: What should the user see while their submission is waiting for manual QC?
How would you degrade the profile dashboard if the stats table is unavailable?
cards.answer: It means the system keeps doing its most important job when a part fails, with less functionality instead of an error page. The analyzer does it: it counts failures from the external ML platform per submission, and after the limit it gives up on that stage and, if the pipeline is configured for it, passes the submission to manual QC, so the user's submission still gets reviewed. You decide ahead of time which features are core and which can go dark.

cards.q: What are load shedding and bulkheads, and how do they keep an overloaded system alive?
cards.k: shed = reject early (503 / 429) so accepted requests succeed, prioritise critical · unbounded queue = overload as latency · bulkheads = separate pools / limits / Lambdas · one Lambda per feature = coarse bulkhead
keys: Load shedding: reject excess requests early (503/429) when over capacity so the requests you accept still succeed; prioritise critical traffic
Queue limits: an unbounded queue only converts overload into huge latency
Bulkheads: isolate resources (separate pools, concurrency limits, separate Lambdas / reserved concurrency) so one noisy workload can't starve others
My Go service's one-Lambda-per-feature layout is a coarse bulkhead
wrong: Accepting every request is always better for users
follow: In a flash sale, what would you shed first?
How does reserved concurrency act as a bulkhead and as a limit?
cards.answer: When demand exceeds capacity, trying to serve everyone means everyone times out. Load shedding rejects the excess fast so the requests you accept still finish, and it should drop low-priority traffic first. Bulkheads split resources so one workload can't drain them all: separate connection pools, concurrency caps, separate functions. Splitting my Go service into one Lambda per feature is a coarse bulkhead: an admin export spike can't eat the submission API's concurrency if each has its own limits.

cards.q: Where in the request path would you put rate limiting, and how do you rate-limit across many app servers?
cards.k: edge / CDN / WAF = volumetric · gateway / LB = per client / key · app = per user + business rules · many servers → shared Redis / DB counters · fixed, sliding, token bucket · 429 + Retry-After · fail-open vs closed
keys: Layers: edge/CDN/WAF (volumetric attacks), API gateway / LB (per client / API key), app (per user / business rules)
Distributed limits need shared state: Redis counters / token buckets, or a database with atomic increments
Algorithms: fixed window (bursty at edges), sliding window (log or weighted counter), token bucket (allows controlled bursts)
Return 429 with Retry-After; decide fail-open vs fail-closed if the limiter store is down
wrong: An in-memory counter per server enforces a global limit
follow: This repo's auth rate limiter weights the previous window: why is that better than a fixed window?
Fail open or fail closed for a login endpoint?
cards.answer: Coarse protection goes at the edge, a CDN or WAF, to soak up floods before they reach you. Per-client quotas fit the gateway. Business limits like 'five OTP requests per email per hour' live in the app. Across many servers the counter must be shared, so you use Redis or an atomic database counter. A sliding window that weights the previous window avoids the burst a fixed window allows at the boundary; this repo's auth rate limiter does exactly that in DynamoDB.

cards.q: How should an API communicate rate limits and overload to well-behaved clients?
cards.k: 429 + Retry-After (+ RateLimit-Limit / Remaining / Reset) · 503 + Retry-After when shedding · clients: exponential backoff + jitter, respect Retry-After, cap · business limits: clear code + when to retry
keys: 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After; optionally RateLimit-Limit / -Remaining / -Reset headers
503 with Retry-After when overloaded / shedding load
Clients: exponential backoff with jitter, respect Retry-After, cap retries
Business-specific limits (OTP resends) return a clear code and when the user may try again
wrong: Return 500 when rate limited
follow: Why add jitter to backoff?
How does auth-feature tell the app how long to wait before resending an OTP?
cards.answer: Rate-limited requests get 429 with a Retry-After header, and many APIs also expose remaining quota and reset time so clients can slow down before hitting the wall. Overload is 503 with Retry-After. Good clients back off exponentially with random jitter so they don't retry in lockstep. User-facing limits, like OTP resends, should say when the user can try again; this repo's error envelope allows extra fields for exactly that.

cards.q: Liveness versus readiness checks: what's the difference, and what should each check?
cards.k: liveness = keep running? fail → restart, cheap + local · readiness = serve now? fail → stop routing (startup, shutdown, missing dep) · never tie liveness to downstream · shutdown: fail readiness first, LB drains
keys: Liveness: is the process healthy enough to keep running? Failing → restart. Keep it cheap and local
Readiness: can it serve traffic now? Failing → stop routing to it (during startup, shutdown, or a missing dependency)
Don't make liveness depend on downstream services: a DB blip would restart every instance
During graceful shutdown, fail readiness first so the load balancer drains traffic
wrong: One /health endpoint that pings the database for everything
follow: What happens to a fleet whose liveness check pings the database during a DB outage?
How does the load balancer's deregistration delay relate to tus-feature's shutdown timeout?
cards.answer: Liveness asks 'is this process stuck?', and failing it gets the instance restarted, so it should only check things local to the process. Readiness asks 'should I get traffic right now?', and failing it just takes the instance out of the load balancer. If liveness pinged the database, a short DB outage would restart every instance at once. On shutdown you fail readiness first, let the load balancer drain, then stop.

cards.q: How do you think about single points of failure and failure domains in an AWS architecture like my Go service?
cards.k: find what stops everything: single EC2 (tusd, analyzer), one region, shared config table, one stream · managed services are multi-AZ, EC2 only if spread + ASG · async can wait, uploads can't · blast radius: stacks, tables, functions
keys: Identify components whose failure stops everything: a single EC2 instance (tusd, analyzer), a single region, a shared config table, one stream
Managed services (Lambda, DynamoDB, SQS, EventBridge) are multi-AZ; EC2 needs you to spread across AZs behind an LB / auto scaling
Decide per component: is a short outage acceptable (analyzer is async, it catches up) or not (uploads)
Blast radius: separate stacks, separate tables, per-feature functions
wrong: The cloud is highly available, so nothing is a single point of failure
follow: The analyzer is a single EC2 instance: what happens if it dies for an hour, and is that acceptable?
What would it take to run tusd on two instances (hint: the DynamoDB upload lock)?
cards.answer: I list what would stop the product if it died. In my Go service most pieces are managed and spread across zones by AWS, but tusd and the analyzer run on EC2 instances. The analyzer is a single instance, which is acceptable because it's asynchronous: if it's down for an hour, submissions wait and it catches up. Uploads are user-facing, so tusd sits behind a load balancer, and the DynamoDB upload lock is what would let several instances share uploads safely.

cards.q: How do you test that the system actually survives failures?
